2027-07-03.title: Saint Thomas, Apostle
readings: You are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone
Go out to all the world and tell the Good News
2027-07-03.alt: Feast of the Apostle Thomas, kept on 3 July in the Roman calendar. Gloria; no Creed, since 3 July is a weekday this year. In India, where Thomas is held to be the Apostle of the nation, many dioceses and shrines keep today with the greater solemnity of the national patron, above all at Mylapore (Chennai) and in Kerala; check the local calendar. The readings of the weekday (Genesis 27:1–5, 15–29; Psalm 135; Matthew 9:14–17) are not used. Several Christian communities in India observe 3 July as Indian Christian Day. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-07-03.verse: Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”
theo: The first reading is a few lines of St Paul about what the Church is. Gentile Christians in Ephesus, who once had no part in Israel's promises, are told: “So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God.” Notice the three pictures. A city, with its citizens. A family, with its household. And a building, the strangest and most beautiful: “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.” In the ancient world the cornerstone was the first block laid, from which the lines of the whole building were measured. Christ is that stone; the apostles, those whom he sent, are the foundation on which each generation of believers is set as a living stone. The Book of Revelation sees the same wall of the new Jerusalem with “twelve foundations, and on them are the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.” This is what we mean when we say in the Creed that the Church is apostolic: she is built on their witness, taught by their successors, and sent as they were sent (Catechism 857). Today's feast honours one of those foundation stones. The psalm, the shortest in the Psalter, sets the mission to music: “Praise the Lord, all you nations! Extol him, all you peoples!” St Paul himself quotes it in the Letter to the Romans for the Gentiles who praise God for his mercy.

The Gospel is the best-known story about Thomas, but in John's Gospel Thomas appears three times, and each time shows a different side of him. His name means “twin,” in Aramaic Te'oma and in Greek Didymus, and the Gospel does not tell us whose twin he was. First, when Jesus is going back to Judea, to Bethany near Jerusalem, where he has enemies, the other disciples hang back. “Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, ‘Let us also go, that we may die with him.’” This is the Thomas of courage, ready to die with his Master. Second, at the Last Supper Jesus says, “You know the way to the place where I am going,” and Thomas says what the others are thinking: “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?” His honest question brought out one of the greatest sentences in the Gospel: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” Third comes today's scene. On Easter evening Thomas was not with them, and we are not told why. The others tell him, “We have seen the Lord.” He answers with a demand that sounds hard and is really very human: “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the mark of the nails and my hand in his side, I will not believe.” Thomas does not ask for anything that the others have not already been given: Jesus had shown them his hands and his side the first evening (John 20:20). Eight days later, on the first day of the week again, “although the doors were shut, Jesus came and stood among them and said, ‘Peace be with you.’” Notice that the Lord does not scold him. He offers exactly what Thomas asked for: “Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.” The Gospel does not say that Thomas actually touched. What follows is the highest confession of faith in the whole Gospel of John: “My Lord and my God!” In four words, Thomas says what the Prologue said at the beginning of the book, that the Word was God. And the risen body bears the wounds: they are not erased but glorified (Catechism 645). Then comes a blessing for all of us who came later: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.” The Evangelist ends this chapter by saying that all this was written “so that you may come to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that through believing you may have life in his name.”

According to tradition, Thomas did not stay in Jerusalem. The ancient Acts of Thomas, written in the third century, probably in Syriac, tells how he travelled to India, and the Christians of Kerala hold that he landed at Muziris, near modern Kodungallur, in the year 52, preached, baptised and founded seven communities, and was martyred by a lance at Mylapore, near Chennai, in the year 72. Historians discuss the details, and the early records are few; but the Church of India has held this memory dear for many centuries, and the ancient Christian communities of the Malabar coast, called the Thomas Christians or Nazranis, are a living witness that the faith came here very early. The tomb at Mylapore, over which stands the Basilica of San Thome, is venerated as the tomb of the Apostle; an ancient tradition says that some of his relics were taken to Edessa and later to Ortona in Italy. The Catholic Churches of India, Latin and Eastern, as well as the Orthodox and Mar Thoma Churches, all look to Thomas as their father in faith, and today we rejoice with all of them. India received the faith, we may say, not from a conqueror or a trader but from a man who first doubted, then adored, and then carried the risen Lord across the sea.
conn: “Household of God.”
The Greek oikeioi theou means members of God's family. In Christ the Gentiles who were once strangers are given a place at the family table, a place that never depended on race or caste.
“Foundation of the apostles and prophets.”

The Church rests on the witness of the apostles, whom Christ chose and sent, and on the Old Testament prophets, whose words they fulfilled. The Catechism calls the Church apostolic in her foundation, her teaching and her mission (Catechism 857).
“Cornerstone.”
The first stone, set at the corner, which fixes the lines of the building. Jesus applied the psalm to himself: the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (Matthew 21:42).
Thomas, the Twin.
The name comes from the Aramaic Te'oma, “twin”; the Greek form is Didymus. John gives it each time he mentions him (11:16; 20:24; 21:2). The Gospel does not say who his twin was.
“Let us also go.”

When Jesus decides to go to Bethany, only two miles from Jerusalem, where the leaders were planning his death, Thomas speaks for the little group: “Let us also go, that we may die with him.” His loyalty precedes his doubt.
“How can we know the way?”

Thomas's honest question at the Last Supper brings out the saying: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:5–6). Honest doubt is not the opposite of faith, and it can be a way to a deeper one.
A week later.
The next Sunday, the first day of the week. From the beginning the Church has gathered on that day to meet the risen Lord, and the Eucharist is celebrated in memory of him.
“Put your finger here.”

Jesus offers what Thomas demanded, and the Gospel does not tell us that Thomas touched. Seeing was enough for him to believe, and the Church's tradition of the risen body bearing its wounds begins here (Catechism 645).
“My Lord and my God!”

In Greek ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou. The Gospel began by saying that “the Word was God” (1:1), and it ends with a disciple who says the same of Jesus. Some scholars add that Suetonius says the emperor Domitian liked to be called “Lord and God,” and that John's readers heard Thomas's cry as an answer to that claim.
“Blessed are those who have not seen.”

The last beatitude of John. Peter says the same of later Christians: “Although you have not seen him, you love him; and even though you do not see him now, you believe in him and rejoice with an indescribable and glorious joy” (1 Peter 1:8).
altar: At the elevation of the Host and the chalice, many Catholics say quietly, in the words of Thomas, My Lord and my God. There is no better prayer at that moment. We do not see the wounds as Thomas saw them, and what we see is bread and wine; but we believe because the Lord says: This is my body. St Thomas Aquinas, who shares the Apostle's name, wrote in the hymn Adoro te devote, in substance: I do not see the wounds as Thomas did, but I confess you to be my Lord and my God. The Church lives by the last beatitude of John: Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.

The feast also points to the apostolic table. The Eucharist we celebrate is celebrated in communion with the bishops, successors of the apostles, and in the faith of those who handed it on. When the priest says, Peace be with you, he speaks the very words of the Lord to Thomas on the first Sunday after Easter.
outline: Opening
Ask: have you ever had doubts about your faith, and what did you do with them?
Point 1 · Built on the apostles
The Church is a family, a city and a house built on the apostles, with Christ the cornerstone.
Point 2 · The three portraits of Thomas
The loyal friend (“Let us also go”), the honest questioner (“How can we know the way?”) and the doubter.
Point 3 · My Lord and my God
The risen Lord comes to Thomas through closed doors, shows his wounds, and receives the greatest confession of the Gospel.
Point 4 · Thomas in India
According to tradition, he brought the faith to this land; we are the living stones of his building.
Take-home line
“My Lord and my God!”
live: Say Thomas's prayer (John 20:28)
At the elevation at Mass, whisper slowly, “My Lord and my God.” Make it your daily prayer in a moment of doubt.
Bring your doubts to Christ (John 20:27)
Write down one question that troubles your faith. Take it to a priest, a catechist or a wise friend, and pray with it before the Blessed Sacrament.
Give thanks for the faith of India (Ephesians 2:20)
Say a prayer of thanksgiving for the Church in India, for the ancient Christian families and for every missionary, priest and sister whose work built on the apostles' foundation.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (Homily 26 on the Gospels, in substance)
The disbelief of Thomas helped our faith more than the faith of the other disciples. By touching, he strengthened us who believe, and by his doubt the Lord removed all our doubts.
St Augustine (Treatise 121 on John, in substance)
Thomas saw and touched the man, and confessed the God whom he neither saw nor touched. What he saw led him to believe in what he could not see.
St Thomas Aquinas (Adoro te devote, in substance)
I do not see wounds as Thomas did, but I confess you to be my God. Make me believe more and more in you, hope in you, and love you.
magis: Catechism 643–644
The disciples did not at first believe the news of the resurrection. Thomas insists on seeing and touching, and the risen Jesus allows it.
Catechism 645
The risen body of Jesus is real and bears the marks of his passion, yet it is no longer confined by space and time.
Catechism 857
The Church is apostolic: built on the foundation of the apostles, she hands on their teaching, and is sent as they were sent.
saints: St Thomas the Apostle (1st century)

One of the Twelve, called the Twin. In John's Gospel he is the loyal friend who says Let us also go, the honest questioner at the Last Supper, and the one who made the greatest confession of faith on the Sunday after Easter: My Lord and my God. According to tradition he preached the Gospel beyond the Roman Empire, and the Christians of India honour him as their Apostle, who landed at Muziris (Kodungallur) in 52 and was martyred at Mylapore in 72. Latin, Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Catholics, and the Orthodox and Mar Thoma Churches, all keep his memory in India. His feast is 3 July (in the older Roman calendar 21 December).
This week
4 Jul: Fourteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time (St Elizabeth of Portugal omitted). 5 Jul: St Anthony Zaccaria (optional memorial). 6 Jul: St Maria Goretti (optional memorial).
2027-07-03.prayer: Almighty ever-living God, who gave blessed Thomas the Apostle grace to believe more through his doubting, grant that we too may believe in your Son, and so may have life in his name. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, who showed your wounds to Thomas, we have not seen you, yet we love you. Strengthen our faith, answer our doubts with your peace, and make us living stones in the house built on your apostles. Bless the Church in India, which looks to Thomas as her father in faith, and make us faithful witnesses wherever you send us. My Lord and my God. Amen.

2027-07-04.title: Fourteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: They shall know that there has been a prophet among them
Our eyes are fixed on the Lord, pleading for his mercy
My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness
Prophets are not without honor, except in their hometown
2027-07-04.alt: Year B. Gloria and Creed. The optional memorial of St Elizabeth of Portugal (4 July) is omitted this year because it falls on a Sunday. The monsoon of Mithunam is still heavy over Kerala. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-04.verse: “Prophets are not without honor, except in their hometown, and among their own kin, and in their own house.” And he could do no deed of power there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and cured them.
theo: The first reading brings us to the river Chebar in Babylon, where a young priest named Ezekiel lives among the exiles from Jerusalem, about 593 years before Christ. The Lord speaks to him, and a spirit enters him and sets him on his feet. God addresses him with a title that he will use ninety times: “Mortal,” in Hebrew ben adam, son of man, a creature of dust. Jesus will take this title for himself. The task is not pleasant: “I am sending you to the people of Israel, to a nation of rebels who have rebelled against me; they and their ancestors have transgressed against me to this very day. The descendants are impudent and stubborn.” God does not promise Ezekiel success. He says: “Whether they hear or refuse to hear (for they are a rebellious house), they shall know that there has been a prophet among them.” A prophet is not measured by his results. His work is to say, “Thus says the Lord God,” and the Lord will look after the rest. The Psalm gives the posture of such a servant: the eyes of the servant fixed on the hand of his master, “so our eyes look to the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us,” even when we have had “more than enough of contempt.”

In the second reading St Paul tells the Corinthians one of the most personal secrets of his life. He has been given extraordinary revelations, he says, and “to keep me from being too elated, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me.” Nobody knows what the thorn was: an illness, a temptation, an opponent, a weakness of speech. What matters is what he did with it: “Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me.” Three times, like Jesus in Gethsemane, and the answer is not what he asked for. The Lord does not take away the thorn; he gives something better: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” Paul's reaction is astonishing: “So, I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.” This is not a love of suffering for its own sake. Paul has learned that God's power does not need our strength; it is more clearly seen when our own strength is out of the way. “For whenever I am weak, then I am strong.” Elsewhere he says that we have this treasure “in clay jars, so that it may be made clear that this extraordinary power belongs to God and does not come from us” (2 Corinthians 4:7). The Church has always seen here a word for all who carry a hidden cross, an illness, a failure, a loneliness: God does not always remove it, but he promises his grace in the midst of it (Catechism 309–314).

The Gospel takes Jesus home. He comes “to his hometown,” Nazareth, a small village in Galilee, with his disciples following him, and on the Sabbath he teaches in the synagogue. At first the people are astounded: “Where did this man get all this? What is this wisdom that has been given to him? What deeds of power are being done by his hands!” But the astonishment turns into offence. “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon, and are not his sisters here with us?” The Greek says tekton, a craftsman who worked with wood or stone, and this is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus is called a carpenter. It is also the only place where Mark calls him “son of Mary.” They know his family, his trade and his face, and for this very reason they cannot see who he is. The Church reads “brothers and sisters” in the sense of near relatives, which the Aramaic and Hebrew word covers, and teaches that Mary remained a virgin throughout her life (Catechism 500). They “took offense at him,” literally they stumbled over him. Jesus answers with a proverb: “Prophets are not without honor, except in their hometown, and among their own kin, and in their own house.” Then Mark says something sobering: “And he could do no deed of power there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and cured them.” It is not that his power is limited, but that faith is needed for it to be received. “And he was amazed at their unbelief.” Jesus, who marvelled at the faith of the centurion (Matthew 8:10), is here astonished by its absence. Yet he does not give up: “Then he went about among the villages teaching.” In the same way, the one who spent thirty years in an obscure village shows us that God hides himself in what is ordinary (Catechism 531–533); and the one who can be rejected by his own continues to knock at the next door.
conn: “Mortal.”
In Hebrew ben adam, “son of man,” used ninety times of Ezekiel to remind him that he is a human being, dust of the earth. Jesus will take the title Son of Man for himself.
“A spirit entered into me.”
The Spirit of the Lord sets the prophet on his feet before he can speak. A call from God is always accompanied by the strength to answer it.
“A rebellious house.”
The exiles in Babylon were in a land of defeat, and many blamed God. The prophets in the Bible often announced what the people did not want to hear (Jeremiah 1:19; 1 Kings 22:8).
“Thorn in the flesh.”
In Greek skolops, a stake or sharp splinter. Paul does not say what it was: an illness, a temptation, an adversary. Since he does not say, every sufferer can recognise their own thorn.
“Three times.”
The same number as Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane (Mark 14:32–42). The apostle prays as his Master prayed, and receives the same answer: not the removal of the cup, but the grace to drink it.
“Power is made perfect in weakness.”
The cross is the greatest example: in the weakness of the Crucified, the saving power of God is revealed (1 Corinthians 1:23–25). Paul's weakness keeps him from boasting in himself.
“His hometown.”
Nazareth, a small village in Lower Galilee that is never mentioned in the Old Testament. Nathanael asks: “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46).
“The carpenter.”

Greek tekton, a craftsman in wood or stone. Mark's phrase is the only place where Jesus himself is called a carpenter; Matthew has “the carpenter's son” (13:55). The Church honours human work in his workshop (Catechism 531, 2427).
“Brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon.”

The Aramaic and Hebrew word for brother also means cousin or relative. The Church teaches that Mary was a virgin before, in and after the birth of Jesus (Catechism 499–500). Mark 15:40 names a Mary who is the mother of James and Joses.
“They took offense at him.”
The Greek word is a form of skandalon, a stumbling block. For Mark, the offence of Jesus is that God has come so close, in the face of a local craftsman.
altar: The people of Nazareth could not believe that God was present in a man they had known from childhood. Every Mass tests our faith the same way: the Lord is there in a piece of bread and a cup of wine, with no sign of power. “Is this not bread?” But because of the Lord's word, This is my body, we believe that he is truly present, and we receive him whom Nazareth could not receive. Jesus could do no deed of power in Nazareth because of unbelief; in the Eucharist his power, the power of his love, is at work in the faith of the Church, healing and strengthening us.

And when we come to Communion, we come as Paul came to the Lord: with our thorns, our weaknesses, our failures. We do not come as the strong. We hear again the answer to Paul: My grace is sufficient for you. The grace of Communion is sufficient for the week ahead, for the illness, the fear, the difficult person.
outline: Opening
Ask: do you find it harder to believe a good word from someone whom you know well?
Point 1 · A prophet among them
Ezekiel is sent to people who may not listen; his task is to speak, and God will look after the results.
Point 2 · Power made perfect in weakness
Paul's thorn: God does not remove it, but gives grace; when I am weak, then I am strong.
Point 3 · Is not this the carpenter?
The people of Nazareth stumble over a Messiah who is too familiar; God hides himself in the ordinary.
Point 4 · He was amazed at their unbelief
Faith opens the door to his healing; he goes on teaching in the villages.
Take-home line
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
live: Name your thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7)
Write down one weakness, illness or problem that you have asked God to remove many times. Offer it to him with Paul's words: My grace is sufficient for me.
Honour the prophet at home (Mark 6:4)
Say a word of thanks and appreciation this week to someone in your own family, workplace or parish whose good example you take for granted.
See God in the ordinary (Mark 6:3)
Offer your daily work, however humble, to the carpenter of Nazareth, and do it as well as you can.
fathers: St Augustine (Letter 130 to Proba, in substance)

The Lord sometimes does not give what we ask, in order to give what is better. The doctor does not always obey the patient, and he is not unkind when he refuses. Even the apostle, who prayed three times, was told: my grace is sufficient for you.
St John Chrysostom (Homilies on 2 Corinthians, in substance)

Paul was not ashamed to speak of his weakness, because it was the place where the power of Christ was seen. A man who is aware of his own weakness is protected from pride, and is the one in whom grace works most.
magis: Catechism 309–314
Why does a good God permit evil and suffering? God draws good from evil, and in everything works for the good of those who love him.
Catechism 531–533
The hidden life of Jesus in Nazareth: thirty years of ordinary life, work and family prayer that make every ordinary life holy.
Catechism 500
The “brothers and sisters” of Jesus are near relatives; Mary is ever-virgin.
saints: St Elizabeth of Portugal (1271–1336; omitted this year)

Born a princess of Aragon and married as a girl to King Denis of Portugal. She gave generously to the poor, built hospitals and a shelter for foundlings, and kept the peace of her kingdom. She stopped a battle between her husband and her son by riding between the armies. After her husband's death she lived as a Franciscan tertiary, and she died on 4 July 1336 at Estremoz, where she had gone to make peace between her son and the king of Castile. Canonised in 1625. Her memorial, 4 July, gives way to the Sunday this year.
This week

5 Jul: St Anthony Zaccaria, priest (optional memorial). 6 Jul: St Maria Goretti, virgin and martyr (optional memorial). From Wednesday the weekday first readings turn to Joseph and his brothers in Genesis.
2027-07-04.prayer: O God, who in the abasement of your Son have raised up a fallen world, fill your faithful with holy joy, for on those you have rescued from slavery to sin you bestow eternal gladness. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you came to your own and your own did not receive you. Give us faith to recognise you in the ordinary, in the poor, in the Eucharist and in those whom we think we know. Like Paul, teach us to boast in our weakness, so that your power may rest on us. Let your grace be sufficient for us this week. Amen.

2027-07-11.title: Fifteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: The Lord took me from following the flock, and said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel’
Lord, let us see your kindness, and grant us your salvation
He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world
He called the twelve and began to send them out two by two
2027-07-11.alt: Year B. Gloria and Creed. The memorial of St Benedict, abbot, patron of Europe, is omitted this year because it falls on a Sunday; the Mass is of the Sunday. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: green. In Kerala the monsoon is at its height and many parishes keep the Sunday with a prayer for the farmers and for the families affected by the rains.
2027-07-11.verse: So they went out and proclaimed that all should repent. They cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them.
theo: The first reading is one of the great scenes of the prophets. Amos was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore trees from Tekoa, a village in Judah, south of Jerusalem. About the middle of the eighth century before Christ, in the prosperous days of King Jeroboam II, God sent him north into the kingdom of Israel to speak against the luxury of the rich and the oppression of the poor (Amos 2:6–7; 5:24). He came to Bethel, the great shrine of the northern kingdom, and preached there. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, reported him to the king and then told Amos to his face: “O seer, go, flee away to the land of Judah, earn your bread there, and prophesy there; but never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king's sanctuary, and it is a temple of the kingdom.” The priest takes it for granted that a prophet is a paid professional who can be sent to find work elsewhere, and that the shrine belongs to the king. Amos does not argue about credentials. “I am no prophet, nor a prophet's son; but I am a herdsman, and a dresser of sycamore trees, and the Lord took me from following the flock, and the Lord said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’” He belongs to no guild of prophets; he has no career, no title and no salary. He has a call. The sycamore fig of Palestine bears the poor man's fruit, and it needs tending to ripen; so the man who looked after sheep and fig trees was taken by the Lord and sent to speak to a nation. Those whom God sends are seldom those whom the establishment would have chosen, and the word they carry belongs neither to the shrine nor to the king. Notice, too, to whom he is sent: “my people Israel.” The hard word of Amos is the word of a Father who wants his people to live justly and be saved. The Psalm gives the answer of those who listen: “Let me hear what God the Lord will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, to his faithful, to those who turn to him in their hearts,” and “Righteousness will go before him, and will make a path for his steps.”

The second reading is one of the most magnificent passages of the New Testament. In the Greek it is a single long sentence of praise, a hymn that sweeps from before the creation of the world to the final gathering of all things in Christ. Paul blesses God because God has first blessed us: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.” Then he unfolds the story of salvation in three movements, one for each Person of the Trinity. The Father chose us: “just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love. He destined us for adoption as his children through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will.” Before there was a world, God had you in mind, in Christ; your life is not an accident. The Son redeems us: “In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace that he lavished on us.” And he makes known the hidden plan, “the mystery of his will,” “as a plan for the fullness of time, to gather up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.” The Greek verb means to sum up under one head; St Irenaeus called it recapitulation. Christ, the new Adam, takes the whole of creation and human history into himself and sets it right. The Spirit seals us. Paul speaks first of “we,” the Jewish believers who were the first to hope in Christ, then of “you also,” the Gentiles; one Church is formed of two peoples. “In him you also, when you had heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and had believed in him, were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit; this is the pledge of our inheritance toward redemption as God's own people, to the praise of his glory.” The seal is the mark of belonging received in baptism and confirmation. The pledge is a first instalment, like the deposit that guarantees a purchase: we already have the Spirit, and are promised the fullness.

The Gospel follows directly on the sad scene of Nazareth, where Jesus was rejected in his hometown and “was amazed at their unbelief.” He does not stop. “He called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits.” They go in pairs: because two witnesses make a testimony valid (Deuteronomy 19:15), because they support one another on the road, and because the Gospel is announced by a community and not by lone individuals. St Gregory the Great said (in substance) that the Lord sends them two by two because charity cannot exist with fewer than two. Their equipment is almost nothing: “He ordered them to take nothing for their journey except a staff; no bread, no bag, no money in their belts; but to wear sandals and not to put on two tunics.” A staff and sandals are exactly what the Israelites had in their hands and on their feet when they ate the Passover, ready to leave Egypt (Exodus 12:11). The missionaries are a people on the road of a new exodus, unburdened, and their security is the word they carry and the welcome they receive. “Wherever you enter a house, stay there until you leave the place”: they are not to shop around for a better table. And when they are rejected: “If any place will not welcome you and they refuse to hear you, as you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.” It is a sign that they have done their part, not a curse. “So they went out and proclaimed that all should repent.” The message is the same as that of Jesus (Mark 1:15). “They cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them”: the Church sees in this anointing a root of the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick (Catechism 1510). The three readings meet in one word: calling. Amos is taken from the flock, the Christian is chosen before the foundation of the world, and the Twelve are called and sent. We are chosen to be sent.
conn: “I am no prophet, nor a prophet's son.”
Amos did not belong to the bands of professional prophets. The call of God does not wait for a title or a training; he calls shepherds, fishermen and tax collectors.
“A dresser of sycamore trees.”
The sycamore fig (Ficus sycomorus) was the fruit of the poor in Palestine; the fruit had to be tended to ripen. Amos worked with his hands before the Lord took him from the flock.
“The king's sanctuary.”
Bethel was a royal shrine of the northern kingdom since the time of Jeroboam I (1 Kings 12:29). The priest Amaziah serves the state; Amos serves the word of God.
“Blessed.”
Greek eulogetos: the Letter opens like a Jewish berakah, a prayer of blessing. Paul praises God first, and only then explains. The Mass opens and closes in the same spirit, with praise.
“Chosen before the foundation of the world.”
The Church's faith is that God's plan of love comes before everything and that every person is willed by him. We are not here by chance (Catechism 257–260).
“To gather up all things in him.”
Greek anakephalaiosasthai: to sum up, to bring under one head. St Irenaeus uses it to say that Christ, the new Adam, takes up the whole story of humanity and heals it (Catechism 518).
“The seal … the pledge.”
The seal (sphragis) is the mark of ownership given at baptism and confirmation (Catechism 1274). The pledge (arrabon) is a first instalment that guarantees the whole.
“Two by two.”
Deuteronomy 19:15 requires two witnesses. In Luke 10:1 the seventy-two also go in pairs. The Church's mission is never a one-man show.
“A staff … sandals.”
The dress of the Passover night (Exodus 12:11). In Matthew and Luke the staff is forbidden; Mark allows it; the Church has always seen the difference as one of emphasis, the same call to trust.
“Shake off the dust.”
A sign familiar from the practice of pious Jews returning from foreign lands. Here it is a sad, solemn witness that the messenger has done his part.
“Anointed with oil.”
Oil was the ordinary medicine of the time (Luke 10:34). The Church sees in this passage and in James 5:14–15 the foundation of the Anointing of the Sick.
altar: The second reading begins with a blessing, and the word for blessing in Greek is eulogia, which is also the root of Eucharist, thanksgiving. At every Mass the priest prays at the preparation of the gifts: “Blessed are you, Lord God of all creation.” Paul would recognise it: God has blessed us first, and we answer by blessing him with the gifts he has given. The Mass is the place where the hymn of Ephesians becomes our own prayer: chosen, redeemed, sealed, and all things gathered in Christ.

At the end of Mass the deacon or priest sends the people out: “Go forth, the Mass is ended,” or “Go and announce the Gospel of the Lord.” This is the Church's version of the Gospel today. We do not leave as we came. Like the Twelve, we are sent with authority that is not our own, with the Word we have heard and the Bread we have received, to be the light and the salt of the world. We go out, by the Lord's will, two by two, a parish and a family together, with nothing to carry but him.
outline: Opening
Ask: if someone asked you for your credentials as a Christian, what would you say?
Point 1 · The Lord took me
Amos is a shepherd with no credentials, and the call of God does not depend on any.
Point 2 · Chosen before the foundation of the world
Ephesians: blessed, chosen, redeemed, sealed, and all things gathered in Christ.
Point 3 · Two by two
The Twelve are sent in pairs, as a community that supports one another.
Point 4 · Take nothing but a staff
The new exodus: trust in God, welcome from others, and a message of repentance and healing.
Closing image
A pair of sandals and a staff by the door, ready for the road.
Take-home line
“Go, prophesy to my people.”
live: Answer your call
Ask in prayer: What is the work you want to give me this week? Then do it, without asking whether you are qualified.
Count your blessings
Write ten spiritual blessings you have received in Christ, as Paul begins with blessing. Read them aloud at supper.
Go two by two
Invite someone to go with you to visit a sick or lonely person, or to Mass on a weekday. Do not walk the path of mission alone.
Travel lighter
Choose one possession, habit or screen time that weighs you down, and set it aside for a week so that you can follow the Lord more lightly and joyfully.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (Homilies on the Gospels 17, in substance)

The Lord sends the disciples two by two because there are two commandments of charity, love of God and love of neighbour, and charity cannot exist with fewer than two. A preacher who does not love cannot speak the Gospel.
St Irenaeus (Against Heresies, in substance)

When the Son of God became man he recapitulated in himself the long history of humanity, giving us salvation in brief, so that what we had lost in Adam, to be the image and likeness of God, we might receive again in Christ.
St John Chrysostom (Homilies on Ephesians, in substance)

Paul says that God has blessed us with every spiritual blessing: not with earthly goods, like the blessings of the old promises, but with heavenly gifts, forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit and the inheritance of the kingdom.
magis: Catechism 857–860
The Church is apostolic: built on the foundation of the Apostles, she keeps their teaching, and the bishops, their successors, carry on their mission until Christ returns.
Catechism 1077–1083
The liturgy opens with the blessing of Ephesians 1:3–6: the Father is the source and goal of all blessing, and the Church blesses him in return.
Catechism 518
Christ's whole life is a mystery of recapitulation: all that Jesus did, said and suffered had the aim of restoring fallen humanity to its original vocation.
Catechism 1510
Mark 6:13 speaks of the apostles anointing many sick people with oil and healing them; the Church has always seen in this a root of the sacrament of Anointing.
Catechism 2544–2547
Poverty of heart: the Lord asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone, and to be detached from goods, so as to enter the kingdom.
saints: St Benedict (omitted this year)

Abbot (c. 480–547), father of Western monasticism and patron of Europe, proclaimed by Pope Paul VI in 1964. His Rule, which sums up the monastic life as prayer and work in a community under an abbot, shaped monasteries for fifteen centuries. His memorial, 11 July, gives way to the Sunday this year.
This week

12 Jul: Monday of the Fifteenth Week. 13 Jul: St Henry (optional memorial). 14 Jul: St Camillus de Lellis, priest (optional memorial). 15 Jul: St Bonaventure, bishop and doctor of the Church (memorial). 16 Jul: Our Lady of Mount Carmel (optional memorial).
2027-07-11.prayer: O God, who show the light of your truth to those who go astray, so that they may return to the right path, give all who for the faith they profess are accounted Christians the grace to reject whatever is contrary to the name of Christ and to strive after all that does it honour. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Father, you chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world; you took Amos from his flock and the Twelve from their nets, and you call us by name. Give us the lightness of those who carry only a staff and sandals, trusting in you. Make us a blessing, as you have blessed us; send us out two by two with the Gospel and the oil of healing; and when we are rejected, keep us from bitterness. Seal us with your Spirit until we enter into our inheritance. Amen.

2027-07-15.title: Saint Bonaventure, Bishop and Doctor of the Church
readings: I AM has sent me to you
Remember the wonderful works he has done
Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest
2027-07-15.alt: Memorial of St Bonaventure (white). The Lectionary gives no proper readings, so the readings of Thursday of the Fifteenth Week (Year I) are used. Psalm 105 has the same numbering in the Lectionary and in the NRSV. The memorial of St Bonaventure is kept on 15 July, the day he died. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-07-15.verse: Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
theo: Moses has met God at the burning bush and been sent to Egypt, and now he asks a practical question: “If I come to the Israelites and say to them, ‘The God of your ancestors has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is his name?’ what shall I say to them?” In the ancient world a name was not a label; it opened a person's character and a way into a relationship. God answers with the most mysterious sentence in the Old Testament: “I am who I am.” The Hebrew, ehyeh asher ehyeh, can mean “I am who I am,” or “I will be who I will be,” or “I will be there as who I will be”: the God who simply is, and who is present and faithful. Then God gives a shorter form that Israel would speak with great reverence, the divine Name written with four Hebrew letters (YHWH), which our Bibles print as “the Lord” in capitals, and which pious Jews never pronounce out of respect. The Church has the same reverence and does not pronounce it in worship. “This is my name forever, and this my title for all generations.” Notice that the name comes joined to a history: “the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob.” God is not an idea; he is the God of a family and a promise. Moses is to gather the elders and say: “I have given heed to you and to what has been done to you in Egypt.” The God who is is the God who looks. He also tells the truth about the road ahead: “the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand.” The liberation will be costly and slow, but God says plainly: “I will stretch out my hand.” The psalm answers with thanksgiving for what he has done: “Remember the wonderful works he has done, his miracles,” and especially that he “sent his servant Moses, and Aaron whom he had chosen.”

From the mountain of God we go to the lake of Galilee, and to words of rest. After the reproach of the towns and the thanksgiving of Jesus, there is this invitation: “Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.” The people who heard him knew about burdens: the labour of poor farmers and fishermen, taxes, and a religion that some teachers had loaded with many rules. In Jewish teaching “the yoke” was a familiar picture for the study and keeping of the Law and for the service of God; Ben Sira had said: “Put your neck under her yoke, and let your souls receive instruction.” Jesus takes up the picture and changes it: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me.” He does not abolish the yoke; he offers his own, which is himself. A yoke was usually worn by two animals together, so to take his yoke is to be joined to him and to walk at his side. And the teacher is not a hard master: “I am gentle and humble in heart.” Learning from Jesus means learning meekness, and rest is the fruit: “you will find rest for your souls.” This is the sentence that echoes Jeremiah's “ancient paths,” where Israel was told to “find rest for your souls.” His yoke is “easy” because love makes burdens light, and because he carries it with us. The Exodus reading and the Gospel fit: the God who says “I am” has come to the weary, and the Son who knows the Father invites everyone to come.
outline: Opening
Ask: what burden are you carrying that nobody knows about?
Point 1 · I am who I am
God gives Moses his name, and the name is joined to faithfulness.
Point 2 · I have seen, and I will stretch out my hand
The God who looks, and tells the truth about the road.
Point 3 · Come to me
The easy yoke of Jesus, gentle and humble of heart.
Point 4 · St Bonaventure, the Seraphic Doctor
Learning that ends in love, and a heart set on the Crucified.
Take-home line
“Come to me … and I will give you rest.”
live: Say his Name with reverence (Exodus 3:14)
Make the Sign of the Cross slowly today, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and let it be a prayer, not a habit.
Carry the light yoke (Matthew 11:29)
Name your heaviest burden to Jesus in a few words tonight, and say: I take your yoke; carry this with me. Ask also whom you can help to carry theirs.
saints: St Bonaventure (c. 1217–1274)

Born in Bagnoregio in Italy, he joined the Franciscans and studied and taught in Paris, where he was a contemporary of St Thomas Aquinas. A story tells that as a child he was healed through the prayers of St Francis; when his mother later told Francis, he is said to have exclaimed: “O buona ventura!” (good fortune). He became Minister General of the Order in 1257 and wrote the Life of St Francis and the Journey of the Mind into God, a guide from creatures to the cross and to God. Named cardinal bishop of Albano, he died during the Council of Lyons on 15 July 1274. Pope Sixtus V declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1588; he is called the Seraphic Doctor.
2027-07-15.prayer: God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, you told Moses your name and you promised to be with your people. Teach us to say your name with love and reverence, and to trust that you have seen what is done to us. Lord Jesus, gentle and humble of heart, we are weary and burdened: we come to you. Take your yoke upon us, and carry it with us, and give us rest. As you gave St Bonaventure a mind enlightened by learning and a heart on fire with love for the Crucified, give us a faith that studies, adores and serves. Amen.
altar: The Mass is the place where the weary come. “Come to me,” says Jesus, and in the Eucharist we come to him: the priest holds up the bread and says, “Behold the Lamb of God,” and we answer, “Lord, I am not worthy.” We lay down the burden of the week and receive his rest. St Bonaventure loved the Eucharist, and he taught that every study of God must end in love, adoration and thanksgiving, which the Mass makes real in the sacrifice of Christ.

2027-07-18.title: Sixteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: I will raise up shepherds over them who will shepherd them
The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want
He is our peace; he has made both groups into one
He had compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd
2027-07-18.alt: Year B. Gloria and Creed. No memorial is omitted this year. Psalm 23 has the same numbering in the Lectionary and the NRSV. This Sunday falls in Karkidakam, the month of the heaviest rains in Kerala, which tradition has long made a month of rest, care of the body and quiet at home; the Gospel's “Come away … and rest a while” fits it well. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-18.verse: As he went ashore, he saw a great crowd; and he had compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.
theo: Today's readings are about shepherds, and they begin with a thunderclap. The prophet Jeremiah speaks around the year 600 before Christ, when Judah's kings and leaders were failing the people, and the Lord says through him: “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!” The accusation is precise: “It is you who have scattered my flock, and have driven them away, and you have not attended to them.” The sheep belong to the Lord (“my flock,” “my pasture”); the shepherds are only stewards, and their failing is neglect: they have not “attended to” the people. Then God turns from judgment to promise, in three steps. First: “I myself will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the lands where I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fold.” God himself is the first shepherd. Second: “I will raise up shepherds over them who will shepherd them, and they shall not fear any longer, or be dismayed, nor shall any be missing.” Good shepherds are a gift from God, and their sign is that no sheep is lost. Third: “The days are surely coming … when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely.” His name will be “The Lord is our righteousness.” Christians read this as a promise fulfilled in Jesus, the descendant of David and the Good Shepherd. The psalm is the best-loved shepherd prayer in the world: “The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures; he leads me beside still waters; he restores my soul.” It moves from green meadow to “the darkest valley” (“for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me”) to a table “in the presence of my enemies” and a cup that “overflows,” and to the house of the Lord “my whole life long.”

In the second reading St Paul tells the Christians of Ephesus, most of them from non-Jewish families, what the Shepherd has done for them. “You who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.” “Far off” and “near” were the old words for Gentiles and Israel. Then he says the sentence at the centre of the letter: “For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.” Everyone in Ephesus knew about a dividing wall: in the Jerusalem Temple a low stone barrier separated the courtyard of the Gentiles from the inner courts, with a notice warning foreigners on pain of death not to go further. Paul says that Christ has taken down that wall, not by a plan or a treaty, but “in his flesh” and “through the cross.” The result is “one new humanity in place of the two, thus making peace.” This peace is not only between people; it is also with God: “through him both of us have access in one Spirit to the Father.” This is the unity of the Church: Jews and Gentiles, and in our parishes Malayalis and migrants, rich and poor, all brought near by one blood and one Spirit. The Church's unity is not our achievement but his gift, and our job is to keep from rebuilding the walls.

The Gospel has a very human opening. The apostles have just come back from their first mission (Mark 6:7–13), when Jesus had sent them out two by two, and “told him all that they had done and taught.” They are full of stories, and tired. Jesus does not say “well done, now go again.” He says: “Come away to a deserted place all by yourselves and rest a while.” Mark adds why: “many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat.” Here is a Lord who cares about the apostles' bodies and their need for food and quiet. Real ministry depends on rest and on prayer. But the plan fails: the crowds run along the shore and arrive before the boat. A shepherd might say, “They are ruining our retreat.” Jesus does the opposite: “As he went ashore, he saw a great crowd; and he had compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.” The Greek for compassion, splagchnizomai, means to be moved in the gut. This is the same verb used of the Good Samaritan and of the father of the prodigal son. And what does he do for people who are like lost sheep? He teaches them. The first food that he gives is his word, and on the next page of Mark he will feed them with bread. In this one scene, Jeremiah's promise is fulfilled: the Lord himself comes to gather the scattered sheep.
conn: “Woe to the shepherds.”

Jeremiah speaks against the kings and leaders of Judah. In Ezekiel 34 the same charge is made, and God promises: “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep.” Jesus gathers both prophecies when he says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).
“The remnant of my flock.”
The remnant is the group that stays faithful through exile. Jeremiah sees God gathering them from all lands: the Church sees this as the gathering of all peoples in Christ (John 10:16).
A righteous Branch.

In Hebrew tsemach, a shoot from the stump of David's family (see also Isaiah 11:1). The name “The Lord is our righteousness” is one that Christians apply to Jesus, who was descended from David (Matthew 1:1).
“Your rod and your staff.”
The rod was a club to ward off wild animals, and the staff a long stick to guide and rescue sheep. Both are signs of protection, not punishment.
“A table in the presence of my enemies.”
The shepherd becomes a host. The Church has always heard in the table, the anointed head and the overflowing cup an image of the sacraments of initiation and of the Eucharist (Catechism 1293, 1333).
“Far off” and “near.”
The words of Isaiah 57:19, “Peace, peace, to the far and the near,” which Paul applies to Gentiles and Jews alike.
The dividing wall.
The soreg, a stone barrier in the Temple, kept non-Jews out of the inner courts. Paul says that Christ has torn down the wall of hostility between peoples.
“Come away … and rest a while.”
Mark has the apostles rest even before the great feeding of the five thousand. From the beginning the Church has joined work with prayer and Sabbath rest (Catechism 2184–2185).
“Compassion.”

Splagchnizomai: to be moved in the gut. Jesus is moved with compassion at a leper (Mark 1:41), at a blind man's plea and at a widow's funeral. The verb is used almost only of Jesus and of the characters of his parables who show God's own heart.
altar: Psalm 23 sings of a table prepared and a cup that overflows, and every Sunday the Church sets that table. In the Eucharist the Good Shepherd feeds his flock with himself. The words of Mark, “he began to teach them many things,” also describe the Mass: first the table of the Word, then the table of the Body and Blood. The crowds ran ahead of the boat to find him; we come to Mass to find him too.

The unity that Paul praises, one body through the cross, is made real at the altar: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17). That is why the priest, who acts in the person of Christ the Shepherd, prays at each Mass for the Pope and our bishop and for the whole Church. And that is why we pray for good shepherds: only the Lord can raise them up.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did someone last notice you were tired, and tell you to rest?
Point 1 · Woe to the shepherds
The neglect of leaders, and God's promise: I myself will gather my flock.
Point 2 · The Lord is my shepherd
Green pastures, the dark valley, the table: the Lord leads and is with us.
Point 3 · He is our peace
Christ has broken down the dividing wall; one new humanity, one Spirit.
Point 4 · Come away and rest
Jesus cares for the tired apostles; rest and prayer are part of mission.
Point 5 · Compassion
The crowd like sheep without a shepherd: Jesus teaches them first.
Take-home line
“He had compassion for them.”
live: Rest a while
Plan one hour this week, perhaps on the Sunday afternoon in the quiet of the monsoon, in which you do nothing useful and simply rest with the Lord. Switch off the phone.
Pray for shepherds
Pray each day this week for your parish priest and your bishop by name, and for vocations to the priesthood and religious life: that the Lord may raise up shepherds who do not lose any sheep.
Take down a wall
Think of a person or group you avoid because of differences in religion, caste, language or politics. Do one small thing this week to reach across.
Be the compassionate eye
On your way to church or work, notice someone who looks lost or tired, a “sheep without a shepherd,” and greet them kindly.
fathers: St Augustine (Sermon 46 on the Shepherds and Sermon 340, in substance)

The Lord is the one Shepherd; those who shepherd in his name are shepherds only because they feed the flock that is his and not their own. To you I am a bishop; with you I am a Christian, and I am glad to be a sheep in his flock.
St Gregory the Great (Pastoral Rule, in substance)

The pastor should be a near neighbour to everyone in compassion, and yet raised above all in contemplation, so that his own pity may carry others' needs and his prayer may lift him above the things of earth.
St John Chrysostom (Homilies on Ephesians, in substance)
Christ did not only make peace between God and us; he joined Jew and Gentile into one body, so that the wall that divided them might not be rebuilt in the Church.
magis: Catechism 754
The Church is a sheepfold whose one door is Christ, and a flock whose shepherd is God himself; Christ the Good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
Catechism 1548–1551
The ordained priest acts in the person of Christ the Head and Shepherd of his flock; bishops and priests serve the flock in his name.
Catechism 820
Christ always gives his Church the gift of unity, and we must pray and work to preserve it, since the Church is one by his gift.
Catechism 2184–2185
Rest on the Lord's day: God rested on the seventh day, and Sunday is a day of joy, of worship and of care for the sick and elderly.
Catechism 2305
Peace is the work of justice and the effect of charity; earthly peace is an image and fruit of the peace of Christ.
saints: Sunday of the shepherds
No memorial is omitted this Sunday. The Church today thinks of her shepherds, the Pope, the bishops and the priests, who serve in the name of the Good Shepherd.
This week

19 Jul: Monday, Week 16. 20 Jul: St Apollinaris, bishop and martyr (optional memorial). 21 Jul: St Lawrence of Brindisi, priest and doctor (optional memorial). 22 Jul: St Mary Magdalene (feast). 23 Jul: St Bridget of Sweden (optional memorial). 24 Jul: St Sharbel Makhluf (optional memorial).
2027-07-18.prayer: Almighty God, show favour to your servants and mercifully increase the gifts of your grace, that, made fervent in hope, faith and charity, they may be ever watchful in keeping your commands. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, Good Shepherd, you saw the crowds and had compassion on them. Look on the scattered and the tired, and gather them in your fold. Raise up for your Church shepherds after your own heart, who attend to the sheep and lose none. You are our peace: take down the walls between peoples, castes and families. Lead us beside still waters, restore our souls, and let us dwell in your house our whole life long. Amen.

2027-07-25.title: Seventeenth Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: They shall eat and have some left
The hand of the Lord feeds us; he answers all our needs
One Lord, one faith, one baptism
Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed them to those who were seated
2027-07-25.alt: Year B. Gloria and Creed. From today the Church sets St Mark aside for five Sundays and reads John 6, the chapter of the Bread of Life. The feast of St James the Apostle (25 July) is omitted this year because it falls on a Sunday; the Mass is of the Sunday. The fourth Sunday of July is the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly (Pope Francis, 2021), kept close to the memorial of Sts Joachim and Anne. Psalm verses are the same in NRSV and the Lectionary. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-25.verse: Then Jesus took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated; so also the fish, as much as they wanted.
theo: Elisha is the prophet of the lean years. Just before today's story the Bible says, “there was a famine in the land” (2 Kings 4:38), and now a man arrives from Baal-shalishah with “twenty loaves of barley and fresh ears of grain in his sack.” They are first fruits, the first of the harvest, which the Law set apart for God and his ministers (compare Numbers 18:12–13; Deuteronomy 18:4). In a famine the man could easily have kept them for his own family; he carries them instead to the man of God. Elisha says only: “Give it to the people and let them eat.” His servant does the arithmetic every hungry community knows: “How can I set this before a hundred people?” Elisha repeats the command and gives the reason: “for thus says the Lord, ‘They shall eat and have some left.’” The servant obeys, and it happens “according to the word of the Lord.” Notice what is not asked: nobody is told to pray bread down from the sky. Twenty real loaves are placed in a servant's hands, and the word of the Lord does the rest. The Psalm names the God behind the sign: “The eyes of all look to you, and you give them their food in due season. You open your hand, satisfying the desire of every living thing.”

In the second reading St Paul writes as “the prisoner in the Lord,” and he begs rather than commands: “lead a life worthy of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, making every effort to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” Then comes the great litany of the “ones”: one body and one Spirit, one hope, “one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in all.” The Church's unity is not something we build; it is a gift to be guarded. And the Gospel shows where that gift is fed. To the Corinthians Paul writes: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17). The many are made one by the one bread.

For five Sundays the Church now reads John 6, and it opens with the sign. Every detail is chosen. “Now the Passover, the festival of the Jews, was near”: we are to think of the Exodus and the manna. Jesus “went up the mountain and sat down there with his disciples,” like a new Moses. He asks Philip, “Where are we to buy bread for these people to eat?” and John adds, “He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do.” Philip does the sums: “Six months' wages would not buy enough bread for each of them to get a little.” Then Andrew, who in this Gospel is always bringing someone to Jesus, brings a boy with “five barley loaves and two fish,” and asks the honest question: “But what are they among so many people?” Jesus says, “Make the people sit down.” Then comes the action that every Mass repeats: “Jesus took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them.” The Greek for “given thanks” is eucharistesas, the word from which we get Eucharist. Nothing is wasted: “Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost,” and twelve baskets are filled. The crowd, seeing the sign, wants “to take him by force to make him king,” but Jesus “withdrew again to the mountain by himself.” He will be king by giving himself, and in the coming Sundays he will say what the bread is: “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35); “the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh” (John 6:51).
conn: “Baal-shalishah.”
A place named only here in the Bible, in the northern kingdom of Israel where Elisha worked. A man from a land of famine still brings the first of his harvest to God's prophet.
First fruits.

The first of the harvest, offered to God in thanks (Exodus 23:19; Numbers 18:12–13; Deuteronomy 26:1–11). St Paul calls the risen Christ “the first fruits of those who have died” (1 Corinthians 15:20).
Barley loaves.
Barley was the grain of the poor; wheat bread cost more. Both the man's loaves and the boy's are barley: God works with what the poor can bring.
“The festival of the Jews.”

John places the sign near Passover, the feast of the Exodus. Jesus, his disciples and the crowd are themselves Jews; the Church honours the Jewish people as God's own people, never to be blamed collectively (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597–598).
The mountain.
As Moses went up Sinai, Jesus goes up “the mountain” and sits as teacher, and the people are fed as Israel was fed in the desert with manna (Exodus 16).
Philip and Andrew.

Both came from Bethsaida (John 1:44). Andrew is the disciple who brings people to Jesus: his own brother Simon (1:41–42), the boy today, and, with Philip, the Greeks who wished to see Jesus (12:20–22).
“Six months' wages.”
Greek: two hundred denarii. A denarius was a labourer's daily pay, so the sum was some seven months of work, far beyond anything the crowd or the disciples could raise.
“Given thanks.”
In Greek eucharistesas. At the Last Supper Jesus “took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it” (Luke 22:19). The Church sees in this sign a foreshadowing of the Eucharist (Catechism 1335).
“The fragments.”

Greek klasmata, “broken pieces.” An early Christian text of the late first or early second century, the Didache, prays over the Eucharistic bread that as it was once scattered on the hills and gathered into one, so the Church may be gathered into God's kingdom (Didache 9, in substance).
Twelve baskets.
Twelve for the tribes of Israel and for the Twelve Apostles: the abundance is for the whole people of God and is entrusted to the apostles to distribute.
altar: Look at the four actions of Jesus: he took, he gave thanks, he distributed, and he asked that nothing be lost. These are the actions of the priest at the altar in every Mass: the gifts are taken, the Eucharistic Prayer gives thanks, the bread is broken and given, and what remains is treated with reverence. In the Eucharist Jesus does far more than multiply bread: he gives himself, Body and Blood, soul and divinity. Yet he still begins, as today, with what we bring: bread and wine, “fruit of the earth and work of human hands,” and the offering of our own lives.

St Paul says there is one bread and so one body. When we receive Holy Communion we are not only united to Christ; we are made one with every other person at the table. That is why quarrels in the family or parish are not a small matter. Before we receive we say: Lord, I am not worthy; and the Lord answers by giving us himself, and by asking us to keep “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”
outline: Opening
Ask: what is the little thing you are holding back because it seems too small to matter?
Point 1 · They shall eat and have some left
Elisha's twenty barley loaves and the word of the Lord: enough, and more than enough.
Point 2 · What are they among so many?
A boy, five loaves and two fish: God asks for our little and does the rest.
Point 3 · He gave thanks
Take, give thanks, distribute: the shape of the Mass, and nothing lost.
Point 4 · One bread, one body
The Eucharist makes us one: humility, gentleness and patience in the Church and at home.
Closing image
Twelve baskets of fragments, and a boy who goes home having watched God use his lunch.
Take-home line
“Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.”
live: Offer your five loaves
Name one small gift you have, an hour, a skill, a bag of rice, a kind word, and put it in Jesus' hands today by giving it to someone in need.
Gather the fragments
Waste no food today. In this lean month of the monsoon, share what is left over with a neighbour, and keep the same reverence for every particle of the Eucharistic bread at Mass.
Guard the unity
In one place where there is quarrelling, at home or in the parish, be the first to speak with humility, gentleness and patience, as St Paul asks.
Honour a grandparent
Today is the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly. Visit or call a grandparent or an elderly neighbour, and ask them to tell you how they learned to pray.
fathers: St Augustine (Tractates on John 24, in substance)

The Lord who multiplied the five loaves is the same Lord who multiplies a few seeds into whole harvests every year. We marvel at the loaves because we have grown used to the field: the government of the whole world is a greater miracle than the feeding of five thousand.
St Ignatius of Antioch (Letter to the Philadelphians 4, in substance)
Take care to keep one Eucharist: there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, one cup for union with his blood, one altar, as there is one bishop with the priests and deacons.
The Didache 9 (in substance)
As this broken bread was scattered over the hills and, gathered together, became one, so may your Church be gathered from the ends of the earth into your kingdom.
magis: Catechism 1335
The miracles of the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord said the blessing, broke and distributed the loaves, foreshadow the superabundance of the one bread of his Eucharist.
Catechism 1396
The Eucharist makes the Church: those who receive it are united more closely to Christ, and through him to one another.
Catechism 813–815
The Church is one by her source, by her founder and by her soul, yet unity must be preserved by bonds of faith, sacraments and apostolic succession.
Catechism 2837
“Give us this day our daily bread”: the bread we ask for is also the bread of the Word and of the Body of Christ, and the prayer sends us to those who lack bread.
Catechism 2208, 2218
The family should care for the young and the old, the sick and the poor; grown children owe their parents gratitude and support in old age.
saints: St James the Apostle (omitted this year)

Son of Zebedee, a fisherman of Galilee, brother of St John, one of the three closest to Jesus on Tabor and in Gethsemane. He was the first of the Twelve to die for the faith, put to the sword by Herod Agrippa (Acts 12:1–2). According to tradition his relics rest at Santiago de Compostela. His feast, 25 July, gives way to the Sunday this year.
This week

26 Jul: Sts Joachim and Anne, parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary (memorial). 28 Jul: St Alphonsa (memorial in India). 29 Jul: Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus (memorial). 30 Jul: St Peter Chrysologus (optional memorial). 31 Jul: St Ignatius of Loyola (memorial).
2027-07-25.prayer: O God, protector of those who hope in you, without whom nothing has firmness, nothing is holy, bestow in abundance your mercy upon us and grant that, with you as our ruler and guide, we may use the good things that pass in such a way as to hold fast even now to those that ever endure. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you saw the hungry crowd and had compassion. Take the little we have, our time, our gifts and our poor loaves, give thanks over them and make them enough. Feed us with your own Body and Blood, make us one body, and teach us to gather up the fragments so that nothing and no one may be lost. Bless our grandparents and all the elderly, who have handed on the faith to us. Amen.

2027-07-01.title: Thursday of the Thirteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son
Not to us, O Lord, but to your name give glory
Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven
2027-07-01.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 13 (Year I). The first reading continues the story of Abraham with its greatest test, the binding of Isaac. The Gospel of the weekdays of Weeks 13 and 14 follows the mighty works of Matthew 8–9. In popular devotion July is the month of the Most Precious Blood. In Kerala the first monsoon rains of the month of Mithunam are still falling. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-01.verse: When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven.”
theo: Today's first reading is one of the most demanding chapters of the Bible. “After these things God tested Abraham.” The old man has waited twenty-five years for Isaac, has sent Ishmael away at God's command, and now hears the voice again: “Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering.” Notice how slowly the command tightens: your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love. Each word presses on the father's heart. The surrounding peoples did sacrifice their children, and the Bible tells this story to show the opposite: the God of Abraham does not want the death of a child. The angel stops the knife, and Israel will never offer her sons. Yet the test is real, and Abraham's answer is a model of faith. He rises early in the morning. He walks for three days. He says to his servants, “we will worship, and then we will come back to you.” He believes, as the Letter to the Hebrews explains, that “God is able even to raise someone from the dead” (Hebrews 11:19). The most moving words are Isaac's: “The fire and the wood are here, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” and Abraham's reply: “God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” The Hebrew name he gives the mountain, Yahweh-yireh, means “The Lord will provide.” The Church has always heard in this story a shadow of the Father who “did not withhold his own Son, but gave him up for all of us” (Romans 8:32): the beloved son who carries the wood, the mountain in the land of Moriah, the three days, the lamb that God himself provides. Our Jewish elder brothers and sisters read this chapter, the Akedah, with deep reverence at the New Year, and we honour their reading as we offer ours. The Psalm gives the right answer to a test passed: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.”

Matthew's Gospel now brings us home to Capernaum, “his own town.” Some people carry a paralysed man to Jesus on a bed, and the first thing Matthew tells us is that Jesus sees something: “When Jesus saw their faith.” The faith of the friends carries the sick man, and Jesus answers with a sentence that nobody asked for: “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven.” The man had come for his legs; Jesus first heals his heart. Some scribes think, “This man is blaspheming,” and from their own point of view they are right: only God can forgive sins. Jesus does not deny it. He reads their thoughts and asks which is easier, to say “Your sins are forgiven” or “Stand up and walk.” Anyone can say the first, since no one can check it; the second can be seen. So he proves the invisible by the visible: “so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,” he says to the paralytic, “Stand up, take your bed and go to your home.” And the man goes home carrying the bed that carried him. The crowds “glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.” The last words are in the plural, and the Church has always understood why: on Easter evening Jesus breathed on his apostles and said, “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them” (John 20:23). This is why we confess our sins to a priest: the one who forgave the paralytic in Capernaum forgives us through the ministry of his Church (Catechism 1441–1442). And the lamb that God provided on Moriah is the One of whom John the Baptist said, “Here is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!”
outline: Opening
Ask: when did someone's faith carry you, when you could not walk by yourself?
Point 1 · The test on Moriah
Abraham trusts that God can raise the dead, and God stops the knife.
Point 2 · God will provide the lamb
From Isaac's question to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
Point 3 · Your sins are forgiven
Jesus heals the heart before the legs, and gives this authority to human beings.
Take-home line
“God himself will provide the lamb.”
live: Be the friend who carries (Matthew 9:2)
Think of one person who is too weak to pray, to hope or to walk to Mass today. Carry them: call, visit, offer a lift, and pray for them by name.
Go to confession (Matthew 9:6–8)
If it has been a long time, choose a day this month for the sacrament of Reconciliation, and thank God for giving such authority to human beings.
2027-07-01.prayer: God of Abraham, you asked everything of your friend and you gave everything back to him. Give us a faith that trusts you on the mountain we do not understand, and teach us that you yourself provide the lamb. Lord Jesus, Lamb of God, who forgave the paralysed man and gave your Church the power to forgive, heal our hearts before our bodies, and make us friends who carry one another to you. Through your Precious Blood, wash away our sins and bring us home. Amen.
altar: At every Mass, before Communion, the priest holds up the Host and says: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world. These are the words of John the Baptist, and behind them stand Isaac's question and Abraham's answer. The Father has provided the Lamb; the Lamb is placed on the altar; and the people answer with the words of another man who sought healing, the centurion of Capernaum: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed. In July, the month of the Precious Blood, we remember that the cup of Mass holds the blood of the covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of sins.

2027-07-02.title: Friday of the Thirteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Isaac loved Rebekah, and was comforted after his mother's death
Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good
2027-07-02.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 13 (Year I). First Friday of the month, the day on which many parishes keep Mass, adoration and confession in honour of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. July is the month of the Most Precious Blood in popular devotion. The first reading skips the long story of the search for a bride (Genesis 24:9–61). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-02.verse: “Go and learn what this means, ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’ For I have come to call not the righteous but sinners.”
theo: The first reading moves in two steps: from a grave to a wedding. “Sarah lived one hundred twenty-seven years.” She dies at Hebron, and Abraham, the man of faith, does what every human being does: he goes in “to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.” Holy Scripture does not hurry grief. Then he rises and does something practical and dignified: he asks the Hittites for a place to bury his dead. “I am a stranger and an alien residing among you; give me property among you for a burying place.” After more than sixty years in the land God had promised him, the only piece of it Abraham owns is a cave and a field at Machpelah, bought for “four hundred shekels of silver” (Genesis 23:16). It is a lesson in the pilgrim life. The Letter to the Hebrews comments: all these died in faith, and “they confessed that they were strangers and foreigners on the earth,” seeking “a better country, that is, a heavenly one.” Jewish, Christian and Muslim traditions all honour that tomb of the patriarchs. The Church too teaches us to respect the bodies of the dead and to pray at their graves (Catechism 2300). The second part of the reading, from chapter 24, is a very different scene. Abraham is old; he sends his oldest servant to find a wife for Isaac among his own kin, and trusts that God “will send his angel before you.” After the long story of the well and Rebekah's kindness, which the Lectionary leaves out, we see the meeting: “Isaac went out in the evening to walk in the field; and looking up, he saw camels coming.” Rebekah looks up too, sees him, and veils herself. Then comes a sentence of great tenderness: “Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah's tent. He took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.” The covenant goes on through the love of husband and wife. The Church sees in the home built on such love a small image of the love of Christ for his people (Catechism 1602–1605).

The Gospel is the call of a man whom everybody despised. Matthew was a tax collector, one who collected tolls for the Roman authorities and for his own pocket, a collaborator in the eyes of his people. “As Jesus was walking along, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth; and he said to him, ‘Follow me.’ And he got up and followed him.” Mark and Luke tell the same story about a tax collector named Levi, and the Church has long understood that this is the apostle Matthew, the author of the Gospel that we read this week.
