Two words in the story are worth pausing on: he saw, and he said. Jesus looked at the man behind the counter and saw a disciple. Then comes the dinner, and with it the scandal. Jesus sits at table with “many tax collectors and sinners.” In the East to eat with someone was to accept him as a friend. The Pharisees ask the disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus answers with a proverb and a quotation. The proverb: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” The quotation is from the prophet Hosea: “Go and learn what this means, ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’” Go and learn: the teachers of the Law are sent back to school! God does not want religion without love. And then the mission statement of Jesus: “I have come to call not the righteous but sinners.” On First Fridays the Church thinks especially of the Heart that has this mercy. Since the revelations to St Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial in France in 1673–75, Catholics have honoured the Sacred Heart pierced by the lance, from which came “blood and water,” and many keep the nine First Fridays with Mass and Communion. The prayer of St Paul fits the day: that we may “know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge.”
outline: Opening
Ask: where do you meet your grief: do you hurry past it, or do you let God comfort you?
Point 1 · A stranger and an alien
Abraham buries Sarah and owns only a tomb in the land of the promise: we are pilgrims.
Point 2 · Comforted by love
Isaac and Rebekah: love in the home is God's comfort in sorrow.
Point 3 · Follow me
Jesus sees a tax collector and calls him; he eats with sinners, because he came for them.
Take-home line
“I desire mercy, not sacrifice.”
live: Pray at a grave (Genesis 23:2)
Visit the grave of someone you love this week, or pray for the dead at home, and thank God for their life. Grief offered to God becomes a prayer.
Eat with someone alone (Matthew 9:10)
Invite to your table or to a cup of tea someone whom others pass by, a widow, a newcomer, someone who has made mistakes.
2027-07-02.prayer: God of Abraham and Sarah, you comfort those who mourn and you make the love of husband and wife a sign of your faithfulness. Teach us to live as pilgrims, strangers and aliens on earth, looking for the better country that you have prepared. Lord Jesus, who saw a tax collector at his table and said, Follow me, call us from whatever keeps us sitting at our counters. Sacred Heart of Jesus, meek and humble, gentle and merciful, make our hearts like yours, and teach us to desire mercy more than sacrifice. Amen.
altar: On the First Friday many Catholics receive Holy Communion and spend time before the Blessed Sacrament. At every Mass the Lord does what he did at Matthew's table: he sits down with sinners, and gives himself to them. Before Communion we say, Lord, I am not worthy; and he says what he said to the tax collector: Follow me. The Eucharist is the meal of the pilgrim people, bread for the road to the better country, and also a foretaste of the wedding feast of the Lamb, of which Isaac and Rebekah's love is a distant image.

2027-07-05.title: Monday of the Fourteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God
My God, in whom I trust
If I only touch his cloak, I will be made well
2027-07-05.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 14 (Year I). From today the first readings turn to the stories of Jacob and Joseph in Genesis, which will be read through the week. Optional memorial of St Anthony Zaccaria, priest. The proper readings from the Common of Pastors may be used. Liturgical colour: green (white for the memorial).
2027-07-05.verse: Then Jacob woke from his sleep and said, “Surely the Lord is in this place—and I did not know it!” And he was afraid, and said, “How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”
theo: Jacob is alone. He has cheated his brother Esau of his blessing and has to run for his life, a man with a staff, a bag and a guilty conscience, walking from Beer-sheba toward Haran, a journey of some five hundred miles. When the sun sets, he stops at “a certain place,” and the Bible does not even name it. He takes “one of the stones of the place” and puts it under his head, and falls asleep. Then he dreams: “there was a ladder set up on the earth, the top of it reaching to heaven; and the angels of God were ascending and descending on it.” And above it stands the Lord himself, who does not scold the runaway but renews the promises made to Abraham and Isaac: the land, a great family, a blessing for all the families of the earth, and then the sentence that Jacob most needs: “Know that I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land; for I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.” Jacob wakes up and says one of the best-known sentences of the Book of Genesis: “Surely the Lord is in this place—and I did not know it!” The cold roadside is the “house of God” and the “gate of heaven.” He sets up the stone as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel, “house of God.” Then he makes a vow, still a bargain, as if God had to prove himself: “If God will be with me ... then the Lord shall be my God.” But the God who gave the promise is patient, and will teach Jacob over the years. The Church uses this very text when she dedicates a church: “This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven” (Catechism 1180–1181). The Psalm answers Jacob's night: “You who live in the shelter of the Most High ... will say to the Lord, ‘My refuge and my fortress; my God, in whom I trust.’”

Matthew compresses two healings into one chapter and weaves them together, and the woman's story is placed inside the ruler's. A leader of the synagogue, whose name Mark and Luke give as Jairus, kneels before Jesus: “My daughter has just died; but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.” This father has no promise to rely on, only a hope. Jesus gets up and follows him. On the road a woman who has had a flow of blood for twelve years comes up behind and touches the fringe of his cloak, one of the tassels that a Jewish man wore by the commandment of the Law. She does not dare to speak; she is ritually unclean, and she does not want to make Jesus unclean. “If I only touch his cloak, I will be made well.” Jesus turns and sees her, and says a tender word: “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.” With that word the nameless woman is received into the family. Then they reach the house. The flute players and the crowd making a commotion are the professional mourners of the day. Jesus says: “Go away; for the girl is not dead but sleeping.” And they laughed at him. When the crowd has been put outside, he goes in and takes her by the hand, and the girl gets up. Jacob learned in the night that the Lord is with him wherever he goes. The ruler and the woman learn that the Lord is with them in the street, in their trouble. And we learn the same on St Anthony Zaccaria's day: this physician from Cremona, who became a priest at twenty-six, knew that a person's deepest sickness is not of the body, and he spent his short life, only thirty-six years, healing souls.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did you last feel completely alone, and where did you meet God unexpectedly?
Point 1 · Surely the Lord is in this place
Jacob, a runaway, sleeps on a stone and finds the gate of heaven.
Point 2 · I am with you
The promise on the road: God stays with the wanderer until his word is done.
Point 3 · Take heart, daughter
A ruler and an unclean woman both reach Jesus, one by asking and one by touching.
Point 4 · St Anthony Zaccaria
A physician who became a priest and treated the sickness of souls.
Take-home line
“Know that I am with you and will keep you wherever you go.”
live: Say Jacob's words (Genesis 28:16)
Several times today, in your workplace, on a bus or in the kitchen, whisper: Surely the Lord is in this place. Look for him there.
Touch with faith (Matthew 9:21)
At the next Mass, make a conscious act of faith as you receive Communion: if I only touch him, I will be made well.
saints: St Anthony Zaccaria (1502–1539)

Born in Cremona in northern Italy; his father died when he was young, and his mother Antonia devoted herself to him. He studied medicine at Padua and practised as a physician in Cremona, then was ordained priest in 1528. In Milan he founded, with two friends, the Clerics Regular of St Paul, later called Barnabites after the church of St Barnabas in Milan, which they received some years after his death. He also helped to found the Angelic Sisters of St Paul and a lay group, the Married of St Paul. He loved the letters of St Paul, promoted devotion to the Eucharist, especially the Forty Hours, and preached missions to renew parish life. He died at Cremona on 5 July 1539, aged thirty-six. Canonised in 1897.
2027-07-05.prayer: God of Jacob, who met a runaway on the road and promised never to leave him, we thank you that you are in this place and in every place where we walk. Give us eyes to see the gate of heaven in the ordinary. Lord Jesus, who took the daughter of the ruler by the hand and called the woman who touched your cloak your daughter, take us by the hand when we are afraid, and let our faith touch you. Through the intercession of St Anthony Zaccaria, physician of body and soul, heal what is sick in us and in your Church, and make us eager to live by the word of St Paul. Amen.
altar: Jacob called the place of his dream Bethel and said, This is none other than the house of God. Every church in which the Eucharist is celebrated is a Bethel: the altar is the stone on which the Lord offers himself, and the Eucharist is the ladder on which heaven comes down to earth and earth rises to heaven. The woman touched the fringe of his cloak and was healed; at Communion we receive not the fringe but the Lord himself. St Anthony Zaccaria taught his Barnabites to keep the Forty Hours of adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, in which the Lord is truly the God who says, I am with you.

2027-07-06.title: Tuesday of the Fourteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: You have striven with God and with humans, and have prevailed
I shall behold your face in righteousness
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few
2027-07-06.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 14 (Year I). Optional memorial of St Maria Goretti, virgin and martyr (red or white). Verse numbering of Genesis 32 and Psalm 17 is given in NRSV numbering; the Lectionary numbers differ slightly. Liturgical colour: green (red for the memorial).
2027-07-06.verse: When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”
theo: Twenty years have passed since Jacob ran away from Esau, and now he is coming home. News has reached him that his brother is coming to meet him with four hundred men. Jacob has done what a man can do: he has prayed (Genesis 32:9–12), sent gifts ahead in droves, divided his camp, and sent his wives and children across the ford of the Jabbok. And then: “Jacob was left alone; and a man wrestled with him until daybreak.” The Bible does not explain who the stranger is. When the man cannot win, he strikes Jacob's hip and puts it out of joint. And Jacob, in pain, holds on: “I will not let you go, unless you bless me.” This is the wrestler's prayer. Then comes the question of the name: “What is your name?” “Jacob.” In Hebrew the name means “heel-grabber,” and at his birth it recalled how he clung to Esau's heel. The man gives him a new name: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with humans, and have prevailed.” Jacob asks for the stranger's name and receives only a blessing; and he calls the place Peniel, “face of God”: “I have seen God face to face, and yet my life is preserved.” “The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel, limping because of his hip.” The prophet Hosea remembers the story and adds a detail that Genesis does not give: “He strove with the angel and prevailed, he wept and sought his favor.” Prayer, says the Catechism, can be a struggle in the night, in which we do not let go until God blesses us (Catechism 2573). The one who wrestled and was wounded walks away with a blessing and a limp: he who grabbed at the heel is now the father of the people of Israel. And the Israelites to this day do not eat the thigh muscle, in remembrance. We honour the Jewish people who bear that name. The psalm adds the prayer of a man who has come through the night and looks forward to the morning: “As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake I shall be satisfied, beholding your likeness.”

Matthew is gathering the Lord's mighty works, and this is the last of the series. A man who is mute and possessed is brought to Jesus; the demon is driven out; “the one who had been mute spoke.” The crowds are astonished: “Never has anything like this been seen in Israel.” But some of the Pharisees say, “By the ruler of the demons he casts out the demons.” This is the first sign of the opposition that will grow in the Gospel, and it is a warning that a heart may see a miracle and still close itself. Then Matthew gives a summary of the Lord's work: Jesus “went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and curing every disease and every sickness.” And a sentence follows that shows his heart: “When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.” The Greek verb for compassion means to be moved in one's innermost being, in the gut. The crowds are people who have been worn down by hunger, taxes, illness and false leaders, and Jesus feels it. He takes up the promise of the prophet Ezekiel: “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep ... I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed, and I will bind up the injured, and I will strengthen the weak.” And then he turns to his disciples: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.” The first thing he asks is that we pray, and in the next chapter the Twelve will be sent. Many people in India, and in Kerala especially, know what a harvest is, and know that the rains are only the start. The harvest of souls is also great today, and it needs workers, priests, religious, catechists and lay people. St Maria Goretti, whom the Church remembers today, was a field that bore a harvest at a very early age. Born in 1890 in a poor farming family in Italy, she was an eleven-year-old girl when, on 5 July 1902, a young man living in the same house, Alessandro Serenelli, tried to force her into sin. She refused: “No, it is a sin. God does not want it.” He stabbed her repeatedly, and she died the next day in the hospital at Nettuno, forgiving him. Alessandro was sentenced to thirty years in prison; some years later he dreamed that Maria offered him lilies, and he changed. Released in 1929, he asked her mother Assunta for forgiveness, and was present at Maria's canonisation in 1950. He died in 1970, as a lay brother of the Capuchins. Her life shows both the cost of purity and the power of forgiveness.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did you last wrestle with God in prayer, and refuse to let go?
Point 1 · I will not let you go
Jacob at the Jabbok: a night of struggle, a new name, a blessing and a limp.
Point 2 · Compassion on the crowds
Jesus sees harassed and helpless people as sheep without a shepherd, and his heart moves.
Point 3 · The harvest and the labourers
Pray to the Lord of the harvest; vocations begin on our knees.
Point 4 · St Maria Goretti
A girl of eleven who said no to sin, and yes to forgiveness.
Take-home line
“I will not let you go, unless you bless me.”
live: Wrestle in prayer (Genesis 32:26)
Choose one real need and pray for it for ten minutes each day this week without giving up, as Jacob did: I will not let you go unless you bless me.
Pray for vocations (Matthew 9:38)
Each day this week say one Hail Mary for priests, sisters and brothers, and for young people who may be called. Ask the Lord of the harvest to send labourers.
saints: St Maria Goretti (1890–1902)

Born at Corinaldo in Italy to a poor farming family; after her father Luigi died of malaria, she took on much of the household work with her mother Assunta. A girl of deep prayer, she prepared with great care for her First Communion at eleven. On 5 July 1902, at Le Ferriere, she was attacked by a nineteen-year-old neighbour, Alessandro Serenelli, who tried to force her into sin. She resisted and was stabbed fourteen times. She died the next day in hospital, having forgiven him. He later repented, and he attended her canonisation by Pope Pius XII in 1950. She is a patroness of youth, and of those who have been victims of violence.
2027-07-06.prayer: God of Jacob, who wrestled with your servant in the night and blessed him with a new name, teach us to hold on to you in prayer, even when it costs us, and to walk in the morning of your blessing. Lord Jesus, shepherd of the harassed and helpless, move our hearts with your compassion, and send labourers into your harvest. Through the intercession of St Maria Goretti, who kept her purity and forgave her murderer, give our young people a love for what is pure and a heart ready to forgive. Amen.
altar: At Mass we hold on to the Lord with Jacob's persistence: we do not let you go, unless you bless us. And he blesses us, not with a new name but with himself. The compassion that moved Jesus when he saw the crowds is present in the Eucharist, where the Good Shepherd feeds his sheep with his own Body. Before Communion we pray for the grace of forgiveness, as we say: forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us. St Maria Goretti received Holy Communion for the first time a few weeks before her death, and the bread of the strong made her ready to forgive.

2027-07-07.title: Wednesday of the Fourteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Go to Joseph; what he says to you, do
Truly the eye of the Lord is on those who fear him
As you go, proclaim the good news, ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near’
2027-07-07.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 14 (Year I). The first reading begins the last great story of Genesis, the story of Joseph and his brothers, which the weekdays of this week follow to the end of the book. The Gospel opens the mission discourse of St Matthew, chapter 10, read all week. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-07.verse: As you go, proclaim the good news, ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near.’
theo: The famine that Joseph foretold has come, and it has spread beyond Egypt. When the Egyptians cry to Pharaoh for bread, his answer is only seven words: “Go to Joseph; what he says to you, do.” The young man who was sold as a slave and forgotten in prison now opens the storehouses, and “all the world came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain.” In Canaan old Jacob hears that there is grain in Egypt and sends ten of his sons, keeping Benjamin at home, for the youngest son of his beloved Rachel is all he has left of her. Then Genesis shows us the scene it has been preparing since chapter 37: “Joseph's brothers came and bowed themselves before him with their faces to the ground.” The dream of the sheaves, which they had mocked, comes true, though not in any way they could have imagined. Joseph recognises them; they do not recognise him. He “treated them like strangers and spoke harshly to them,” and he tests them. It is not cruelty for its own sake. He wants to know whether these men have changed, and whether they will again abandon a favoured brother as they once abandoned him. After three days in prison he sends them home on one condition: one brother stays behind, and the rest must bring Benjamin. And now the guilt that more than twenty years of silence could not bury comes to the surface. “Alas, we are paying the penalty for what we did to our brother; we saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen.” Reuben adds, “So now there comes a reckoning for his blood.” They suppose that Joseph cannot understand them, since he speaks through an interpreter. But he understands every word, and “he turned away from them and wept.” The reading does not say what the tears meant: sorrow for what was done, or hope that his brothers have begun to repent. Nothing in the story is wasted: the famine, the prison and the awakened conscience are the road by which God will bring the family home. The Psalm names the secret of it: “The counsel of the Lord stands forever,” and “the eye of the Lord is on those who fear him, ... to keep them alive in famine.”

In the Gospel Jesus “summoned his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to cure every disease and every sickness.” St Matthew gives their names, and he gives them with some honesty: Simon Peter and Andrew, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew the tax collector, James son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus, Simon the Cananaean, and “Judas Iscariot, the one who betrayed him.” A fisherman, a tax collector who worked for Rome, a Cananaean who may have belonged to the zealot party, and a man who would betray his Master: Jesus builds his Church from the most unlikely materials. The number is not an accident. Jacob had twelve sons, and from them came the twelve tribes of Israel; now Jesus calls twelve, the foundation of a renewed people of God. We have just heard about those twelve sons and how their family was almost broken by jealousy and cruelty; here are twelve others who are sent out to bring peace and healing. Then comes the first instruction: “Go nowhere among the Gentiles, and enter no town of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” This does not close the door on the nations. God's promise came through Abraham to Israel, and the Messiah comes first to his own people, to gather them. After the resurrection the same Jesus will say, “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19), and the Gospel itself has already shown a Roman centurion and the Magi from the East honoured for their faith. The message the Twelve carry is the message of Jesus himself, and of John the Baptist before him: “The kingdom of heaven has come near.” They do not preach their own wisdom, and they do not heal by their own power; the authority was given to them. Pharaoh sent the hungry to Joseph; Jesus sends his apostles to the hungry of every age, with the word that heals and the bread that feeds. Christian devotion has long heard in Pharaoh's command, “Go to Joseph,” an echo of the trust we place in St Joseph, the guardian of the Holy Family and the protector of the Church. And only four days after the feast of St Thomas, the Apostle of India, we may notice his name in the list, one of the Twelve who were sent.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did your conscience last speak about something you thought was buried and forgotten?
Point 1 · Go to Joseph
In the famine, the world comes to the man who was once thrown into a pit.
Point 2 · We are paying the penalty
The brothers remember what they did, and conscience awakens.
Point 3 · He turned away and wept
Joseph tests his brothers in love, and weeps in secret.
Point 4 · The kingdom has come near
Jesus calls twelve, gives them authority and sends them to the lost.
Take-home line
“The kingdom of heaven has come near.”
live: Listen to your conscience (Genesis 42:21)
Is there a wrong you have not set right, a word of sorrow you have never spoken? This week, name it before God, and ask for the sacrament of Reconciliation.
Be sent (Matthew 10:7)
Choose one person who is hungry for hope, a neighbour, a relative, a colleague, and say or do one thing this week that tells them God is near.
2027-07-07.prayer: Lord God, you were at work in a famine, in a prison and in a brother's tears, to bring a divided family home. Awaken our conscience when it sleeps, and give us the courage to say: we have sinned. Lord Jesus, you called the Twelve by name and gave them your own authority; you still call ordinary and imperfect people and send them to the lost. Make us messengers of your kingdom, patient with those who wrong us, generous to the hungry, and glad to hear your word: the kingdom of heaven has come near. St Joseph, guardian of the Holy Family, pray for us. Amen.
altar: Joseph opened the storehouses, and the world came to him for grain. At every Mass the Church opens two storehouses: the table of the Word, where the Scriptures are read as they are today, and the table of the Bread, where Jesus gives himself to us as food for the journey. The Twelve whom Jesus sent are the root of the Church's ministry: the bishops are their successors, and the priests share in their mission, so that in every parish the Lord may still say to the hungry: take and eat. We come, like Joseph's brothers, hungry and not worthy; we leave, as they did, with food for our households.

2027-07-08.title: Thursday of the Fourteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt
He had sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave
You received without payment; give without payment
2027-07-08.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 14 (Year I). The first reading is the climax of the story of Joseph: Judah's plea and the revelation of Joseph to his brothers. The Gospel continues the mission discourse of St Matthew, chapter 10. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-08.verse: Cure the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. You received without payment; give without payment.
theo: The story of Joseph reaches its turning point. The silver cup has been found in Benjamin's sack, and Joseph, still unrecognised, has ruled that only Benjamin shall stay behind as his slave; the rest may go home in peace. Then Judah steps forward, and he makes the longest speech in the Book of Genesis. He does not defend himself and he does not bargain. He simply tells the story of an old father: “We have a father, an old man, and a young brother, the child of his old age. His brother is dead; he alone is left of his mother's children, and his father loves him.” He reports what Jacob said when asked to let Benjamin go: “You know that my wife bore me two sons; one left me, and I said, Surely he has been torn to pieces; and I have never seen him since. If you take this one also from me, and harm comes to him, you will bring down my gray hairs in sorrow to Sheol.” In the verses the Lectionary passes over, Judah makes the offer that settles everything: “please let your servant remain as a slave to my lord in place of the boy; and let the boy go back with his brothers.” This is the same Judah who, twenty years earlier, had proposed that Joseph be sold to traders. Now he offers himself as a slave so that another favoured son will not be lost to his father. The test is passed: these brothers will not abandon a beloved brother again. Joseph can no longer control himself. “Send everyone away from me,” he cries, and weeping so loudly that the Egyptians hear it, he says, “I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?” His brothers cannot answer him, “so dismayed were they at his presence.” “Come closer to me,” he says, and they come closer. There is no reproach. Joseph does not pretend that nothing happened: “I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.” But he looks at the wrong with the eyes of faith: “do not be distressed, or angry with yourselves, because you sold me here; for God sent me before you to preserve life.” Later in the chapter he will say it more boldly still: “it was not you who sent me here, but God.” Joseph does not call the evil good; he sees that God has brought good out of it. The Christian tradition has long seen in Joseph a figure of Christ, handed over by his own brothers for silver, brought low, and then raised up to give life to the world, forgiving those who wronged him; and in Judah, one who offers himself in the place of another. The Psalm sings the whole story: “he had sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave. His feet were hurt with fetters, his neck was put in a collar of iron; until what he had said came to pass, the word of the Lord kept testing him.”

In the Gospel Jesus goes on instructing the Twelve. “As you go, proclaim the good news, ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near.’ Cure the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons.” These are the very works Jesus himself has done in chapters 8 and 9 of St Matthew: the leper cleansed, the girl raised, the demons driven out. Now he hands them on. And then comes the sentence that sums up the whole of grace: “You received without payment; give without payment.” Nothing the apostles have, they earned. Healing, forgiveness and the word of God are gifts, and a gift cannot be sold. So the messengers travel light: “Take no gold, or silver, or copper in your belts, no bag for your journey, or two tunics, or sandals, or a staff.” Their poverty is a sign that the message does not belong to them and that they trust the One who sends them. They are not beggars, however, for Jesus adds, “laborers deserve their food”: those who serve the Gospel have a right to be supported by the people they serve, and the Church still lives by that rule. They depend on the hospitality of ordinary homes. “Whatever town or village you enter, find out who in it is worthy, and stay there until you leave.” Anyone who knows the welcome of a Kerala household, where the priest or the visitor is given the best chair and a hot meal, will understand how much the early Church grew in family homes. At the door the messenger offers the greeting of the East: “As you enter the house, greet it,” that is, say Shalom, peace. The peace is real, not a polite formula: “If the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it; but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you.” A gift refused is not wasted; it comes back to the giver. When a place will not listen, the disciples are to “shake off the dust from your feet.” It is a solemn sign that they have done their part and that responsibility now rests with those who refused; it is not an act of hatred, and Jesus himself weeps over the towns that do not receive him. The warning about Sodom and Gomorrah teaches how serious it is to reject the word of God, not that any people may be despised. Joseph asked no payment for his forgiveness, though his brothers owed him everything. That is the way of God, and the way of the disciple: you received without payment; give without payment.
outline: Opening
Ask: what is the most valuable thing you have ever been given without having earned it?
Point 1 · In place of the boy
Judah, who once sold a brother, now offers himself for another.
Point 2 · I am Joseph
The reveal: no reproach, only tears and the words “Come closer to me.”
Point 3 · God sent me before you
Joseph sees the hand of God in the wrong done to him.
Point 4 · Without payment
The Twelve receive a gift they can neither earn nor sell, and carry it lightly.
Take-home line
“You received without payment; give without payment.”
live: Offer yourself in place of another (Genesis 44:33)
This week take on a burden that belongs to someone else, quietly: a chore, a worry, a night watch with a sick person, so that they can rest.
Give without payment (Matthew 10:8)
Do one good thing this week for which you ask nothing back: no thanks, no credit, no return favour.
2027-07-08.prayer: Lord God, you brought good out of a brother's betrayal and you taught Joseph to forgive. Give us Judah's courage to offer ourselves for the people we love, and Joseph's tears to forgive those who have wronged us. Lord Jesus, you have given us healing, pardon and your own Body and Blood without any payment from us. Make us light travellers on your road, trusting in you, glad to be welcomed, and quick to give what we have received. Where we are refused, let your peace return to us and keep us from bitterness. St Joseph, pray for us. Amen.
altar: Judah offered himself as a slave in place of his brother. At every Mass we remember One who offered himself in the place of all of us: “This is my Body, which will be given up for you.” We could never have bought what we receive at the altar; it is given without payment. Then the priest greets the people with the peace of the Lord, as the apostles greeted every house, and at the Sign of Peace we offer that gift to those around us. And at the end of Mass, when we are sent forth, we hear again the command: give what you have received.

2027-07-09.title: Friday of the Fourteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Augustine Zhao Rong and Companions, Martyrs
readings: I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again
The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord
I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves
2027-07-09.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 14 (Year I). The optional memorial of St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, the martyrs of China, may be kept; the readings are those of the weekday. The first reading is Jacob's journey into Egypt, the Gospel the warning of persecution in the mission discourse of St Matthew. Liturgical colour: green (red if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-09.verse: See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.
theo: Jacob is an old man, and the journey he now takes is the hardest of his life. Joseph is alive and has sent wagons, and the whole family sets out for Egypt. But Egypt is not the land of the promise; it is a place where the patriarchs went in times of famine, and Isaac had once been forbidden to go there (Genesis 26:2). So at Beer-sheba, on the southern edge of Canaan, Jacob stops. He does not simply go. “When Israel set out on his journey with all that he had and came to Beer-sheba, he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.” And God answers: “God spoke to Israel in visions of the night, and said, ‘Jacob, Jacob.’ And he said, ‘Here I am.’” The double call is the call of the great vocations, the call of Abraham on Mount Moriah and of Moses at the burning bush. Then come three promises. “I am God, the God of your father; do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make of you a great nation there.” That is the first: the promise of a people. “I myself will go down with you to Egypt.” That is the second: God himself will travel with him into the foreign land. “And I will also bring you up again; and Joseph's own hand shall close your eyes.” The third is the promise of a return, and of a gentle death in the arms of a son. So the whole house of Jacob goes down, sons, grandsons, daughters, little ones, flocks, in the wagons that Pharaoh sent; the chapter counts seventy persons, the seed of the people of God. At the end of the road comes the meeting. Israel sends Judah ahead to Goshen, and it is the man who once offered himself in place of Benjamin who leads the way. Then “Joseph made ready his chariot and went up to meet his father Israel in Goshen. He presented himself to him, fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a good while.” The father's first words are among the most moving in all the Bible: “I can die now, having seen for myself that you are still alive.” For more than twenty years he had grieved for a son he thought dead. Now he asks nothing more of life. The Psalm is the song of an old believer who has seen it all: “Trust in the Lord, and do good,” “Take delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart,” and the sweet promise that “in the days of famine they have abundance.” It ends: “The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord; he is their refuge in the time of trouble.”

In the Gospel the mission discourse takes a darker turn. Jesus does not promise his messengers an easy road: “See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.” The disciples must be shrewd, not naive, and pure, not cunning. They will be handed over to councils and flogged in the synagogues; they will be dragged before governors and kings “as a testimony to them and the Gentiles.” Even this is mission: a trial becomes a pulpit. Jesus promises help for exactly those moments: “When they hand you over, do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say; for what you are to say will be given to you at that time; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” The words about family betrayal are harsh: “Brother will betray brother to death, and a father his child.” In every age, in lands where the Church is persecuted, they have been true. “You will be hated by all because of my name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.” Jesus also allows the prudent step: “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next.” The martyr does not go looking for death; he goes on bearing witness, and if it comes, he does not run from it. The saying that closes the passage, “you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes,” is a difficult one, read in several ways in the tradition of the Church; it tells at least that the work of the mission will not be finished before the Lord comes. The Church may keep today the memorial of St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, the 120 martyrs of China whom Pope John Paul II canonised in the Jubilee Year 2000. Bishops, priests, religious and lay women and men, Chinese and foreign, they died for the faith in the centuries from 1648 to 1930. Augustine Zhao Rong was a Chinese priest who, according to the usual account, had first been a soldier guarding a captive missionary and was so moved by his faith that he asked for baptism; he died in prison in 1815. Closer to home, India too has her martyrs; St Devasahayam, a layman of the Tamil country who was killed in 1752 for his faith, was canonised in 2022. They show how Jacob's three promises hold good: God gives a people, he goes down with them into every foreign land, and he brings them up again.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did you last set out on a journey that frightened you, not knowing whether God was in it?
Point 1 · Do not be afraid to go down
At Beer-sheba God calls Jacob by name and promises to travel with him.
Point 2 · I can die now
Father and son meet in Goshen: the tears of a lifetime.
Point 3 · Sheep among wolves
Jesus warns the disciples of trials, and promises the Spirit's help.
Point 4 · The martyrs
The 120 martyrs of China and all who bear witness to the end.
Take-home line
“I myself will go down with you.”
live: Pray before you go (Genesis 46:1)
Before any big decision or journey this week, stop and offer a prayer, as Jacob offered sacrifice at Beer-sheba, and ask God to go with you.
Pray for the persecuted (Matthew 10:22)
Pray for Christians who suffer for their faith, in China and elsewhere, and for those who persecute them, that they may come to know Christ.
2027-07-09.prayer: God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, you called Jacob by name at Beer-sheba and promised to go down with him into Egypt and bring him up again. Be with all who set out into the unknown this day, and with all who are afraid. Lord Jesus, you sent your disciples out like sheep among wolves and promised them the Spirit of your Father. Give us the wisdom of serpents and the innocence of doves; give us courage when we are brought before the powerful, and words from the Holy Spirit when we have none. Receive into your glory the martyrs of every land, St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, and the martyrs of India, and by their prayers keep us faithful to the end. Amen.
altar: Jacob offered sacrifices at Beer-sheba before he went down into Egypt, and received the promise of God's company on the road. Every Mass makes present the one sacrifice of Christ, to which all those earlier sacrifices pointed, and is a promise kept: “I am with you always, to the end of the age.” The early Christians were nourished by the Eucharist before they went to face the wolves; the word martyr means witness, and at Mass the Church remembers her martyrs by name in the Eucharistic Prayer and asks to be given a place with them. We receive the Lord's Body so that, like them, we may bear him into the world, by the way we live, even when it costs us something.

2027-07-10.title: Saturday of the Fourteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: God intended it for good, in order to preserve a numerous people
Seek the Lord and his strength; seek his presence continually
So do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows
2027-07-10.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 14 (Year I). The first reading closes the Book of Genesis with the death of Jacob and Joseph. The Gospel continues the mission discourse of St Matthew, chapter 10. The Saturday memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary may be kept. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial of Mary is kept).
2027-07-10.verse: Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. And even the hairs of your head are all counted. So do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.
theo: The Book of Genesis, which began with the creation of the heavens and the earth, ends with a coffin. Jacob is dying, and his last concern is where he will be buried: not in Egypt, but with his fathers in the cave at Machpelah, near Mamre, “in the field that Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site. There Abraham and his wife Sarah were buried; there Isaac and his wife Rebekah were buried; and there I buried Leah.” The patriarchs own no land but a grave, and in that grave is their claim on the promise. Then the old man dies, Joseph weeps and has him embalmed, and the family goes up to Canaan to bury him; the Egyptians mourn for seventy days. But once the father is gone, an old fear awakens in the brothers. “Realizing that their father was dead, Joseph's brothers said, ‘What if Joseph still bears a grudge against us and pays us back in full for all the wrong that we did to him?’” They send a message in their father's name, begging Joseph to forgive “the crime of the servants of the God of your father.” Genesis does not say whether Jacob really spoke those words. It tells us that the brothers, after seventeen years of living in Egypt on Joseph's bounty, have still not grasped how completely they are forgiven. “Joseph wept when they spoke to him.” It grieved him that they could think so little of his love. When they fall down before him, he says the sentence that is the summit of the whole book: “Do not be afraid! Am I in the place of God? Even though you intended to do harm to me, God intended it for good, in order to preserve a numerous people, as he is doing today. So have no fear; I myself will provide for you and your little ones.” He forgives them and does not diminish the evil that was done; he sets it inside a larger story that God is writing. “In this way he reassured them, speaking kindly to them.” Genesis ends with Joseph's own death at one hundred and ten. His last words look beyond Egypt: “I am about to die; but God will surely come to you, and bring you up out of this land to the land that he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.” He makes them swear: “When God comes to you, you shall carry up my bones from here.” The book closes: “he was embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt.” It is a coffin with a promise inside it. Moses will carry those bones out of Egypt (Exodus 13:19), and the Letter to the Hebrews will say that Joseph, at the end of his life, “made mention of the exodus of the Israelites” by faith (Hebrews 11:22). The Psalm is the song of such a people: “O give thanks to the Lord, call on his name, make known his deeds among the peoples,” “Seek the Lord and his strength; seek his presence continually,” and “O offspring of his servant Abraham, children of Jacob, his chosen ones.”

The Gospel takes up the same word that Joseph spoke twice: do not be afraid. Jesus has told his disciples that they will be hated and brought before courts; now he tells them what to do with their fear. First he reminds them who they follow: “A disciple is not above the teacher, nor a slave above the master; it is enough for the disciple to be like the teacher, and the slave like the master. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they malign those of his household!” Beelzebul is a name for the prince of the demons, the very name the enemies of Jesus have already thrown at him (Matthew 9:34). The disciples are not to be surprised if they share his treatment. And then three times comes the command: “So have no fear of them.” The first reason is that truth will come out: “nothing is covered up that will not be uncovered, and nothing secret that will not become known.” What Jesus has taught them in the quiet of the circle of disciples, they must now proclaim: “What I say to you in the dark, tell in the light; and what you hear whispered, proclaim from the housetops,” the flat roofs from which news was shouted across the village. The second reason is that there is a greater fear that drives out the lesser: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.” Jesus is not asking us to be afraid of God as of a tyrant; the next verse shows the same God counting sparrows. The holy fear of the Lord, which the Church counts among the gifts of the Holy Spirit (Catechism 1831), is the fear of losing God and the life he gives, and it is the beginning of wisdom. The third reason is the tenderness of the Father. “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. And even the hairs of your head are all counted. So do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.” The sparrow was the cheapest bird sold for food in the market, the poor man's meat. If the Father knows each of them, how much more his children. The passage ends with the choice of every disciple: “Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven; but whoever denies me before others, I also will deny before my Father in heaven.” Joseph's brothers feared a master who had loved them all along; we are asked to trust a Father who has loved us all along.
outline: Opening
Ask: is there a fear you carry, long after the cause has gone, that you have never handed to God?
Point 1 · The fear of the forgiven
The brothers still fear, though Joseph has already forgiven them.
Point 2 · Am I in the place of God?
Joseph forgives, and sees the larger story God is writing.
Point 3 · A coffin with a promise
Genesis ends with Joseph's bones, and a promise that God will come.
Point 4 · Do not be afraid
Three times Jesus says it; the sparrows and the hairs of your head.
Take-home line
“Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.”
live: Let yourself be forgiven (Genesis 50:17)
If you have been to confession and still carry the old guilt, say to God today: I trust that I am forgiven, and let the matter rest.
Speak kindly to the one you have forgiven (Genesis 50:21)
Tell someone clearly and kindly that you have forgiven them, so that they do not go on living in fear.
2027-07-10.prayer: Lord God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, you wrote the story of Joseph and his brothers and brought good out of the evil that was done. When we are afraid of those we have wronged, and when we cannot believe that we are forgiven, teach us to trust in your mercy. Lord Jesus, you tell us not to be afraid of those who can kill the body, because the Father counts the sparrows and numbers the hairs of our heads. Give us courage to speak in the light what you tell us in the dark, and to acknowledge you before others. Holy Mary, who stood by the Cross without fear, pray for us. Amen.
altar: Joseph's last request was that his bones be carried out of Egypt when God came to visit his people. Every Mass is a visit of God to his people, and the Church has a name for the Communion given to a dying Christian: Viaticum, food for the journey. Like Joseph, the Christian goes out of this world carrying a promise, and the Lord who is received at the end is the same Lord who is received every Sunday. In the Creed we acknowledge Jesus before others, as he asks today, and in Communion he acknowledges us. And the Lord's Prayer, which we say before Communion, asks him to forgive us as we forgive, as Joseph forgave.

2027-07-12.title: Monday of the Fifteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: A new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph
Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth
2027-07-12.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 15 (Year I). From today the first reading is the Book of Exodus, read on the weekdays of weeks 15 and 16 and into week 17, the story of the oppression, the call of Moses and the liberation of Israel. The Gospel closes the mission discourse of St Matthew, chapter 10. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-12.verse: Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.
theo: With today's reading the Book of Exodus begins, and the story changes. A family has become a people, and a people has become a problem for a new regime. The book opens with names: the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, seventy persons in all. In a few lines a whole era passes: “Then Joseph died, and all his brothers, and that whole generation. But the Israelites were fruitful and prolific; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them.” God's blessing from the first pages of Genesis, “Be fruitful and multiply,” is being fulfilled in the foreign land. Then comes the sentence that turns the page: “Now a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.” Joseph, who saved Egypt from famine, has been forgotten; gratitude is short-lived when power is at stake. The king speaks like a frightened man: “Look, the Israelite people are more numerous and more powerful than we. Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase and, in the event of war, join our enemies and fight against us and escape from the land.” A minority has become a threat to national security, and the answer is to be “shrewd,” step by step. First forced labour: “they set taskmasters over them to oppress them with forced labor. They built supply cities, Pithom and Rameses, for Pharaoh.” Then harsher: “The Egyptians became ruthless in imposing tasks on the Israelites, and made their lives bitter with hard service in mortar and brick and in every kind of field labor.” The bitterness will be remembered every year at the Passover table. But the plan does not work. “The more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread, so that the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites.” The blessing of God cannot be stopped by a decree. So the king turns to murder. The Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah, whom the Lectionary passes over, “feared God” and let the boys live: the first act of conscientious refusal in the Bible, and Scripture records their names while the king's name is not given. Then Pharaoh orders all his people: “Every boy that is born to the Hebrews you shall throw into the Nile, but you shall let every girl live.” The river that gives Egypt its life becomes a place of death, and in tomorrow's reading a baby in a basket will be drawn out of it. Notice that it is one king and one policy, not a whole people: the next chapter shows an Egyptian princess saving the child. The Psalm is the song of those who came through such a time: “If it had not been the Lord who was on our side, when our enemies attacked us, then they would have swallowed us up alive.” “We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped. Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

The Gospel brings the mission discourse to its end with some of the hardest words of Jesus. “Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.” In the same discourse he has told his disciples to bring peace into every house (Matthew 10:13), and he is the Prince of Peace. The sword is not a weapon of war. It is the knife that cuts, the line that falls between those who accept him and those who refuse him; the words that follow are taken from the prophet Micah, who described how families break up in a time of trial (Micah 7:6). Jesus is not telling anyone to quarrel with their parents; elsewhere he defends the duty to honour father and mother (Matthew 15:4–6). He is saying that no loyalty, however sacred, may stand above him: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.” In many families, in every age, the decision to follow Christ has cost a person the peace of the home, and Jesus does not hide it. “And whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” It is the first mention of the cross in the Gospel of Matthew, before Jesus speaks of his own passion. His hearers knew the Roman cross as an instrument of shame; he turns it into the sign of the disciple. Then comes the paradox at the heart of the faith: “Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.” The midwives of Egypt lost their safety and found the lives of children. And then the tone changes, and the discourse ends with welcome. “Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.” It is a chain of presence: the Father, the Son, the disciple, the host. A prophet or a righteous person welcomed in his name brings a reward, “and whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple ... none of these will lose their reward.” The smallest hospitality counts: in Kerala, the people who set up water-sheds for travellers in the hot months know what a cup of cold water is worth. “Now when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and proclaim his message in their cities.” The instruction is done; the teacher goes on preaching. When, many years later, Herod will try to kill another child, the Holy Family will go down into Egypt for refuge (Matthew 2:13–15), and the land of Pharaoh will again shelter a Hebrew child.
outline: Opening
Ask: who are the people in your country or neighbourhood whom someone has decided are a threat, and what does the Bible say about them?
Point 1 · A king who did not know Joseph
Forgetting the good done by others leads to fear, and fear to oppression.
Point 2 · The more they were oppressed
God's blessing grows under the whip; the midwives refuse to kill.
Point 3 · Not peace but a sword
Jesus cuts through every loyalty that stands above him.
Point 4 · A cup of cold water
The smallest welcome given in his name is never lost.
Take-home line
“Whoever welcomes you welcomes me.”
live: Remember with gratitude (Exodus 1:8)
Write the names of three people to whom you owe your life, your faith or your livelihood, and thank at least one of them this week, in person or by a call.
Offer a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42)
Do one small act of hospitality for a stranger or a worker: a glass of water, a seat, a meal, a kind word, in the name of Christ.
2027-07-12.prayer: Lord God of the oppressed, you saw the misery of your people in Egypt and you did not let the whip or the river destroy them. Give us a good memory, so that we may never forget those who have served us. Give us fearless consciences, like the midwives who feared you more than the king. Lord Jesus, you did not come to bring a false peace; teach us to love you above every other love, and to take up the cross and follow you. Bless those who give a cup of cold water in your name, and those who receive it. Our help is in your name, Lord, who made heaven and earth. Amen.
altar: The Church has long prayed these very words from the Psalm: “Our help is in the name of the Lord,” and the people answer, “Who made heaven and earth.” In the older form of the Mass the priest says them at the foot of the altar. At the Eucharist we remember what the Lord has done, as the Israelites remembered their bitter slavery each Passover, and we hear his words, “Do this in memory of me.” He is the one who does not forget us. And the Eucharist is the cup of cold water, and much more, that he gives us: “Whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.”

2027-07-13.title: Tuesday of the Fifteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Henry
readings: She named him Moses, “because I drew him out of the water”
You who seek God, let your hearts revive
Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!
2027-07-13.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 15 (Year I). From today the first reading follows the story of Moses, which runs through the weekdays of weeks 15 and 16. Optional memorial of St Henry, the emperor who ruled as a servant of the poor; the Mass is of the weekday unless the priest chooses the memorial. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. In Kerala the monsoon rivers are full this month, and the baby in the basket among the reeds is easy to picture. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-13.verse: When the child grew up, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and she took him as her son. She named him Moses, “because,” she said, “I drew him out of the water.”
theo: The book of Exodus opens with a people under pressure. Pharaoh has ordered every Hebrew boy to be thrown into the Nile, and today's reading begins with one family's answer. A man and a woman of the house of Levi have a son. His mother sees that he is “a fine baby” and hides him for three months. When she can hide him no longer she does a remarkable thing: she obeys Pharaoh's order, and defeats it. She does put the child in the Nile, but in a “papyrus basket” plastered with bitumen and pitch. The Hebrew word for this basket, tebah, is the word used for Noah's ark; the Bible is quietly telling us that another great rescue through water has begun. The child's sister, who is later named Miriam, stands at a distance and watches. Three women save him: the mother who lets go, the sister who keeps watch, and the daughter of Pharaoh who “took pity on him” although she knows at once that he is “one of the Hebrews’ children.” The tyrant's own house shelters the one who will break the tyrant's power, and the boy's mother is even paid wages to nurse her own son. Then comes the name: “She named him Moses, ‘because,’ she said, ‘I drew him out of the water.’” The name echoes the Hebrew for “to draw out.” The one drawn out of the water will draw a whole people out of the sea. The reading then jumps forward. Moses, grown up, sees an Egyptian beating one of his kinsfolk and kills him, and the next day one of his own people asks: “Who made you a ruler and judge over us?” Moses flees to Midian and sits down by a well. St Stephen will later say that Moses thought his people would understand that God was rescuing them through him, “but they did not understand,” and yet this very Moses was the one “whom God now sent as both ruler and liberator” (Acts 7:25, 35). The psalm is the prayer of a person in deep water: “I have come into deep waters, and the flood sweeps over me,” and yet “the Lord hears the needy.”

In the Gospel Jesus speaks hard words, and they have to be heard as words of grief. “Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his deeds of power had been done, because they did not repent.” The cities are Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, small towns around the Sea of Galilee. Capernaum was the base of his ministry, and Bethsaida was the town of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). The cry “Woe to you!” is the cry of the prophets over a city they love; it is closer to a mourner's “Alas for you!” than to a curse. The reason is not that these towns were worse than others but that they had been given more. They had seen the deeds of power, the healings and the teaching, and had not repented, which in the Bible means turning round and changing direction. Jesus compares them with Tyre and Sidon, pagan harbour cities that the prophets had condemned, and even with Sodom, the byword for sin. If those cities had seen what you saw, he says, they would have repented “long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” On the day of judgment it will be “more tolerable” for them: grace that is received and not used becomes a weight. Jesus speaks here as a son of Israel to his own neighbours in Galilee, in the manner of the prophets, and the Gospels show that many from these very towns did follow him; the first disciples came from them. The words are a family's lament, not a verdict against a people. The two readings meet in one question. Moses was drawn out of the water, and his people did not at first know their deliverer. Jesus was among his people, and many of his towns had seen and not yet turned. What have we done with what we have been given: our baptism, the Word, the Mass? Nothing in the Gospel is said to make us anxious; it is said to wake us up while there is still time to turn.
outline: Opening
Ask: who held you up when you could not hold yourself, and have you ever thanked them?
Point 1 · Drawn out of the water
A mother, a sister and a princess save the child who will save a people.
Point 2 · Who made you a ruler?
The deliverer is not yet recognised; God's time is longer than ours.
Point 3 · Woe to you
Jesus laments over the towns that saw most and turned least: gifts bring responsibility.
Point 4 · St Henry, an emperor who served
A crown understood as a trust for the poor and for peace.
Take-home line
“Because I drew him out of the water.”
live: Remember your baptism (Exodus 2:10)
Find the date of your baptism, thank God for it, and sign yourself with holy water when you come into church or when you leave home today.
Count what you have been given (Matthew 11:21)

Write down five gifts of faith you have received, such as the Mass, the Bible, a praying grandmother or a good priest, and ask what you have done with each. Plan one act of turning back, perhaps confession.
saints: St Henry (973–1024)

Born in Bavaria, he became King of Germany in 1002 and Holy Roman Emperor in 1014. With his wife Kunigunde, who is also a saint, he founded the diocese of Bamberg and supported monasteries and the renewal of Church life. He understood his crown as a trust from God for justice, for the poor and for peace, and he is remembered as an oblate of the Benedictines. He died on 13 July 1024 and was canonised in 1146.
2027-07-13.prayer: Lord God, you saw the cry of your people and drew Moses out of the water to be their deliverer. Draw us out of every flood that threatens to carry us away, and teach us to thank those who held us up when we could not hold ourselves. Lord Jesus, you grieved over the cities that saw your works and did not turn: give us hearts that are quick to repent and quick to be grateful. Through the intercession of St Henry, make all who hold power servants of the poor and makers of peace. Amen.
altar: At every Mass the priest pours a little water into the wine, and prays that we may share in the divinity of Christ who humbled himself to share our humanity. It is a small sign of baptism: we have been drawn out of the water. And the Mass is the greatest deed of power we shall ever see. The towns of Galilee saw healings; we see bread become his Body, and we are asked the same question as they were: will we turn to him? That is why the Mass begins with “Lord, have mercy.”

2027-07-14.title: Wednesday of the Fifteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Camillus de Lellis
readings: Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground
The Lord works vindication and justice for all who are oppressed
You have hidden these things from the wise and have revealed them to infants
2027-07-14.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 15 (Year I). The first reading is the burning bush; the Mass of the weekday may be replaced by the optional memorial of St Camillus de Lellis, priest and founder, the patron of the sick, of hospitals and of nurses (white). The Lectionary leaves out verses 7–8 of Exodus 3, the heart of the passage, and they are quoted below. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-14.verse: Then he said, “Come no closer! Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.” He said further, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”
theo: Forty years have gone by since Moses fled from Egypt. He is now a shepherd in Midian, looking after the sheep of his father-in-law Jethro, and he has led the flock “beyond the wilderness” to Horeb, “the mountain of God.” He is an old man doing the humblest work; the prince of Egypt has become a herdsman, and it is to the herdsman that God appears. “The angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of a bush; he looked, and the bush was blazing, yet it was not consumed.” Notice what Moses does: “I must turn aside and look at this great sight.” The whole story turns on that small decision. “When the Lord saw that he had turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush, ‘Moses, Moses!’ And he said, ‘Here I am.’” God speaks only to someone who stops. Then come two commands that shape all worship: “Come no closer! Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.” Ground becomes holy because God is present in it. And God names himself, not first by power but by relationship: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hides his face. The Lectionary skips two verses, and they are the heart of it: “I have observed the misery of my people who are in Egypt; I have heard their cry on account of their taskmasters. Indeed, I know their sufferings” (Exodus 3:7). The holy God is the God who sees suffering, hears the cry, and knows it from the inside. And so he sends Moses. Moses objects: “Who am I?” and God answers, not with a list of Moses' strengths, but with himself: “I will be with you.” The psalm sings it: “The Lord works vindication and justice for all who are oppressed. He made known his ways to Moses.”

In the Gospel Jesus bursts into thanksgiving: “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants.” The passage comes right after he has grieved over the towns that saw most and turned least, and the contrast is deliberate: those who thought they knew did not see, and the little ones did. “Infants” (Greek nepioi) are the unlearned, the humble, those with nothing to defend. The Bible has many of them: a shepherd at a bush, a boy David, fishermen from Galilee. St Paul would write that God chose “what is low and despised in the world” (1 Corinthians 1:28). Then Jesus lifts the veil on his own mystery: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father; and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” This is the most intimate sentence in the first three Gospels; it sounds like the Gospel of John. Jesus is not only a messenger of God: he knows the Father as only a Son can, and he opens that knowledge to those he chooses, and he chooses the humble. The burning bush and this prayer fit together. At the bush God revealed his name and his compassion to a shepherd; in Jesus the Father reveals his whole heart to those who come like children. And the holy ground is no longer only a mountain in Sinai: it is wherever the Son is, and wherever the least of his brothers and sisters are found.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did you last stop, turn aside and look at something that you did not understand?
Point 1 · I must turn aside
God speaks to the one who stops; the shepherd at the bush.
Point 2 · Holy ground
Remove your sandals: God's presence makes every place holy, and he knows our sufferings.
Point 3 · Revealed to infants
The Father reveals himself to the humble through the Son.
Point 4 · St Camillus
A sickbed is holy ground, and the sick are Christ himself.
Take-home line
“I will be with you.”
live: Turn aside (Exodus 3:3)
Choose one moment today, on a bus, in the kitchen or at the roadside, to stop completely for two minutes, put the phone away and be quiet before God.
Take off your sandals (Exodus 3:5)
Visit or phone someone who is ill. When you enter their room, treat it as holy ground: sit, listen, and do not hurry.
saints: St Camillus de Lellis (1550–1614)

Born at Bucchianico in Italy, he became a soldier, a gambler and a restless young man with an incurable wound on his leg. In Rome he was treated, and then worked, in a hospital for incurables, and a sermon in 1575 turned his life round. He later founded the Ministers of the Sick, the Camillians, who wear a red cross on their habit, and he asked them to care for the sick with the love of a mother for her only child. He cared for the sick in plague and in war, and is the patron of the sick, of hospitals and of nurses. He died in Rome on 14 July 1614 and was canonised in 1746.
2027-07-14.prayer: Lord God, you appeared to Moses in the burning bush and said: I have heard the cry of my people and I know their sufferings. Make us people who turn aside to look, who take off their sandals before holy ground, and who see in every sickroom a place where your Son is present. Father, Lord of heaven and earth, we thank you that you reveal yourself to the little ones. Through the intercession of St Camillus, give strength and tenderness to all who nurse the sick, healing to those who suffer, and to each of us the knowledge that you are with us. Amen.
altar: In the Mass we, too, take off our sandals in our own way: we bow, we kneel, we are silent before the altar, because the ground of the church is holy ground. The Lord who spoke from the bush now comes in bread and wine. In the Eucharist the Son gives us the knowledge of the Father that he promised in today's Gospel. And the same Christ who is present on the altar is present, in another way, in the sick person we are asked to visit; that is why the Church has always joined the Mass to the care of the sick.

2027-07-16.title: Friday of the Fifteenth Week in Ordinary Time · Our Lady of Mount Carmel
readings: When I see the blood, I will pass over you
I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord
I desire mercy and not sacrifice
2027-07-16.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 15 (Year I), with the optional memorial of Our Lady of Mount Carmel (white), much loved in India and in Kerala, where the brown scapular is widely worn. The weekday readings above are shown; the Mass of the memorial has its own proper readings, which are Zechariah 2:14–17 (NRSV 2:10–13), Luke 1:46–55 (the Magnificat) and Matthew 12:46–50. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-16.verse: Elijah went up to the top of Carmel … At the seventh time he said, “Look, a little cloud no bigger than a person’s hand is rising out of the sea.”
theo: Today's first reading is the last night in Egypt, and it is the most important night in the Old Testament. Nine plagues have fallen; “the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go out of his land.” Now God gives Moses and Aaron the instructions for the night of liberation. First, a new calendar: “This month shall mark for you the beginning of months.” The liberation of the people becomes the beginning of the year. Then, a meal in each home: “a lamb for each family,” “without blemish, a year-old male,” kept until the fourteenth day and then slaughtered at twilight by the whole assembly. Some of its blood is put “on the two doorposts and the lintel” of the house. It is eaten “with unleavened bread and bitter herbs,” in haste: “your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand.” “It is the passover of the Lord.” The word means passing over: “when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague shall destroy you.” And then the command that turns an event into a tradition: “This day shall be a day of remembrance for you. You shall celebrate it as a festival to the Lord; throughout your generations you shall observe it as a perpetual ordinance.” Jews celebrate this meal today, in every generation, in the Seder; and the Church, from the beginning, has seen in the unblemished lamb a picture of Christ: John the Baptist calls him “the Lamb of God,” and Paul writes, “our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The psalm is the answer of someone who has been saved: “What shall I return to the Lord for all his bounty to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord.” We say these words at the Mass, because they are the grateful prayer of the Passover and the Eucharist.

In the Gospel the disciples walk through the grainfields on the sabbath and, being hungry, pluck some heads of grain. The Pharisees object: “Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the sabbath.” Plucking grain was counted as reaping, one of the kinds of work forbidden on the day of rest. Jesus does not abolish the sabbath; he explains it, with three arguments from Scripture. First, David and his men, when hungry, ate the bread of the Presence, which only the priests might eat. Need and mercy come before the letter. Second, the priests in the temple work on the sabbath, offering the sacrifices, and are guiltless: the service of God takes precedence. Then the astonishing sentence: “I tell you, something greater than the temple is here.” He means himself. And then he quotes the prophet Hosea: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.” Mercy is the key that opens the law. The passage ends with a claim of authority: “the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.” The Passover lamb and this Gospel meet in the same truth: the God who passes over his people in mercy has come among them in his Son, who is greater than the temple, greater than the sabbath, and who will be the Lamb.

Today the Church also remembers Our Lady of Mount Carmel, and the day has its own beauty. Carmel is a mountain ridge by the sea in the Holy Land, near present-day Haifa, and its name is bound up with Elijah. On Carmel he called down fire on the altar and challenged the prophets of Baal; and at the end of the drought he “went up to the top of Carmel; there he bowed himself down upon the earth and put his face between his knees,” and sent his servant to look toward the sea. Six times there was nothing. “At the seventh time he said, ‘Look, a little cloud no bigger than a person’s hand is rising out of the sea.’” In a little while the heavens grew black with rain. Christian tradition, and the Carmelites in particular, have seen in that little cloud a sign of Mary, a small and humble figure out of whom came the rain of grace, her Son. In the twelfth century hermits settled on Mount Carmel and built a chapel in honour of Our Lady, and they became the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel, who gave the Church Teresa of Avila, John of the Cross and Thérèse of Lisieux, and whose spirituality also shaped, in Kerala, the religious family of St Kuriakose Elias Chavara. The proper readings for today are the Magnificat, in which Mary sings “the Mighty One has done great things for me, and holy is his name”; the prophet Zechariah's words, “Sing and rejoice, O daughter Zion! For lo, I will come and dwell in your midst”; and the Gospel in which Jesus says that his true family are those who do the will of his Father. Mary is the first and best of them: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). The brown scapular, a small piece of cloth worn on the shoulders, is a sign of belonging to Mary and of the wish to follow her way. A tradition says that Our Lady gave it to the English Carmelite St Simon Stock in 1251, though historians are cautious about the details. The Church teaches that the scapular is a sacramental: a sign that helps us to pray, to trust Mary's care and to imitate her, not a charm. Salvation is always Christ's gift. In July, when Kerala watches the sky for the monsoon, a cloud bringing rain is a good picture of Mary: small, humble, and carrying the water of life.
outline: Opening
Ask: when everything seems dry, what do you do while you wait for the rain?
Point 1 · When I see the blood
The Passover night and the Lamb without blemish.
Point 2 · Mercy and not sacrifice
Something greater than the temple is here; the Lord of the sabbath.
Point 3 · A little cloud
Elijah on Carmel, persistent prayer, and Mary as the small cloud that brings the rain.
Point 4 · Do whatever he tells you
Mary the first disciple, and the scapular as a sign of belonging.
Take-home line
“Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
live: Pray like Elijah (1 Kings 18:42–44)
Choose one need that is still unanswered and bring it to God every day this week, even seven times, without giving up.
Wear Mary's sign (Luke 1:38)
If you have a scapular, wear it today and offer it as a promise to imitate Mary's yes. If not, say a Hail Mary at midday with the words: Mother, teach me to do whatever he tells me.
2027-07-16.prayer: Lord God, on the night of the Passover you saw the blood on the doorposts and passed over your people. Through Christ, our Passover lamb, you have saved us and given us the cup of salvation. Teach us mercy rather than the letter. Lord Jesus, you who are greater than the temple, and lord of the sabbath, receive our thanks. Father, as Elijah looked to the sea and saw a little cloud, so we look to Our Lady of Mount Carmel and see in her the one who bore your Son and who did your will. Through her prayers, make us faithful in waiting, humble in service and generous in mercy. Amen.
altar: At every Mass the priest takes the cup, and we remember Psalm 116: “I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord.” The Mass is the Passover of the New Covenant: Christ, the Lamb without blemish, whose blood saves us, is offered, and we eat the Lamb at his table. “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.” Mary stands close to this mystery: she gave him his body and blood, and at the foot of the cross she stood united with his sacrifice.

2027-07-17.title: Saturday of the Fifteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: That was for the Lord a night of vigil, to bring them out of the land of Egypt
His steadfast love endures for ever
He will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick
2027-07-17.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 15 (Year I). On Saturdays in Ordinary Time, when there is no obligatory memorial, the optional memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary may be kept. Psalm 136 has the same numbering in the Lectionary and the NRSV. The Malayalam month of Karkidakam, the month of the heaviest monsoon rain, begins about now. Liturgical colour: green.
