2027-07-17.verse: A bruised reed he will not break, and a dimly burning wick he will not quench; he will faithfully bring forth justice.
theo: Today's first reading is the departure. After the last night in Egypt the people of Israel march out from Rameses to Succoth, “about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children.” They carry unleavened dough, because they were “driven out of Egypt and could not wait.” The Bible records the exact length of the slavery, “four hundred thirty years,” and says that on the very day the years were completed, “all the companies of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt.” There is one detail that is easy to miss: “A mixed crowd also went up with them.” Not all who left Egypt were descendants of Jacob; there were other slaves and foreigners who saw that the God of Israel was acting and went along with them. From the start the people of God has been bigger than a single family. And then comes the heart of the passage: “That was for the Lord a night of vigil, to bring them out of the land of Egypt. That same night is a vigil to be kept for the Lord by all the Israelites throughout their generations.” The night belonged to the Lord, who kept watch; now the people keep watch in return. For this reason the Jewish people stay up on Passover night to tell the story, and the Church, in the same spirit, keeps the greatest vigil of the year on Holy Saturday night, when the Easter Candle is lit and the deacon sings that this is the night when God led our ancestors out of Egypt and the night when Christ broke the chains of death. The psalm repeats the refrain after every line, “for his steadfast love endures forever,” and names what he did: “brought Israel out from among them … with a strong hand and an outstretched arm,” and “remembered us in our low estate.”

In the Gospel the shadow falls. After the argument about the sabbath, “the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him.” Some of the Pharisees, we must remember, were friends of Jesus, and some warned him of danger; Matthew is speaking of the party that plotted against him. What does Jesus do? “When Jesus became aware of this, he departed.” He does not argue, he does not threaten, and he does not run away in fear. He withdraws, and goes on healing: “Many crowds followed him, and he cured all of them.” And he commands silence: “he ordered them not to make him known.” Matthew explains why by quoting the first Servant Song of Isaiah: “Here is my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved, with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles.” The King is a Servant, and the Servant is gentle: “He will not wrangle or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. He will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick until he brings justice to victory.” A bruised reed is a stem that is cracked and about to snap, and a smoldering wick is a flame about to die; they are pictures of the weak, the discouraged and the sinful, and Jesus does not throw them away: he bends over them to heal. And the passage ends with the word that rings like the “mixed crowd” of Exodus: “in his name the Gentiles will hope.” The people who left Egypt were already a mixed company, and the Servant opens the way for all nations. Both readings are about God's quiet, patient strength: the night watch of the Lord over his people, and the gentle hand over the bruised reed.
outline: Opening
Ask: who keeps vigil for you at night, and for whom do you keep it?
Point 1 · A night of vigil
God watches over his people on the night of the Exodus, and we keep watch with him.
Point 2 · A mixed crowd
The people of God is wider than one family: the foreigners who went out with Israel, and all nations who hope in his name.
Point 3 · Jesus departs
He does not answer a plot with force; he withdraws and heals.
Point 4 · A bruised reed
The Servant who does not break the weak and does not put out the faintest flame.
Take-home line
“A bruised reed he will not break.”
live: Keep a small vigil (Exodus 12:42)

Before sleeping tonight, spend ten minutes in silence, thanking God for watching over your day and asking him to watch over those who are alone tonight: the sick, the night-shift workers, the travellers.
Handle someone gently (Matthew 12:20)
Think of a person who is discouraged or fragile, a bruised reed, and give them an encouraging word or small kindness today. Do not argue with them; strengthen them.
2027-07-17.prayer: Lord God, you kept a night of vigil to bring your people out of slavery, and your steadfast love endures for ever. Watch over us tonight and always, and teach us to keep watch with you in prayer. Lord Jesus, chosen Servant, beloved of the Father, you did not break the bruised reed or quench the smoldering wick: be gentle with our weakness, and make us gentle with the weakness of others. Open your house to the mixed crowd of all nations, and let your name be the hope of every people. Amen.
altar: The Mass is the Church's vigil and the Church's Exodus. We come out of the week to gather around the Lord's table, and what we celebrate is a passage: from slavery to life, from death to resurrection, in Christ. Before Communion we say, “Behold the Lamb of God,” and the Lamb who is gentle with the bruised reed feeds us with himself. Every Mass is a small Easter night.

2027-07-19.title: Monday of the Sixteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Do not be afraid, stand firm, and see the deliverance that the Lord will accomplish for you today
I will sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously
Something greater than Jonah is here
2027-07-19.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 16 (Year I). The first readings of this week follow Israel through the Exodus: the crossing of the sea, the manna, Sinai and the covenant. The responsorial psalm is the Song of Moses (Exodus 15), given here in NRSV numbering (Lectionary 15:1bc–2, 3–4, 5–6 = NRSV 15:1–6); the same song is sung every year at the Easter Vigil. In these monsoon weeks of Kerala, with the rivers full and the roads cut off, the story of a people with the sea in front of them and an army behind them is heard with fresh ears. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-19.verse: But Moses said to the people, “Do not be afraid, stand firm, and see the deliverance that the Lord will accomplish for you today; for the Egyptians whom you see today you shall never see again. The Lord will fight for you, and you have only to keep still.”
theo: Israel has walked out of slavery on the night of the Passover, and for a few days it seems that the story has ended happily. Then comes the news in Pharaoh's palace: the people “had fled,” and “the minds of Pharaoh and his officials were changed.” “What have we done, letting Israel leave our service?” The king takes “six hundred picked chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt,” the most advanced army of the age, and goes after a crowd of ex-slaves, women, children and flocks. The Israelites are camped by the sea, at Pi-hahiroth, in front of Baal-zephon, and when they look back they see the dust of the chariots. “In great fear the Israelites cried out to the Lord.” That is a good prayer. But the next words are not: they turn on Moses. “Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness?” Fear can make a person forget that slavery was slavery; “it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians,” they say. Moses answers with three short commands: “Do not be afraid, stand firm, and see the deliverance that the Lord will accomplish for you today.” Not only the Lord's strength but his timing is announced: “today.” “The Lord will fight for you, and you have only to keep still.” To keep still does not mean to do nothing. Immediately the Lord says to Moses, “Why do you cry out to me? Tell the Israelites to go forward.” There is a time to stand and trust and a time to move; faith is knowing which is which, and trusting that the God who opens a way will also tell us when to step on it. The Lord adds that he will “gain glory for myself over Pharaoh,” so that “the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord.” The reading stops before the sea opens; the psalm gives us the answer in advance, the song Israel sang on the far shore: “I will sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.” Jewish tradition keeps a gentle comment on this song: an old rabbinic story says that when the angels wished to sing as the Egyptians drowned, God said, “My creatures are drowning in the sea, and you would sing?” Even in victory, the God of Israel does not rejoice in the death of any human being. The Church sings this canticle at the Easter Vigil, because the sea is also a picture of baptism, and St Paul says that our ancestors “were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2).

In the Gospel, some scribes and Pharisees say to Jesus, “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.” They have just watched him heal a man who could not see or speak (Matthew 12:22), and they have heard his teaching on the kingdom. A sign for them means a proof they can examine on their own terms. Jesus answers sharply: “An evil and adulterous generation asks for a sign.” In the prophets, “adulterous” is the word used for a people that is unfaithful to the covenant, as a spouse is unfaithful to a spouse; it is not an insult against a race. Jesus is himself a son of Israel, and he speaks as the prophets spoke to their own people, with grief and love. The Church has always taught that what was done in his Passion cannot be charged to all the Jews of that time, still less to the Jews of our own day (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597). The only sign that will be given is “the sign of the prophet Jonah.” “For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster, so for three days and three nights the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth.” Jesus points to his own death and rising, the sign above all signs. He names two figures from outside the circle of those who asked. The people of Nineveh, a pagan city, “repented at the proclamation of Jonah”; the queen of the South, a foreign monarch, “came from the ends of the earth to listen to the wisdom of Solomon.” Each of them recognised God's word when it came in a modest and costly way. “And see, something greater than Jonah is here! … something greater than Solomon is here!” In the first reading Moses stood by the sea and said, “Stand firm”; here the One greater than Moses stands among the people and gives himself as the sign. At the Red Sea God opened a path through the waters of death for Israel; in the Resurrection of Jesus he opens a path through death itself for the whole human race.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did you last feel that you had the sea in front of you and an army behind you?
Point 1 · Do not be afraid, stand firm
Moses' three commands and the God who fights for his people.
Point 2 · Tell them to go forward
Trust and action together: why do you cry out to me?
Point 3 · The sign of Jonah
Jesus' death and Resurrection, the sign that is given; something greater than Jonah and Solomon is here.
Take-home line
“The Lord will fight for you, and you have only to keep still.”
live: Name your sea (Exodus 14:10)
Write down the one difficulty that frightens you most this week, and under it Moses' words: Do not be afraid, stand firm. Pray them each morning.
Go forward (Exodus 14:15)
After praying about that difficulty, take one small, concrete step today: make the call, begin the paperwork, ask for forgiveness.
2027-07-19.prayer: Lord God, you led your people out of Egypt with a mighty hand and made a path for them through the sea. When we are afraid, give us Moses' faith: to stand firm, to keep still before you, and to go forward when you say go. Lord Jesus, you gave us the sign of Jonah, your death and Resurrection; through the waters of baptism lead us out of every slavery into your freedom. Make us people who sing your praise even when the way is not yet open. Amen.
altar: The story of the crossing is read every year at the Easter Vigil. Every baptism is a passage through the sea, and every Eucharist is the meal of those who have been brought through it. Jesus, the sign of Jonah, is present on the altar: the Crucified and Risen One, the gift greater than Jonah and Solomon, who tells us in the sacrament what he told the frightened disciples on the lake: Do not be afraid.

2027-07-20.title: Tuesday of the Sixteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Apollinaris
readings: The Israelites went into the sea on dry ground, the waters forming a wall for them
Sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously
Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother
2027-07-20.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 16 (Year I). The optional memorial of St Apollinaris, first bishop of Ravenna and martyr, may be kept (red if kept). The responsorial psalm is again the Song of Moses, in NRSV numbering (Lectionary 15:8–9, 10 and 12, 17 = NRSV 15:8–10, 12, 17). On Tuesdays many parishes in Kerala keep the devotion to St Anthony; today the Church is invited to think of the family that the Lord gathers through water and word. Liturgical colour: green (red if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-20.verse: The Israelites went into the sea on dry ground, the waters forming a wall for them on their right and on their left.
theo: The night of the sea is the centre of the whole Old Testament, and today's reading tells it slowly. “Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. The Lord drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night, and turned the sea into dry land; and the waters were divided.” Notice that the work of the night is God's, and that Moses' part is the stretched-out hand. The Israelites walk into the sea “on dry ground,” the waters forming a wall on the right and on the left. The Egyptians follow. At “the morning watch,” the last part of the night, the Lord “in the pillar of fire and cloud looked down upon the Egyptian army, and threw the Egyptian army into panic.” The pillar that was a light for Israel is a terror for the pursuers. The wheels clog, and the Egyptians themselves cry: “Let us flee from the Israelites, for the Lord is fighting for them against Egypt.” Moses stretches out his hand again, and at dawn the sea returns. The Bible makes no triumph out of the scene: it says simply, “not one of them remained,” and then describes the Israelites seeing the dead on the shore. After this the Bible tells us how Israel's faith began: “Israel saw the great work that the Lord did against the Egyptians. So the people feared the Lord and believed in the Lord and in his servant Moses.” Faith in Israel does not begin with an idea; it begins with a rescue. Then they sing. The psalm shows the singing in Hebrew poetry: “At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up, the floods stood up in a heap.” The poet speaks of God with the picture of breath and wind, because the image of a mighty breath matches the east wind of the night. And the song looks past the sea to the destination: God brought his people in and “planted them on the mountain of your own possession, the place, O Lord, that you made your abode.” The sea is not the goal; the sanctuary is. From earliest times Christians have read this night as a picture of baptism: St Paul says that our ancestors “were all under the cloud and all passed through the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1), and the great Easter hymn, the Exsultet, says to God, “This is the night when once you led our forebears, Israel's children, from slavery in Egypt, and made them pass dry-shod through the Red Sea.”

In the Gospel, Jesus is teaching the crowds when “his mother and his brothers” arrive and stand outside, “wanting to speak to him.” Someone passes on the message. Jesus asks, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” and stretches out his hand toward his disciples: “Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.” This is not a rejection of his family. In the Jewish world, a teacher's family could be expected to look after him, and Jesus is lifting the question to a higher level: the new family of God, whose bond is not blood but obedience to the Father. The Church has always understood this verse in the light of what Luke tells us about Mary. At the Annunciation she said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word,” and Elizabeth called her blessed because she believed (Luke 1:38, 45). When a woman in the crowd praised the womb that bore Jesus, he answered, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!” (Luke 11:28), and no one has heard and obeyed more perfectly than his Mother. The Second Vatican Council teaches that in the course of her Son's preaching Mary “received the words whereby in extolling a kingdom beyond the calculations and bonds of flesh and blood, he declared blessed those who heard and kept the word of God, as she was faithfully doing” (Lumen Gentium 58). So Jesus' word does not diminish Mary; it points to the reason for her greatness. The “brothers” mentioned here are, according to the Church's constant understanding and the Semitic way of speaking, his close relatives; the Catechism recalls that James and Joseph, called his brothers, are the sons of another Mary, a disciple of Christ (Catechism 500), and the Church holds Mary ever-virgin. The Gospel opens a door to all of us: whoever does the Father's will belongs to Jesus' own household. Today the Church also remembers St Apollinaris, traditionally the first bishop of Ravenna in Italy and a disciple of St Peter, who is said to have been sent from Rome to Ravenna and to have suffered many tortures for the faith before dying as a martyr in the second century. Historians cannot prove all the details, but his cult in Ravenna is very ancient, and in the great basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe a sixth-century mosaic shows him in the apse, in his bishop's vestments, with his arms raised in prayer in the middle of a green meadow, with twelve sheep looking up at him. He is the good shepherd's image of the family that the Lord gathers from the waters: sheep who hear their shepherd's voice.
outline: Opening
Ask: who are the people who are truly your family in faith, not only in blood?
Point 1 · Through the sea on dry ground
The night of the sea: God's work and Moses' outstretched hand.
Point 2 · They believed in the Lord
Faith born of a rescue; the sea as a picture of baptism.
Point 3 · My brother and sister and mother
The new family gathered by the Father's will, and Mary, the first to hear and obey.
Point 4 · St Apollinaris, shepherd of Ravenna
A bishop who watched over his flock, even at the cost of his life.
Take-home line
“Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”
live: Remember your baptism (Exodus 14:22)
Today, when you touch holy water at church or at home, make the sign of the cross slowly and say: Lord, you brought me through the water; I belong to you.
Do the Father's will (Matthew 12:50)
Choose one concrete thing you know the Father asks of you in your household or parish, a visit, a debt of kindness, a duty put off, and do it today.
saints: St Apollinaris of Ravenna (second century, according to tradition)

According to tradition a disciple of St Peter, sent to Ravenna as its first bishop, who evangelised the region, suffered persecution and several times was driven out, and died as a martyr. The details come from a later Life and cannot all be verified; what is certain is that his veneration in Ravenna is very ancient. St Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna in the fifth century, preached in his honour. His relics rest in the basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe, outside Ravenna, consecrated in 549. Patron of Ravenna.
2027-07-20.prayer: God of our fathers, you brought Israel through the sea on dry ground and made them your own people. Bring us through the waters of baptism into your family, and let us be those who hear your word and do it. Lord Jesus, you call us your brothers and sisters and your mother: make us faithful to the Father's will, as the Blessed Virgin Mary was faithful. Through the prayers of St Apollinaris, shepherd and martyr, give your Church shepherds who watch over their flocks with love, and keep us in your sheepfold. Amen.
altar: At the beginning of Mass, and when we enter the church, we are reminded of our baptism by the holy water. The Eucharist is the table of the family that was born in that water: those who hear the word of God and do it, with Mary and all the saints. Before Communion we say Our Father together, because in Christ we have become brothers and sisters of one another and sons and daughters of the same Father.

2027-07-21.title: Wednesday of the Sixteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Lawrence of Brindisi
readings: I am going to rain bread from heaven for you
The Lord gave them bread from heaven
Other seeds fell on good soil and brought forth grain
2027-07-21.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 16 (Year I). The optional memorial of St Lawrence of Brindisi, priest and doctor of the Church, may be kept. His day of death, 22 July, is now the feast of St Mary Magdalene, so his memorial is placed one day earlier. Psalm 78 has the same verse numbers in the Lectionary and the NRSV. Next Sunday the Gospel turns to John 6, the bread from heaven, and the first reading today prepares for it. The month of Karkidakam has just begun in Kerala. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-21.verse: Then the Lord said to Moses, “I am going to rain bread from heaven for you, and each day the people shall go out and gather enough for that day.
theo: A month after leaving Egypt, in the wilderness of Sin, the whole community of Israel grumbles against Moses and Aaron. The reading is honest about hunger: it is the same hunger we feel when food is short and the future is uncertain. But look at what the hunger has done to their memory. “If only we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the fleshpots and ate our fill of bread; for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger.” The slave camp has become a restaurant. Hunger has a way of making the old chains look like comfort. The Lord does not answer with a rebuke; he answers with a promise: “I am going to rain bread from heaven for you, and each day the people shall go out and gather enough for that day. In that way I will test them, whether they will follow my instruction or not.” Daily bread, and no more than daily: the test is whether Israel can live from one day's gift to the next without hoarding and without fear. On the sixth day they will gather twice as much, so that the seventh day can be a day of rest (verse 5), the first hint of the Sabbath before the Law is given at Sinai. The reading skips Moses' words to the people, that their complaint is really against the Lord, and goes straight to the moment when Aaron calls them to “draw near to the Lord, for he has heard your complaining,” and “the glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud.” That evening quails cover the camp; in the morning a layer of dew lifts and leaves “a fine flaky substance, as fine as frost on the ground.” The Israelites ask “What is it?”; in Hebrew man hu, which is why the bread was called manna. Moses answers: “It is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat.” The manna is not earned and not understood; it is received. The psalm remembers both sides of the story: “Can God spread a table in the wilderness?” was the people's doubtful question, and the answer was that he “rained down on them manna to eat, and gave them the grain of heaven. Mortals ate of the bread of angels; he sent them food in abundance.” Jesus will teach us to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11). In the old Kerala memory, Karkidakam, the month that has just begun, was the lean month, when the granary was low and the new harvest not yet ripe; many a family has known what a day's bread means.

In the Gospel Jesus has just met misunderstanding in the house (Matthew 12). Now “that same day” he goes out and sits beside the sea; the crowds are so great that he gets into a boat, and the boat becomes his pulpit and the shore his church. He begins to teach “many things in parables,” the third great discourse of Matthew's Gospel, which contains seven parables. The first is the Sower. In Galilee, a farmer scattered the seed by hand and ploughed it in afterwards, so some seed would naturally fall on the footpath that crossed the field, on the thin soil over the limestone, and among the thorn roots. The picture is not of a careless sower but a generous one: seed is thrown with open hands because the harvest depends on the soil as well as the sower. Three kinds of soil fail, each for a different reason: the path where birds eat the seed, the rock where the sun scorches the shoot, the thorns that choke it. The fourth soil is good, and brings forth “grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.” A hundredfold was a blessing of the patriarchs: Isaac reaped “in the same year a hundredfold” (Genesis 26:12). The point of this parable is both warning and hope: the word of God will be heard in many different hearts, and some will bear great fruit. Jesus closes with a call: “Let anyone with ears listen!” The seed is, as Jesus will explain, “the word of God” (Luke 8:11). Let us hold the two readings together. The manna was bread from heaven for the body on the journey; the word is bread from heaven for the heart. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church has always venerated the Scriptures as she venerates the Body of the Lord, receiving the bread of life from the table of the word of God and of the Body of Christ (Dei Verbum 21). Today the Church remembers St Lawrence of Brindisi, a Capuchin friar of the sixteenth century, one of the great preachers of the Church, who handed the bread of the word to the hungry in many countries and languages. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1959 and is called the Apostolic Doctor.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did you last feel real hunger, and what did it do to your memory of the past?
Point 1 · Enough for that day
The manna and the test of daily trust: give us this day our daily bread.
Point 2 · What is it?
The bread that is received, not earned; the road from manna to the bread of life.
Point 3 · A sower went out to sow
The generous Sower, four soils, and the good soil that bears fruit.
Point 4 · St Lawrence of Brindisi, preacher of the word
A Capuchin who gave the bread of the word to princes, soldiers and the poor.
Take-home line
“Let anyone with ears listen!”
live: Receive your daily bread (Exodus 16:4)
Before each meal today, say the grace slowly and name one person who has no food today. Give something to the parish food fund or the poor.
Prepare the soil (Matthew 13:8)
Spend ten minutes today with the Gospel of the day, read slowly. Ask the Lord to make your heart good soil, and note one word that stays with you.
saints: St Lawrence of Brindisi (1559–1619)

Born Giulio Cesare Russo at Brindisi in southern Italy on 22 July 1559; entered the Capuchin Order at sixteen, studied in Padua and Venice, and was ordained priest in 1582. He was remarkable for his gift of languages: besides Latin and Italian he knew Hebrew, Greek, German, French, Spanish and others, and it is said that his knowledge of Hebrew and of the Bible astonished Jewish scholars. He preached throughout Italy and in Germany and Bohemia, helped to found Capuchin houses north of the Alps, and served his order as minister general. In 1601 he went as chaplain with the imperial army that defended Hungary against the Ottoman advance and, with a crucifix in his hand, rode among the soldiers. He also served the Church as a diplomat for peace between princes. He died at Lisbon on 22 July 1619, on his sixtieth birthday. Canonised in 1881; declared a Doctor of the Church by Pope St John XXIII in 1959. Among his writings are many sermons and a collection of sermons on the Blessed Virgin, the Mariale. He taught in substance that the word of God is a light for the mind and a fire for the will, so that we may know and love God, and that for the one who lives by love it is bread and water.
2027-07-21.prayer: God of mercy, you rained bread from heaven on your people in the wilderness and you sow your word in our hearts. Teach us to receive each day's bread with thanks, without fear and without greed. Lord Jesus, the Sower who goes out to sow, make our hearts good soil: take the stones from them, pull out the thorns, and let your word bear fruit thirty, sixty and a hundredfold. Through the prayers of St Lawrence of Brindisi, who preached your word with courage and love, make us hearers and doers of what we hear. Give us this day our daily bread, and the bread of life that is yourself. Amen.
altar: At Mass the Church sets two tables. First comes the table of the word, where the Sower scatters his seed in the readings and the homily; then the table of the Eucharist, where the bread from heaven is given. The manna in the desert was a sign, and Jesus will say in Capernaum, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). The faithful receive Christ's Body and Blood in Holy Communion, and the word they have heard is meant to bear fruit in their lives.

2027-07-22.title: Saint Mary Magdalene
readings: I sought him whom my soul loves; I held him and would not let him go
My soul is thirsting for you, O Lord my God
Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”
2027-07-22.alt: Feast. Gloria; no Creed. Since 2016, by a decree of the Congregation for Divine Worship (Apostolorum Apostola, 3 June 2016, issued at the wish of Pope Francis), the memorial of St Mary Magdalene has the rank of a feast, like the feasts of the apostles, because she was the first witness of the Resurrection and the first to announce it. The Lectionary offers 2 Corinthians 5:14–17 (“the love of Christ urges us on … everything has become new”) as an alternative to the Song of Songs; the weekday readings (Exodus 19:1–2, 9–11, 16–20b; Matthew 13:10–17) are not used today. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-07-22.verse: Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”; and she told them that he had said these things to her.
theo: The Church gives us today two of the most loving texts in the Bible. In the first, from the Song of Songs, a woman is awake in the night, searching for the one she loves. “Upon my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not; I called him, but he gave no answer.” She does not stay in bed with her longing; she says, “I will rise now and go about the city, in the streets and in the squares; I will seek him whom my soul loves.” The watchmen on their rounds find her, and she asks them at once, “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” Then, “Scarcely had I passed them, when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go.” Since early times the Church has read this poem as the story of God and the human soul, and the Christian tradition has heard in it the voice of Mary Magdalene at the tomb. The third-century writer Hippolytus of Rome, in one of the oldest Christian commentaries on the Song of Songs, already compares the women who went to the tomb with the bride who seeks her beloved. The setting matches: the Song's bride seeks him at night in a garden city; John says that Mary came “while it was still dark,” and that the tomb was in a garden (John 19:41). The psalm is the prayer of the same seeker: “O God, you are my God, I seek you, my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you, as in a dry and weary land where there is no water.” And it knows the answer: “Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you.” If the alternative reading is used, St Paul gives us the other side of the same love: “The love of Christ urges us on,” and “if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!” (2 Corinthians 5:14, 17). Mary of Magdala is the first person who sees what that new creation looks like.

Magdala was a fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, and excavations there have uncovered a synagogue of the time of Jesus. Mary of Magdala is named in all four Gospels. Luke tells us that among the women who travelled with Jesus and supported him and the Twelve “out of their resources” was “Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out” (Luke 8:2). The Gospels say nothing more about the nature of her illness. She remained with Jesus to the end: she stands near the cross with his mother (John 19:25), she sees where he is laid (Mark 15:47), and on Sunday morning she comes back. Here we need to be careful. A tradition in the Western Church, which became widespread after a homily of Pope St Gregory the Great in the sixth century, joined her with the unnamed sinful woman who anointed Jesus' feet in Luke 7:36–50 and also with Mary of Bethany, the sister of Martha. The Gospels never say so. Today the Church keeps these figures distinct, and reads on this feast only what Scripture tells us about Mary of Magdala: a woman healed by Jesus, a faithful disciple, a witness of the cross and the empty tomb, and the first to see the risen Lord. John's account is among the most moving in the Gospels. “Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark,” she sees that the stone has been removed, and runs to Simon Peter and the beloved disciple: “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.” The reading omits the visit of Peter and John to the tomb. The two men see the burial cloths and go home. “But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb.” She bends down and sees two angels in white, who ask, “Woman, why are you weeping?” and she says, “They have taken away my Lord”: it is my Lord, not only the Lord. Then she turns round and sees Jesus standing there but does not recognise him, taking him for the gardener, and says to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.” Her love will carry the body of Jesus herself if she must. And then the whole scene turns on one word: “Jesus said to her, ‘Mary!’” The Good Shepherd “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3). “She turned and said to him in Hebrew, ‘Rabbouni!’ (which means Teacher).” She turned a second time: the first was her body, the second her heart. It is the moment of faith.

Then Jesus says something strange: “Do not hold on to me, because I have not yet ascended to the Father.” The Greek is a command to stop clinging, as if she were taking hold of him to keep him as before. Jesus is not rejecting her; he is telling her that the old way of being with him is over and a new one begins. He will not be held in the garden; he will be with his disciples always through the Spirit, in the Church. He sends her: “But go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’” For the first time he calls the disciples his brothers, and he gives them, through her, the whole meaning of Easter: his Father is now our Father. Mary Magdalene “went and announced to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord.’” In these few words the Church's whole message is already present, and she is the first to say it. That is why the Church, since the early centuries, has called her the “apostle of the apostles”: apostle means “one who is sent,” and the risen Lord sent her to the apostles. St Thomas Aquinas, commenting on this passage, uses exactly this title. The Catechism puts it plainly: Mary Magdalene and the holy women “were the first to encounter the Risen One. Thus the women were the first messengers of Christ's Resurrection for the apostles themselves” (Catechism 641). The apostles, at first, did not believe the women's words (Luke 24:11), as people sometimes do not believe the testimony of those who are overlooked; but the Church, which rests on the testimony of Peter and the Twelve, rests also on this first testimony. In 2016 the Church raised her day to the rank of a feast, so that all the faithful, and women in particular, may remember the place of this witness. This is also a day for those who weep. In the monsoon weeks, when for days together the sky itself seems to weep, we remember that Mary's tears were seen by someone: the Lord was already there, and he was calling her by name.
conn: Magdala.

A town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, near Tiberias. Mary is called “Magdalene,” of Magdala, to distinguish her from the other Marys of the Gospels. Excavations have found a first-century synagogue there.
Seven demons.
Luke 8:2 and Mark 16:9. Seven is the biblical number of fullness; the Gospels do not describe her illness further. Nothing in the Gospel text says that she was a sinner of any particular kind.
Not named as the sinful woman of Luke 7.

A Western tradition from the sixth century identified Mary Magdalene with the unnamed sinful woman of Luke 7:36–50 and with Mary of Bethany. The Gospels do not say so, and the Church today keeps them distinct. The Roman Mass of this day now reads John 20.
“While it was still dark.”
John often uses darkness as a sign of unbelief and night (John 3:2; 13:30); here the first light of faith appears while it is still night.
“We do not know.”
Mary says “we,” which fits the Synoptic accounts in which several women go to the tomb (Mark 16:1; Luke 24:10). She speaks for the group.
“My Lord.”
Mary calls Jesus “my Lord” twice (verses 2 and 13); the title grows from “the Lord” to a personal bond.
“Rabbouni.”
An Aramaic form of “Rabbi,” “my teacher,” more affectionate. John gives it in Aramaic (“in Hebrew,” as he calls it) and translates it.
“Do not hold on to me.”
In Greek, a present command: stop clinging. In the Latin tradition, noli me tangere. The risen Jesus is the same and yet transformed; he cannot be possessed but only received in faith.
“My brothers.”
The first time that Jesus calls the disciples his brothers; in the Resurrection they become sons in the Son, with the same Father and God.
“Apostle of the apostles.”
A title in Latin, apostola apostolorum, that goes back to the early centuries. It means that she was sent to those who would be sent. It does not make her one of the Twelve.
altar: In the Mass the risen Lord makes himself present to us under the signs of bread and wine, and we do not cling to him as Mary might have; we receive him in faith, and are sent: “Go in peace, glorifying the Lord by your life.” Every Communion is a Magdalene moment: he calls us by name, and then sends us to tell what we have received. After the consecration we say: “We proclaim your Death, O Lord, and profess your Resurrection until you come again.” The first to proclaim the Resurrection was a woman at a tomb.

On Easter Sunday the Church sings the ancient Sequence, which even puts the question to Mary herself: “Tell us, Mary, what did you see on the way?” and she answers, “The tomb of the living Christ and the glory of the risen one.” Today the Church lets her answer be heard again.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did you last weep and find that someone you did not recognise was standing beside you?
Point 1 · Seeking in the dark
The Song of Songs, the garden, and a love that rises and goes out to search.
Point 2 · Why are you weeping?
Mary stays at the tomb when the others go home; her love will carry the body.
Point 3 · Mary!
The Shepherd calls her by name; she turns, and recognises him.
Point 4 · Go to my brothers
Do not cling, but go: Mary is sent as the first witness and the apostle of the apostles.
Closing image
A woman running through the dawn with the news: I have seen the Lord.
Take-home line
“I have seen the Lord.”
live: Stay when others go (John 20:11)
Choose one person who is grieving or one situation that others have given up on, and stay with them in prayer and presence this week.
Listen for your name (John 20:16)
Take five minutes of silence today and read John 20:11–18 slowly, hearing the Lord call you by name. Then write one sentence about what you have heard.
Announce it (John 20:18)
Say aloud to someone this week, in your own words, what the risen Lord has done in your life.
Do not cling (John 20:17)
Name one thing from the past that you are holding on to, a grievance or a lost time, and ask the Lord for the grace to let it go and go forward.
fathers: St Augustine (Sermon 232, in substance)

In the beginning a woman brought death to the man, and now a woman announces life to the men. The Lord let a woman be the first herald of the Resurrection, to heal by faith what had been wounded by disobedience.
St Hippolytus of Rome (Commentary on the Song of Songs, in substance)
Christ appeared first to the women, so that they might be apostles to the apostles, and so that the women who had been made the first to weep might be the first to rejoice and tell the good news.
St Thomas Aquinas (Commentary on John 20, in substance)

Mary Magdalene was given the office of announcing the Resurrection to the apostles: so she is called the apostle of the apostles, because she announced to the apostles what they would announce to the whole world.
magis: Catechism 641
Mary Magdalene and the holy women were the first to encounter the Risen One, and so the first messengers of the Resurrection to the apostles themselves.
Catechism 642–644
The apostles' witness, and their first disbelief: the Resurrection is a fact grounded on testimony before it is a feeling.
St John Paul II, Mulieris Dignitatem 16
Women were the first witnesses of the Resurrection, and so “apostles to the apostles.”
Decree Apostolorum Apostola (2016)
The decree that raised the memorial of St Mary Magdalene to a feast, with a new Preface that calls her the “apostle of the apostles.”
Catechism 640
The empty tomb is the first sign of the Resurrection: the first witnesses found it empty, and Peter, the beloved disciple and the women went from it to faith.
saints: St Mary Magdalene (first century)

Mary of Magdala, healed by Jesus of seven demons, follows him with the women who supported his ministry, stands near the cross, and is the first witness of the Resurrection (John 20). The Eastern Churches call her “equal to the apostles.” Later traditions about her life, whether in Ephesus, as the East tells, or in southern France, as the Western legend tells, cannot be verified. Her day, 22 July, has been kept in the Roman Calendar for many centuries; it was raised to a feast in 2016.
This week

23 Jul: St Bridget of Sweden, a mother and widow who founded an order (optional memorial). 24 Jul: St Sharbel Makhluf, the Lebanese hermit-priest (optional memorial). 25 Jul: the Seventeenth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
2027-07-22.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you called Mary of Magdala by her name and sent her to announce your Resurrection to the apostles. Make us seekers like her, who rise before dawn, do not stop weeping before the empty tomb, and know your voice when you call us by name. Teach us not to cling to what is past, but to go to our brothers and sisters and say: I have seen the Lord. Through the prayers of St Mary Magdalene, the apostle of the apostles, give your Church the faith that proclaims you without fear, and bring us all to the joy of your presence, where you live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.

2027-07-23.title: Friday of the Sixteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Bridget of Sweden
readings: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery
Lord, you have the words of everlasting life
The seed sown on good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it
2027-07-23.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 16 (Year I). The optional memorial of St Bridget of Sweden, religious, may be kept (white if kept). The psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering (Lectionary 19:8, 9, 10, 11 = NRSV 19:7, 8, 9, 10). Today the first reading is the Ten Commandments, the Decalogue, which the Catholic Church numbers as in the Catechism (CCC 2052–2557). In the month of Karkidakam many Hindu homes in Kerala read a portion of the Ramayana each day; it is a good month to give the Word of God its daily hour. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-23.verse: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other gods before me.
theo: Today's first reading is the centre of the Old Testament: “Then God spoke all these words.” They are given at Sinai, three months after the Exodus, to a people just brought out of slavery. Before any commandment comes a name and a deed: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” The law is not given to slaves to bind them again, but to keep a liberated people in their liberty. In Hebrew the ten are called the Ten Words, and the Catechism teaches that they are a path of life, the “ten words” by which God says to his people what love of God and of neighbour require (Catechism 2056–2057). The Catholic tradition counts them in this way: the first three are about God (no other gods and no idols; the name of the Lord not misused; the sabbath kept holy), and the last seven about our neighbour (father and mother; no murder; no adultery; no theft; no false witness; no coveting of the neighbour's wife; no coveting of the neighbour's goods). The first word is stern because it protects what love is: “for I the Lord your God am a jealous God.” A jealous God is a God whose love wants all of us, as a faithful spouse wants a faithful spouse. The sabbath is not a rule that makes life harder but a gift: a day of rest, in imitation of the Creator, for family, servants, the foreigner and even the cattle. “Honor your father and your mother” is the first commandment with a promise attached, and the one that holds family and society together. The last words go to the heart: “You shall not covet.” The law reaches inside the heart where every sin begins. For Christians, the sabbath rest is fulfilled on the Lord's Day, the day of the Resurrection (Catechism 2174–2176), and Jesus has told us that he came “not to abolish but to fulfill” the law (Matthew 5:17) and that all of it hangs on the love of God and of neighbour (Matthew 22:37–40). The psalm is the sung answer of a people who delight in this gift: “The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul; the decrees of the Lord are sure, making wise the simple … More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey, and drippings of the honeycomb.” We honour the Jewish people, who first received these words and who still cherish the Torah as their delight.

In the Gospel the disciples have heard Jesus tell the parable of the sower, and now he explains it. It is one of only two parables in Matthew's thirteenth chapter that Jesus explains in detail (the other is the parable of the weeds), and he explains it to those who ask. “When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what is sown in the heart; this is what was sown on the path.” The word is heard but never allowed inside. “As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy; yet such a person has no root, but endures only for a while, and when trouble or persecution arises on account of the word, that person immediately falls away.” This is the enthusiast whose joy is shallow. “As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the lure of wealth choke the word, and it yields nothing.” This is the busy person, caught up in worries and wanting more. “But as for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it, who indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty.” In Matthew to “understand” is not only to follow an argument; it is to take the word to heart and put it into practice. Put the two readings side by side. At Sinai God gives the law on tablets of stone; the prophets promised that one day he would do something more: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). The parable of the sower shows how this happens: the word is a seed that must be received into the soil of the heart, where it takes root and bears fruit. The law of the Lord, as Psalm 19 says, revives the soul only when it is received. Today the Church remembers St Bridget of Sweden, a medieval noblewoman, wife and mother of eight children, a widow, a mystic and the founder of an order. Her life shows what good soil looks like: a heart in which the word of God took root, and in which the cares of the court did not choke it. The Church calls her one of the patron saints of Europe.
outline: Opening
Ask: if someone asked you for the ten commandments by heart, how many could you give? And which one does your heart find hardest?
Point 1 · The gift before the command
I am the Lord your God, who brought you out: law as a path of freedom.
Point 2 · Sweeter than honey
The psalm of those who delight in the law; love of God and neighbour as its fulfilment.
Point 3 · The seed in the heart
The path, the rock, the thorns and the good soil; the law written on the heart.
Point 4 · St Bridget of Sweden
A mother, widow and mystic who gave good soil to the word.
Take-home line
“The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul.”
live: Learn the ten (Exodus 20:1–17)
Write the Ten Commandments on a sheet this week, and place a small cross beside the one you most need the Lord's help with. Say it in your evening prayer.
Give the word its hour (Matthew 13:23)
Set aside a fixed time each day this week, even ten minutes, for reading the Gospel of the day; put the phone away while you read.
saints: St Bridget of Sweden (c. 1303–1373)

Born c. 1303 in Uppland, Sweden, of a noble family; married at about thirteen to Ulf Gudmarsson and the mother of eight children, among them St Catherine of Vadstena. She served at the court of King Magnus. After Ulf's death in 1344 she gave herself to prayer and penance and began to receive visions that she wrote down (the Revelations); the Church does not oblige anyone to believe private revelations (Catechism 67). She founded the Order of the Most Holy Saviour (the Bridgettines) at Vadstena, approved by Pope Urban V in 1370. From 1349 she lived in Rome, where she worked and prayed for the return of the Pope from Avignon, cared for the poor and pilgrims, and made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land in 1372. She died in Rome on 23 July 1373 and was canonised in 1391. In 1999 Pope St John Paul II named her, with St Catherine of Siena and St Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (Edith Stein), a co-patron of Europe. Her order was renewed in the twentieth century by St Elizabeth Hesselblad, canonised in 2016.
2027-07-23.prayer: Lord our God, you gave your people the ten words on Mount Sinai and wrote your law in the hearts of those who love you. Make us hear your word and understand it; take the stones out of our hearts and cut away the thorns, so that your word may take root in us and bear fruit thirty, sixty and a hundredfold. Through the prayers of St Bridget of Sweden, mother, widow and servant of your word, make us faithful to your commandments, glad in your law and generous to the poor. Lord Jesus, who fulfilled the law by love, write your law on our hearts, and let us love you with all our heart and our neighbour as ourselves. Amen.
altar: At the beginning of Mass we say the Lord, have mercy, because we know that we have not always kept the commandments. At the Gospel we make a small sign of the cross on forehead, lips and heart, so that the word may be in our minds, on our lips and in our hearts. And in Communion the One who fulfilled the law by love gives himself to us, to write the commandments of love in us. St Bridget meditated daily on the Passion of Christ.

2027-07-24.title: Saturday of the Sixteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Sharbel Makhluf
readings: See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you
To the upright I will show the saving power of God
Let both of them grow together until the harvest
2027-07-24.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 16 (Year I). The optional memorial of St Sharbel (Charbel) Makhluf, a Lebanese Maronite monk, priest and hermit, may be kept (white if kept), or the optional Saturday memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The Syro-Malankara Church of Kerala also remembers St Sharbel today, in the Panchangam of the Church. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering; Psalm 50 has the same verse numbers in the Lectionary. Tomorrow, the Seventeenth Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year B), the Gospel turns to John 6, the bread of life. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-24.verse: Then he took the book of the covenant, and read it in the hearing of the people; and they said, “All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.” Moses took the blood and dashed it on the people, and said, “See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you in accordance with all these words.”
theo: Today's first reading ends the long scene of the giving of the law at Sinai with the sealing of the covenant, and it is one of the great liturgies of the Old Testament. Moses has received the words and the ordinances of the Lord, and he comes down to tell the people everything. They answer “with one voice”: “All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do.” Moses does not let the words go with the wind: he “wrote down all the words of the Lord.” Early the next morning he builds an altar at the foot of the mountain, and around it he sets up twelve pillars, “corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel.” The altar is God's side of the covenant, the pillars are the people's; between them is the sacrifice. Young men offer burnt offerings and “offerings of well-being,” meals shared in joy with God. Then comes the central action. Moses takes the blood of the sacrifice, which in the Old Testament stands for life, and divides it: half is put in basins; half is dashed against the altar. He reads the “book of the covenant” in the hearing of the people, who answer again, “All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.” In Hebrew, na'aseh ve-nishma: we will do, and we will hear. And then Moses takes the blood in the basins and “dashed it on the people, and said, ‘See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you in accordance with all these words.’” The same blood touches the altar and the people: God and Israel are bound together in one life. The Letter to the Hebrews will remember this moment (Hebrews 9:18–20), and Jesus will use almost the same words at the Last Supper: “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (Mark 14:24). The Christian Church sees in Sinai a shadow of what Christ does at the Eucharist: the new covenant sealed in his blood, shared at the table. The psalm takes up the same theme from the other side. God summons the earth: “Gather to me my faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice!” and he teaches what pleases him: “Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and pay your vows to the Most High. Call on me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.” The Greek word for thanksgiving is eucharistia. The sacrifice that God most loves is a grateful heart.

In the Gospel Jesus gives another parable of the kingdom, found only in Matthew: the wheat and the weeds. A householder sows good seed in his field; “while everybody was asleep, an enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and then went away.” The weed meant here, probably the bearded darnel, looks very like wheat until the ears appear, when the difference is clear. “So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared as well.” The slaves ask, with amazement, “Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? Where, then, did these weeds come from?” The householder answers, “An enemy has done this.” Evil in the world and in the Church is not God's doing; there is an enemy. And the slaves, quite naturally, ask, “Then do you want us to go and gather them?” The householder says, “No; for in gathering the weeds you would uproot the wheat along with them. Let both of them grow together until the harvest.” Only at harvest will the reapers separate them, and the wheat be gathered “into my barn.” Jesus will explain the parable in a few days (Matthew 13:36–43). Meanwhile the point is plain: patience. The Church on earth is a field where good and bad grow together, and it is not our work to decide, before the time, who is wheat and who is weed. Often we cannot tell: the harsh person may be the one who most needs mercy, and a seeming saint may be a weed. The Catechism teaches that the Church is “at once holy and always in need of being purified” (Catechism 827, quoting Lumen Gentium 8). This is not an excuse for indifference to evil: the householder knows there is an enemy, and the harvest will come. But it is a strong teaching on God's patience, which gives everyone time to repent: “Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, says the Lord God, and not rather that they should turn from their ways and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23). Today the Church remembers one who quietly allowed God to cultivate him: St Sharbel Makhluf, a Lebanese Maronite monk and hermit of the nineteenth century, who spent his last twenty-three years in a mountain hermitage, hidden and silent, and who now draws pilgrims of all faiths to his tomb at Annaya.
outline: Opening
Ask: when you promise God something at Mass, how much of it do you actually do the next day?
Point 1 · We will do
Israel's two answers at Sinai; the people who hear and do.
Point 2 · The blood of the covenant
Moses' altar, the sprinkled blood, and the Eucharist of the new covenant.
Point 3 · Let both grow together
The enemy sows weeds; the householder's patience and the harvest.
Point 4 · St Sharbel, hidden in prayer
A Maronite monk who lived in silence and obedience, and the fruit of a hidden life.
Take-home line
“See the blood of the covenant.”
live: Do what you have heard (Exodus 24:7)
After the readings of tomorrow's Sunday Mass, choose one thing you will do in the week that follows, and tell one person about it.
Be patient with the weeds (Matthew 13:29)
Pray today by name for one person who annoys or troubles you, and ask God to give both of you time to grow. Do not give up on the good that is in them.
Keep a little silence (Matthew 6:6)
Spend at least ten minutes in silence today, with no phone, radio or conversation, speaking only to your Father who is in secret.
saints: St Sharbel Makhluf (1828–1898)

Born Youssef Antoun Makhlouf on 8 May 1828 in Bekaa Kafra, a mountain village in northern Lebanon, to a poor family; his father died when he was three. As a young man he left home to join the Lebanese Maronite Order, took the name Sharbel (Charbel), a name of an early martyr of Syria, and was ordained priest in 1859. He lived for sixteen years in the monastery of St Maron at Annaya, and from 1875 until his death in a hermitage nearby, in obedience to his superiors, in silence, poverty and prayer, with deep devotion to the Eucharist and to Our Lady. While celebrating the Divine Liturgy on 16 December 1898 he suffered a stroke; he died on 24 December 1898. Soon after his death a light was reported at his tomb, and many healings have been reported there among Christians and Muslims alike. Beatified in 1965 at the close of the Second Vatican Council, and canonised in 1977, both by Pope Paul VI. The Maronite Church is one of the Eastern Catholic Churches in communion with Rome; its liturgy belongs to the ancient Syriac tradition of Antioch, which still uses Syriac, a later form of Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke. Optional memorial in the Roman Calendar on 24 July.
2027-07-24.prayer: God of the covenant, you bound yourself to your people at Sinai by the sprinkled blood, and in your Son you sealed a new and everlasting covenant. Make us a people who say, We will do, and then do what we say. Lord Jesus, you teach us patience with the wheat and the weeds; give us the patience of the householder and the mercy of the Father who wills that all should come to repentance. Through the prayers of St Sharbel, who sought you in silence and hidden prayer, teach us to seek you in secret and to give you a sacrifice of thanksgiving. Keep Lebanon and all the Middle East in your peace. Amen.
altar: At every Mass the priest takes the cup and says the words of Jesus: this is the chalice of my blood, the blood of the new and eternal covenant, which will be poured out for you and for many. Moses sprinkled blood on the people; in the Eucharist Christ gives us his own blood to drink, so that his life flows in us. The Church calls this sacrifice a Eucharist, a thanksgiving, because it is the thanksgiving for all that the Lord has done. St Sharbel, a hermit, never lived without the Eucharist: he said that the Mass was the most important hour of his day, and he is said to have prepared for it, and to have given thanks after it, for long hours.

2027-07-26.title: Saints Joachim and Anne, Parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary
readings: Alas, this people has sinned a great sin; they have made for themselves gods of gold
Remember us, O Lord, as you favor your people
The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed ... like yeast
2027-07-26.alt: Memorial. The weekday readings of Week 17 (Year I) are given; the proper readings of the memorial (Sirach 44:1, 10–15; Psalm 132:11, 13–14, 17–18; Matthew 13:16–17) may be used instead. The names Joachim and Anne come from an early Christian writing, the Protoevangelium of James (second century), not from the Gospels. Yesterday, the fourth Sunday of July, was the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly. Psalm verses are the same in NRSV and the Lectionary. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-07-26.verse: Their bodies are buried in peace, but their name lives on generation after generation. The assembly declares their wisdom, and the congregation proclaims their praise.
theo: Moses comes down from Sinai carrying “the two tablets of the covenant,” written on both sides, “the work of God.” Below him is the noise of a party. Joshua thinks it is the sound of war; Moses knows better: “it is the sound of revelers that I hear.” When he sees the calf and the dancing his anger burns, and he shatters the tablets at the foot of the mountain, a picture of a covenant broken. He burns the calf, grinds it to powder and makes the people drink it, to show that the idol is nothing. Then he faces Aaron, who gives one of the most comic and most tragic excuses in the Bible: “I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf!” Scripture knows our habit of blaming everything but ourselves. The next day Moses does what the great intercessors do. He tells the people the truth, “You have sinned a great sin,” and then he goes back up the mountain: “perhaps I can make atonement for your sin.” His prayer breaks off in the middle of a sentence: “if you will only forgive their sin” and then, “if not, blot me out of the book that you have written.” He puts his own name on the line for a people who have just betrayed God. The Psalm remembers it: “had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them.” The Church sees in Moses a shadow of Christ, who “always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

In the Gospel Jesus tells two short parables, the mustard seed and the yeast. The kingdom of heaven does not arrive with trumpets; it begins small, hidden, and works from within. The seed is “the smallest of all the seeds,” yet it becomes a tree where birds nest; the yeast is hidden in “three measures of flour,” enough for a whole village's bread, “until all of it was leavened.” St Matthew adds that Jesus speaks in parables to fulfil the word of the Psalm: “I will proclaim what has been hidden from the foundation of the world” (Psalm 78:2). Beside these parables the Church today places the memory of two hidden people, Joachim and Anne. The Gospels never name them. Their names come from the Protoevangelium of James, a second-century writing that the Church does not count as Scripture, but whose names the faithful have honoured in East and West for many centuries. What the Church knows with certainty is simple: Mary had parents. They received her as God's gift, taught her the psalms and the promises of Israel, and handed on a faith in which she could answer the angel: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord.” The Church teaches that Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception, yet she was born into a human family, nursed, and taught like any child. A mustard seed of faith passed from grandparents to a girl in Nazareth, and from her the Lord of all took flesh. In Kerala the name of Anne is in every parish, in Annamma and Anna and Ann, and the old stories of Joachim and Anne praying for a child echo the stories of Sarah and Hannah, whose prayer we hear in the Book of Samuel: “if only you will look on the misery of your servant, and remember me” (1 Samuel 1:11).
outline: Opening
Ask: who first taught you to pray, and what did they hand on to you without knowing it?
Point 1 · Moses in the breach
He puts his own name on the line for a people who betrayed God; Christ always lives to intercede.
Point 2 · The mustard seed and the yeast
The kingdom begins small and hidden, and grows from within.
Point 3 · Joachim and Anne
Two hidden people, a faith handed on, and the girl who said: Here am I.
Take-home line
“A faith that lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice.”
live: Stand in the breach (Exodus 32:32)
Choose one person who has gone far from God, and pray for them by name each day this week, as Moses prayed for his people.
Pass on the seed (2 Timothy 1:5)
Tell a child or grandchild one story of how God has been faithful to your family, or ask a grandparent to tell it to you, and write it down.
saints: Sts Joachim and Anne

According to the Protoevangelium of James, Joachim and Anne were an elderly, childless couple who prayed for a child, and Mary was born to them. The Church honours them as the parents of the Mother of God and, therefore, as the grandparents of Jesus according to the flesh. Anne was honoured in the East from early centuries, and her feast spread to the West in the Middle Ages; Joachim, who had a separate day in the older Roman calendar, was joined to her on 26 July in 1969.
2027-07-26.prayer: O God of our fathers, who gave Saints Joachim and Anne the grace of bringing forth the Mother of your incarnate Son, grant, through the prayers of both, that we may attain the salvation you have promised to your people. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord God, you hide your kingdom in small seeds and quiet lives. Bless our grandparents and parents, who plant the faith in the heart of a child. Make us faithful to what they handed on, and, like Moses, ready to stand in the breach for those who have strayed. Amen.
altar: In every Mass the Church does what Moses did on the mountain: she stands before God for a sinful people, but not with her own merits. She offers the one sacrifice of Christ, “who always lives to make intercession for them.” And in the Eucharistic Prayer we ask to share the company of Mary, the apostles and “all the Saints”: among them, in the hidden ranks of the saints, are the grandparents and parents who taught us to pray and who now pray for us.

2027-07-27.title: Tuesday of the Seventeenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: The Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend
The Lord is kind and merciful
Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field
2027-07-27.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 17 (Year I). The first reading continues the story of Moses and the covenant at Sinai, read on the weekdays of weeks 15 to 17. In Kerala this is the season when farmers weed and tend the young paddy in the rain. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-27.verse: The Lord passed before him, and proclaimed, “The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness
theo: After the golden calf the Lord said he would not go in the midst of this people (Exodus 33:3), and so Moses does something quiet and brave: he takes the tent, pitches it “outside the camp, far off from the camp,” and calls it the tent of meeting. “Everyone who sought the Lord would go out to the tent.” It is a place open to anyone who wants to pray. When Moses enters, the pillar of cloud comes down at the entrance, and the whole people, each at the door of their own tent, rise and bow down. Then comes the sentence that is at the heart of today's reading: “Thus the Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend.” Moses returns to the camp, but young Joshua “would not leave the tent.” Some people cannot bear to leave the place where God speaks. In chapter 34 Moses goes up the mountain a second time, and the Lord comes down in the cloud and “proclaimed the name”: “The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for the thousandth generation, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin.” This is the great self-portrait of God in the Old Testament, repeated by the Psalms, the prophets and Jonah. It holds mercy and justice together (“yet by no means clearing the guilty”), but notice the proportions: judgment reaches “the third and the fourth generation,” while steadfast love reaches “the thousandth.” Moses bows quickly and prays, and his prayer is bold: “Although this is a stiff-necked people, pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for your inheritance.” He uses their stubbornness as his argument for God to come with them. Then he spends “forty days and forty nights” with the Lord, neither eating nor drinking, and writes the words of the covenant. The Psalm sings it back: “The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. As far as the east is from the west, so far he removes our transgressions from us.”

In the Gospel, away from the crowds and “in the house,” the disciples ask Jesus: “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.” He gives them a key: the one who sows is the Son of Man; the field is the world; the good seed are “the children of the kingdom”; the weeds are “the children of the evil one”; the enemy is the devil; the harvest is the end of the age and the reapers are angels. We should read the explanation together with the parable itself. When the servants asked whether they should pull up the weeds, the householder said: “No; for in gathering the weeds you would uproot the wheat along with them. Let both of them grow together until the harvest.” That is God's patience, the “slow to anger” of Exodus 34. We are not the reapers. We are told to sow, to weed our own hearts and to leave the final sorting to the Lord, because we cannot always tell wheat from weeds, and a person who looks like a weed today may be wheat tomorrow. The saints began as sinners. But the parable is serious too. There will be a harvest; “all causes of sin and all evildoers” will be gathered, and the end is described in terrible words. The Church teaches that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead (Catechism 678–679) and she does not soften the warning; yet she does not name anyone as lost. And the parable ends in light: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father,” echoing the prophet Daniel: “those who lead many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.” The Church herself is a field where wheat and weeds grow, “holy and always in need of purification” (Catechism 827), and the patience of God is what gives each of us time to turn. St Peter says it plainly: the Lord “is patient with you, not wanting any to perish, but all to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).
outline: Opening
Ask: with whom can you talk as you talk to a friend, and is God one of them?
Point 1 · Face to face
The tent outside the camp: God speaks to Moses as to a friend, and Joshua will not leave.
Point 2 · The name of the Lord
Merciful and gracious, slow to anger: mercy reaches to the thousandth generation.
Point 3 · Wheat and weeds
The patience of God gives time; we sow and weed our own hearts, and the harvest is the Lord's.
Take-home line
“The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.”
live: Visit the tent of meeting
Spend ten minutes before the tabernacle or in silent prayer today, and speak to God plainly, as to a friend: tell him what is on your mind.
Wait for the harvest (Matthew 13:30)
Before you judge someone this week, pray for them, and name one good seed in them. Weed your own heart first, with the help of confession.
2027-07-27.prayer: Merciful and gracious God, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, you spoke to Moses face to face as to a friend, and in your Son you call us your friends. Give us the courage to pitch our tent of prayer outside the noise of the camp, and to stay near it like Joshua. Teach us your patience, that we may not pull up the wheat while we judge the weeds, but leave the harvest to you. Make us shine like the sun in the kingdom of our Father. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: In every church the tabernacle is the tent of meeting. The little red lamp tells us that he is there, the Lord who spoke to Moses as to a friend and who now says to us in the Gospel: “I have called you friends” (John 15:15). At Mass, in the Kyrie, we cry out to the Lord for mercy, and just before Communion we pray: Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. The name proclaimed to Moses, “merciful and gracious,” is placed in our hands in the Eucharist; and the same Lord who is patient with weeds feeds us with his own Body and Blood so that we may become wheat.

2027-07-28.title: Saint Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception, Virgin
readings: Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God
Holy is the Lord our God
In his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field
2027-07-28.alt: Memorial in the calendar of the Church in India (verify the rank locally); the weekday readings of Week 17 (Year I) are used, and the prayers may be taken from the Common of Virgins. St Alphonsa died on 28 July 1946 and was canonised on 12 October 2008. Psalm verses are the same in NRSV and the Lectionary. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-07-28.verse: Moses came down from Mount Sinai. As he came down from the mountain with the two tablets of the covenant in his hand, Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God.
theo: Moses comes down Mount Sinai for the second time, with the new tablets in his hands, and he does not know that his face is shining. “Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God.” He has spent forty days in the presence of the Lord, and the glory has left its mark on him, though he himself is the last to notice. Aaron and the Israelites see it and are afraid to come near, so Moses calls them, speaks to them, and gives them the commands he has received; then he puts a veil over his face. Whenever he goes in to speak with the Lord he takes the veil off, and when he comes out he tells the people what he has been told, and they see again that his face is shining. The Psalm recalls this friendship: “Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel also was among those who called on his name. They cried to the Lord, and he answered them. He spoke to them in the pillar of cloud.” The holiest people in Scripture are those who have been with God and do not realise how much of him they carry. St Paul will say that in Christ the veil is removed and that “all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

The Gospel gives two tiny parables, each of one sentence. A man finds a treasure hidden in a field, hides it again, and “in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.” A merchant who knows pearls finds “one pearl of great value” and sells everything to buy it. Notice the word “joy.” Neither man calls it a sacrifice. They give up everything because they have found something better, and the finding comes first. This is how the Church understands the call to follow Christ, and the consecrated life in particular: not a loss but a discovery. St Paul says the same of himself: “whatever gains I had, these I have come to regard as loss because of Christ... because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:7–8). The poor man with the field and the rich merchant show that the kingdom is for every kind of person, and that the price is the same for both: all that one has.

Today the Church in India keeps the memorial of a woman who found the pearl early and whose face shone without her knowing it. Alphonsa was born Anna, called Annakutty, on 19 August 1910 at Kudamaloor, near Kottayam in Kerala, into a Syro-Malabar Catholic family. Her mother died when she was small, and she grew up in the care of relatives. From childhood she wanted to belong wholly to Jesus. As a young girl, to avoid a marriage that others were arranging, she injured her feet in a fire, a rash act that the Church does not hold up for imitation, but which shows how single her desire was. She entered the convent of the Franciscan Clarist Congregation at Bharananganam in 1927, received the habit in 1928 and the name Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception, and made her first vows in 1931 and her final vows in 1936. Her life was short and hidden, and full of illness. She taught young children for a time and could do little of the work that the world counts as important. Yet in her letters and in the memory of her sisters she appears as a woman who took her sufferings in union with the Cross of Christ, offered them for others, and met everyone with gentleness. She died at Bharananganam on 28 July 1946, aged thirty-five. Her tomb in the church of St Mary there became a place of pilgrimage. Pope St John Paul II beatified her at Kottayam on 8 February 1986, and Pope Benedict XVI canonised her in Rome on 12 October 2008: she is the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised and the first canonised saint of the Syro-Malabar Church. Like Moses, she did not know that her face was shining; the people of Kerala saw it and came near. Like the merchant, she found one pearl and sold everything. And like the grain of wheat of the Gospel, she fell into the earth and bore much fruit (John 12:24).
conn: “The skin of his face shone.”
