But Elisha says: thus says the Lord, they shall eat and have some left. And they did. The man's first fruits fed a hundred.

In the Gospel there is an even bigger crowd, five thousand, and again Jesus asks a question to test his disciples: where are we to buy bread for these people? Philip does the sums: six months' wages would not be enough. And then Andrew finds a boy. Notice, it is a boy, a child, with five barley loaves and two fish, the poor man's lunch. And Andrew says honestly: but what are they among so many people? (John 6:9). I think every one of us has said that about our own gifts. What is my little time, my little money, my little talent among so many needs?

But look at what Jesus does. He does not ask the crowd for more. He takes what the boy offers, and he gives thanks. Not a complaint that it is too little, but thanks. Then he distributes it, and they all eat as much as they wanted. The boy did not make the miracle. But there would have been no miracle that day without his five loaves. God asks us for our little, and he does the rest.

And then Jesus says: gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost (John 6:12). In God's house nothing is thrown away, no crumb and no person. Twelve baskets are filled. That is how we should look at the Eucharist, at the food on our tables, and at the old and the weak among us, whom the world is tempted to call leftovers. Today is the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly. They are not fragments to be discarded; they are the baskets of the faith, and they hold what was handed down to us. Let us visit them and listen.

St Paul tells us what this bread is for. There is one body and one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism. At every Mass Jesus takes, gives thanks, breaks and gives, and from many grains makes one bread, from many persons one Church. So let us leave the altar with humility, gentleness and patience, bearing with one another in love. And when we feel that our gift is too small, let us remember the boy with the barley loaves, and bring it to Jesus. Amen.
kids: Children, a big crowd followed Jesus and they were all hungry. A little boy had five small loaves and two fish. He gave them to Jesus. Jesus said thank you to God, and he shared the food, and everybody ate until they were full! There were even twelve baskets left. Jesus can do great things with the little we give him. What small thing can you share this week? And please give your grandparents a big hug today!

homily: Dear friends, today the first reading takes us up the mountain with Abraham and Isaac. It is a hard story, and we should not hurry past it. God asks Abraham for his son, his only son, whom he loves. Abraham does not argue. He rises early. He walks for three days. And on the way a boy asks the question every child would ask: where is the lamb? And the father who has no answer except trust says: God himself will provide the lamb, my son (Genesis 22:8).

At the last moment, the angel calls: Abraham, Abraham! Do not lay your hand on the boy (Genesis 22:12). The God of Abraham does not want children sacrificed. He wanted Abraham's heart, and Abraham gave it. And the story does not end with a test passed. It ends with a promise: in your offspring all the nations of the earth will gain blessing (Genesis 22:18). That offspring is Christ. Centuries later another Father would not withhold his own Son, but gave him up for all of us (Romans 8:32), and John would point to Jesus and say: Here is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). God did provide the lamb.

In the Gospel the lamb is already at work, in a small town by the lake. Friends bring a paralysed man, and Matthew says: when Jesus saw their faith (Matthew 9:2). Think of that. The friends say nothing in the story, and yet Jesus hears them. Their faith carried a man who could not walk. Who in your life has carried you? A mother, a grandmother, a teacher, a friend who prayed? And whom are you carrying?

Then Jesus says the unexpected words: Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven (Matthew 9:2). The paralytic's real burden was not his legs. Jesus heals the heart first, and then, to show that he has the right, he heals the body. And the crowds glorify God who had given such authority to human beings. Dear friends, that is the sacrament of Reconciliation. This month, the month of the Precious Blood, let us make the time. Let the Lamb of God lift the burden off our hearts, and then let us go home, like the paralytic, carrying the bed that carried us.
kids: Children, Abraham loved his son Isaac. One day God asked Abraham to trust him in a very hard way. Abraham got up early and walked to a mountain. Isaac asked: where is the lamb? Abraham said: God will provide the lamb. And God did! He stopped Abraham and gave a ram. God never wants a child to be hurt, and he always keeps his promise. In the Gospel, some friends carried a man who could not walk to Jesus. Jesus said: your sins are forgiven, and he made the man walk! Let us be good friends who help carry others.

homily: Dear friends, today's first reading begins with a funeral. Sarah has died, and Abraham goes in to weep for her. The Bible does not tell us to hide our tears. Abraham mourns, and then he does the practical thing. He asks for a place to bury his wife. And we learn something that is almost strange: after all those years with God's promise of the whole land, Abraham owns one cave. I am a stranger and an alien residing among you (Genesis 23:4).

That is the life of faith. We are pilgrims. The Letter to the Hebrews says that the patriarchs confessed that they were strangers and foreigners on the earth, because they desired a better country, that is, a heavenly one (Hebrews 11:13–16). We have homes, jobs and plans, and we should look after them well. But our true home is where Christ is, and our dead are not lost: they have gone ahead of us.

And God comforts his pilgrims through each other. Isaac goes out in the evening to walk in the field. He is grieving for his mother. And he looks up and sees camels coming. Rebekah looks up too. Then the Bible says something simple and beautiful: he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death (Genesis 24:67). Husbands and wives, parents and children, friends: love is the way God consoles. Let us not forget to say to those near us that they are a comfort.

In the Gospel Jesus walks by a tax booth and sees a man. Not a tax collector, not a thief, but a man, and he says: Follow me. Matthew gets up. Then at the dinner Jesus eats with sinners, and when he is criticised he answers: Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick (Matthew 9:12). Go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, not sacrifice. On this First Friday we look at the Heart that was pierced for sinners. If you feel you are too bad to come, this Gospel was written for you. And if you think you are too good to need him, it was written for you too. Let us all come to the physician, and let us make room at our own table for those whom he has called.
kids: Children, a man named Matthew collected taxes, and nobody liked him. One day Jesus walked by and said: follow me. Matthew stood up and went with Jesus! Then he gave a big dinner, and Jesus sat down with all his friends, even those whom others did not like. Some grown-ups were cross. But Jesus said: I came for those who need help, like a doctor for sick people. Jesus loves everybody, and today is First Friday, the day we thank him for his Sacred Heart. Let us be kind to a child who sits alone!

homily: Dear friends, think of Jacob on that night. He is a man on the run. He has cheated his brother, he has left his father's house, he is going to a place he does not know. When the sun sets, he does not even have a bed. He puts a stone under his head. We all know what it is to be at a low point, alone, ashamed, unsure of the future. And that is where God meets him. In a dream he sees a ladder, and angels going up and down, and the Lord standing beside him. And what does God say? Not a scolding. He says: Know that I am with you and will keep you wherever you go (Genesis 28:15).

When Jacob wakes he says one of the great lines of the Bible: Surely the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it! (Genesis 28:16). How many times has God been in our place, in the hospital room, in the bus, in the kitchen, in the dark, and we did not know it? Today's reading invites us to open our eyes. The stone that was a pillow becomes a pillar. The roadside becomes the gate of heaven. And centuries later Jesus tells Nathanael: you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man (John 1:51). Jesus himself is the ladder: God and man in one person. In him heaven has come down.

In the Gospel we meet two people who need that ladder. A ruler of the synagogue: his daughter has just died, and he comes to Jesus with nothing but a request. And a woman, who has suffered for twelve years, who is afraid to speak: she touches the fringe of his cloak. And Jesus turns and sees her. Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well (Matthew 9:22). Perhaps nobody had spoken so tenderly to her in twelve years. Then he comes to the ruler's house, where the flute players are already playing. The girl is not dead but sleeping. And they laughed at him. He takes her by the hand, and she gets up (Matthew 9:24–25).

Dear friends, if you are at a low point today, if you are far from home or from God, remember Jacob's stone. The Lord is in this place. And remember the fringe of the cloak: you do not need great words, only a touch of faith. Today the Church remembers St Anthony Zaccaria, a doctor who became a priest because he saw that souls too need a physician. May he help us to notice the sickness of the heart, in us and around us, and to bring it to the one who takes us by the hand.
kids: Children, Jacob was far from home, and it was night, and he was afraid. He lay down with a stone for a pillow. In his dream he saw a ladder up to heaven, and God said: I am with you wherever you go! When Jacob woke up he said: God is here, and I did not know it! In the Gospel a girl was very sick, and Jesus took her by the hand and made her well. Jesus is with us too, when we are at home and when we are far away. Today we remember St Anthony Zaccaria, a doctor who became a priest to help people love Jesus.

homily: Dear friends, have you ever prayed all night? Not just words, but a real struggle? Jacob did. He is returning home after twenty years, and his brother Esau is coming with four hundred men. Jacob has prayed, sent gifts, arranged his camp. And now, alone at the river in the dark, a man wrestles with him until morning (Genesis 32:25). We do not know exactly who he is. But in the end Jacob says: I have seen God face to face.

Why does God wrestle with Jacob? Because Jacob has to be changed. All his life, he has gripped, grabbed and bargained. That is the meaning of his name: heel-grabber. Now he is gripping God. And God lets him, because this struggle is a prayer. The man touches his hip, and Jacob will limp for the rest of his life. And still he says: I will not let you go, unless you bless me (Genesis 32:26). And God blesses him and gives him a new name: Israel. He walks away limping, but he walks away blessed.

Dear friends, are there nights in your life like that? A sick child, a failing business, a broken marriage, a doubt that will not leave? Do not be afraid to wrestle with God. He can take it. And he does not mind if we say, I will not let you go. In the morning we may be limping, but we will have a blessing, and we will have seen his face.

In the Gospel Jesus walks through the towns and villages, and he sees the crowds. And Matthew says he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36). What does Jesus do with that compassion? He turns to his disciples and says: The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest (Matthew 9:37–38). Notice, he does not say: go! He says: pray! The first step is prayer. Let us pray today, for priests, religious sisters, brothers, catechists and for our own children, that they may hear the call.

Today the Church remembers St Maria Goretti. She was eleven. She was attacked by a young man in her own home, and she said no, because she knew that it was a sin. She died the next day, forgiving him. And that forgiveness bore fruit: Alessandro repented, and years later he knelt beside her mother, asking pardon. That is a harvest. A girl of eleven, a poor farm child, was a labourer in the Lord's harvest. May all our young people have her courage and her forgiving heart.
kids: Children, Jacob was alone by a river in the night, and a stranger wrestled with him until morning. Jacob would not let go! He said: bless me! And God blessed him and gave him a new name, Israel. Jacob walked away with a limp, but happy, because he had seen God. When we pray for something, we can keep on praying, like Jacob. Today we remember St Maria Goretti. She was only eleven. When someone wanted her to do something bad, she said: no, God does not want it! And before she died, she forgave the man who hurt her. Let us say no to sin, and let us forgive.

homily: Dear friends, the story of Joseph and his brothers is a great story of conscience. Twenty years and more have gone by. The brothers have a family, flocks and a good name. They have told their father a lie and they have kept it. And then a famine comes, and they stand before a powerful man in Egypt, and suddenly they remember. Alas, we are paying the penalty for what we did to our brother (Genesis 42:21). Nothing had been forgotten. A sin we do not confess does not die; it sleeps, and it wakes when we are afraid.

Notice what Joseph does. He knows them at once, and he does not take revenge. He tests them. He speaks harshly, he puts them in prison for three days, and then he sends them home, keeping only one of them. Why? Because he wants his brothers back, not their punishment. And when he hears them confess, he turns away and weeps (Genesis 42:24). That is how God works with us too. God sometimes lets the famine come, so that we may stop and remember, and in secret God weeps for us and waits.

The Gospel today begins the long instruction of Jesus to his twelve apostles. He calls them by name. A fisherman, a tax collector, a zealot, even one who will betray him. Jesus gives them authority, and sends them with one message: the kingdom of heaven has come near (Matthew 10:7). It has come near like a brother who forgives, like bread for the hungry, like a door that is open.

What are we sent to do? The same as Joseph and the Twelve: to feed and to forgive. If there is a wrong in your past that you have never put right, this is a good week to go to a brother, to a sister, to a priest in the sacrament of Reconciliation. And if someone has wronged you, remember Joseph's tears. Pharaoh said: go to Joseph. Jesus says to us: go to the lost. Amen.
kids: Children, Joseph's brothers were not kind to him. Years later they were hungry, and they came to ask him for food. Joseph knew them, but they did not know him! He wanted to see whether they were sorry. And they were. They said: we were wrong to hurt our brother. Joseph cried when he heard it. In the Gospel Jesus chooses twelve friends and sends them to tell everybody that God is near. Jesus wants us to be his friends too. When we say sorry and forgive each other, we are telling people that God is near!

homily: Dear friends, Judah is one of the most moving men in the Bible. In the first part of the story he is the brother who proposes to sell Joseph, because it will be more profitable than killing him. Twenty years later, he stands before the governor of Egypt and offers himself as a slave in place of the youngest brother (Genesis 44:33). Something has happened to Judah. He has looked at his father's grief, he has learned what his sin cost, and he has become another man. That is what repentance is: not only feeling sorry, but changing.

Then Joseph cannot hold back any longer. Send everyone away from me (Genesis 45:1). In the privacy of the room he says: I am Joseph. Is my father still alive? His brothers cannot speak. They are afraid. They remember the pit, the silver, the lie. But Joseph says: Come closer to me. And then: do not be distressed, or angry with yourselves, because you sold me here; for God sent me before you to preserve life (Genesis 45:5). Not a word of reproach. This is how God forgives: he draws the sinner closer, and he uses even the evil done to bring about good.

In the Gospel Jesus sends out the Twelve with a few words of instruction: proclaim, heal, cleanse. And then he says the sentence we should write on our hearts: You received without payment; give without payment (Matthew 10:8). We have received so much. Life, faith, baptism, forgiveness, the Eucharist. None of it was earned. How, then, can we hold it back or sell it? The apostles are to travel light, trust in God and the welcome of ordinary people, and bring peace into every house.

So this week, let us give something without payment. A visit, a favour, a forgiveness. And if someone has done you wrong, imagine Joseph standing in front of his brothers and saying: come closer to me. Pharaoh's palace was not too small for that mercy. Neither is your home. Amen.
kids: Children, Joseph's brothers were mean to him when he was young. Years later they came to him for food, and they were afraid. But Joseph did not shout at them. He cried, and he said: I am your brother Joseph! Come close. God has used even this to save our family. In the Gospel Jesus says to his friends: God gave you his love as a gift, so give it as a gift to others. Let us share what we have, and say sorry and forgive, just like Joseph!

homily: Dear friends, Jacob is old, and he is afraid. He has to leave the land of the promise and go down to Egypt, a foreign country and the land of Pharaoh. And what does he do? He does what believers always do: before he sets out, he stops at Beer-sheba and offers sacrifice. And in the night God calls him: Jacob, Jacob. Here I am. And God says: do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make of you a great nation there. I myself will go down with you (Genesis 46:3–4).

I myself will go down with you. That is one of the most beautiful sentences in the Bible. God does not wave from the shore. God goes down. Later God will go down in the Incarnation, in the womb of Mary, and down to the grave, and in the Mass he goes down on the altar. Wherever you go, whatever you fear, God goes down with you. And then the meeting of father and son: Joseph wept on his neck a good while, and old Jacob said: I can die now, having seen for myself that you are still alive (Genesis 46:30). A life that has seen God's faithfulness can be ended in peace.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks plainly to the Twelve: I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves (Matthew 10:16). He does not hide it. Many of his followers have been put to death. Today the Church remembers St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, the martyrs of China. We think too of St Devasahayam, who gave his life for Christ in the south of our own land. How could they do it? Jesus had promised: it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you (Matthew 10:20).

Few of us will be asked to die for the faith. But all of us are asked to witness: at work, at home, in the family. To be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. To say a word for the Lord when it is not easy. Do not worry about how you are to speak. Go, trusting the God who said to Jacob: I myself will go down with you. Amen.
kids: Children, old Jacob was going to a new country, and he was afraid. But at night God called: Jacob, Jacob! And God said: do not be afraid, I will go with you. Later Jacob saw his son Joseph again, and he cried with joy. In the Gospel Jesus tells his friends that it will not always be easy to follow him, but the Holy Spirit will help them to find the right words. Some brave Christians, like the martyrs of China, died because they loved Jesus so much. When you feel afraid, say: Jesus, you are with me.

homily: Dear friends, today we read the last pages of the Book of Genesis. Jacob has died. Seventeen years have passed since the family came down to Egypt, and Joseph has looked after them all. But when their father dies, the brothers are afraid again. What if Joseph still bears a grudge against us? (Genesis 50:15). It is a very human fear. They have been forgiven, and they have not believed it. How many of us have gone to confession, and still carry the old guilt, as though God had not meant what he said?

Joseph wept when they spoke to him. It hurt him that they could think so little of his love. And then he says one of the great sentences of the Bible: Do not be afraid! Am I in the place of God? Even though you intended to do harm to me, God intended it for good (Genesis 50:19–20). He does not say the evil was good. He says that God was greater than the evil. And he comforts them, speaking kindly to them. That is how God speaks to the penitent.

In the Gospel Jesus says it three times: do not be afraid. He knows that his disciples will meet opposition. But the Father who counts the sparrows, the cheapest birds in the market, also counts the hairs of your head. You are of more value than many sparrows (Matthew 10:31). The only fear we need is the holy fear of losing God, and that fear leads us to him.

Genesis ends with a coffin. But Joseph said: God will surely come to you, and carry up my bones. His body was a promise. Our graves too are waiting rooms. Let us hand our fears to God today, forgive without counting the cost, and speak up for Jesus when it matters. And let us ask Mary, who stood without fear at the Cross, to pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, Joseph's brothers were frightened again after their father died. They thought Joseph would punish them. But Joseph cried, and said: do not be afraid! God turned the bad thing into a good one. In the Gospel Jesus says: do not be afraid. God looks after even the smallest sparrow, and he knows how many hairs you have on your head! You are very, very precious to him. So when you are scared in the dark, or about school, or about anything, say: Jesus, I trust you.

homily: Dear friends, a new chapter begins today. A new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph (Exodus 1:8). Joseph had saved the country in the famine. But a new generation has forgotten him. How quickly we forget those who did us good. And the king is afraid. Look, he says, the Israelites are too many. They may join our enemies. So he deals shrewdly with them: forced labour, hard work in mortar and brick, and at last the order to throw the baby boys into the Nile. When we forget, we begin to fear; when we fear, we begin to oppress.

But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied (Exodus 1:12). You cannot stop the blessing of God with a decree. And God has allies in unexpected places: two midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, who feared God and let the boys live. The Bible gives their names, and forgets the king's. Whenever you see the powerful oppressing the weak, remember the midwives. Small people who say no can change the course of history.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks plainly: I have not come to bring peace, but a sword (Matthew 10:34). He means: following me will cut through everything, even the dearest loyalties. Nobody and nothing may stand above God. And whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it (Matthew 10:39). The midwives lost their safety and found the lives of many children.

But the passage ends with welcome. Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me. And a cup of cold water. Such a small thing. Yet Jesus says: none of these will lose their reward. This week, let us do a small thing for someone nobody welcomes, a migrant, a worker, a stranger. And let us give thanks to those who have done us good, and whom we may have forgotten. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time after Joseph, there was a new king in Egypt, and he forgot everything good that Joseph had done. He was afraid of the Israelites, and he made them work as slaves. But two brave women, Shiphrah and Puah, would not do what the king said, because they loved God. God was pleased with them. Jesus tells his friends: whoever gives even a cup of cold water to someone in my name will get a reward from God. A smile, a glass of water, a hello to someone who is new: Jesus sees all of these!

homily: Dear friends, picture a river and a basket among the reeds. In the basket is a three-month-old baby. His mother has done everything she can; now she has to trust God. And God does what he so often does: he uses ordinary people. A mother who lets go, a sister who stands and watches, and a princess who does not look away from a crying baby. Look at how many small hands it takes to save one child. The woman who draws him out of the river names him Moses: because I drew him out of the water (Exodus 2:10). He will draw out a whole people.

We too have been drawn out of the water. In baptism, God lifted us out of the old life and gave us a name. Who were the hands that held you? A mother, a grandmother, a teacher, a priest, a neighbour. Today is a good day to remember them and to thank God for them, and to ask: whom am I holding up?

The story goes on. Moses grows up, sees his people suffering, and tries to help in his own way, with violence, and it goes badly. His own people say: Who made you a ruler and judge over us? (Exodus 2:14). He runs away. It looks like the end, but it is only the beginning: forty years later God will send this same Moses from a burning bush. God's time is longer than ours. When our own good plans fail, God has not stopped.

In the Gospel Jesus grieves over three towns. Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! (Matthew 11:21). It sounds harsh, but listen to the heart behind it: it is the cry of a friend who has done everything and sees his friends still not turning. They saw the most miracles and changed the least. How much have we seen? The Mass every Sunday, the Bible in our own language, the sacraments, the saints. St Henry, whom we remember today, was an emperor who knew that much had been given to him, and so much would be asked. Let us turn back with gratitude today, and let us not wait. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago a baby was in great danger. His mother made a little basket, put him inside it and placed it by the river. His big sister watched to see what would happen. Then a king's daughter came, found the baby and loved him. She called him Moses, which means “drawn out of the water.” Moses grew up and became a great helper of God's people. God uses many people to look after one child: a mother, a sister and a princess. Who looked after you? Let us say thank you to them today, and let us look after someone smaller too.

homily: Dear friends, imagine Moses at the end of a long ordinary day. He is eighty years old, with the sheep, in the desert. Nothing special is happening. And then he sees a bush that burns and does not burn up. He could have walked on. A lot of us walk on. But Moses says: I must turn aside and look at this great sight (Exodus 3:3). And when the Lord saw that he had turned aside to see, God called to him: Moses, Moses! (Exodus 3:4). God does not shout; he waits for someone who stops.

Then God says: Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground (Exodus 3:5). It is just a patch of desert, and it is holy because God is there. When we enter a church we feel it. But God's holy ground is also the sickroom, the kitchen where someone is crying, the hospital bed. And hear what God says in the verses we did not read: I have observed the misery of my people; I have heard their cry; I know their sufferings (Exodus 3:7). Our God is no distant ruler. He knows suffering from the inside, and in his Son he entered it.

That is why St Camillus saw what he saw. A soldier with a wound that would not heal, he lay in a hospital and saw how the poor sick were treated, and he said: this is holy ground. He gave his life to nursing the sick, because Jesus himself said: I was sick and you took care of me (Matthew 25:36). Moses asked: who am I? God answered: I will be with you (Exodus 3:12). That is the only answer any of us needs when we are afraid to help.

And Jesus thanks the Father today that these things are revealed not to the wise and learned but to infants (Matthew 11:25). You do not need a degree to meet God. You need the heart of a child, which stops, looks and says: Here I am. Let us turn aside today and ask for that heart. Amen.
kids: Children, Moses was looking after the sheep one day when he saw a bush on fire, but the bush was not burning up! He went to have a look. And God called: Moses! Moses! God said: take off your sandals, this is holy ground. Then God told him: I have seen my people hurting, and I will send you to help them. Moses was afraid, but God said: I will be with you. A man called Camillus knew that God is with sick people. He looked after them with all his heart. When we are kind to someone who is sick, we are standing on holy ground too.

homily: Dear friends, imagine the night of the Passover. In every Hebrew home a family is eating in haste, shoes on, staff in hand. On the doorpost is the blood of a lamb without blemish. And God says: when I see the blood, I will pass over you (Exodus 12:13). Every year, for three thousand years, the Jewish people have kept that night. And we, in the Mass, keep our Passover: Christ is the Lamb without blemish, his blood saves us, and every time we receive him we pass from slavery to life. Let us remember what Paul says: our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7).

In the Gospel the disciples are hungry and pluck some grain, and the Pharisees say: it is not lawful! And Jesus answers with a sentence that should wake us up: I desire mercy and not sacrifice (Matthew 12:7). Rules matter; worship matters. But if a rule makes us forget a hungry person, we have lost its point. Something greater than the temple is here, he says (Matthew 12:6). It is he himself, the Lord of the sabbath. Mercy is the key to the whole law.

Today we also remember Our Lady of Mount Carmel. On Mount Carmel the prophet Elijah prayed for rain, and he said to his servant: look toward the sea. Six times: there is nothing. The seventh time: a little cloud no bigger than a person's hand (1 Kings 18:44). Dear friends, sometimes our prayer feels like that. We look and see nothing. Elijah teaches us to go back, again and again. And the tradition of the Church saw in that little cloud Mary: a humble young woman from Nazareth, no bigger than a hand in the eyes of the world, and out of her came Jesus, the rain of grace for the whole world.

The Carmelites took Mary as their mother and their model. They wear the scapular, a small cloth, as a sign that they belong to her and want to live as she lived. And what was her life? Here am I, the servant of the Lord (Luke 1:38). And at Cana: do whatever he tells you (John 2:5). Today let us ask Our Lady of Carmel to teach us that, to pray like Elijah, to be merciful like Jesus and to say yes like her. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago on a mountain called Mount Carmel there was a prophet named Elijah. There was no rain, and everything was dry. Elijah prayed. He told his helper: look at the sea! The helper looked and said: nothing! Elijah said: look again! Seven times! The seventh time the helper saw a little cloud, as small as a hand. And then came the rain! We remember Mary today as Our Lady of Carmel. She is like the little cloud: small and humble, and she brought us Jesus. Some people wear a little brown scapular to remember that Mary is our mother. Let us say a Hail Mary and ask her to help us to wait and pray like Elijah, and not give up.

homily: Dear friends, picture the night the people leave Egypt. After four hundred and thirty years, in a hurry, with unleavened dough on their backs, six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children. And the Bible says: that was for the Lord a night of vigil (Exodus 12:42). Think of that: while the people are rushing and afraid, God is awake. He is keeping watch. That is the first good news: when you cannot sleep, when you are afraid, someone is awake over you. And so every year the people keep that night, and every year at Easter we keep the greatest vigil of all.

Notice also: a mixed crowd also went up with them (Exodus 12:38). It was not only the family of Jacob. Other slaves, other peoples, saw what God was doing and joined in. God's people has never been a closed club. In Jesus, the prophet says, the Gentiles will hope (Matthew 12:21). The door is wide. Who is the mixed crowd today, the migrant worker, the newcomer in the parish, the one who does not look like us? Let us make room.

In the Gospel there is a plot. The enemies of Jesus meet and decide to destroy him. And what does Jesus do? He leaves. He does not shout, he does not fight. He goes on healing. Matthew says that he fulfils Isaiah: he will not wrangle or cry aloud; he will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick (Matthew 12:19–20). Brothers and sisters, we are all bruised reeds in some way: weak, discouraged, close to snapping. And he does not break us. He does not put out the little flame of our faith, even when it is only smoking. He bends over it and protects it with his hand.

Let us take that gentleness with us. When we meet someone who is weak, let us not snap them; let us shield the flame. And when we ourselves are bruised, let us remember that the Lord who watched over Israel in the night is watching over us, and that his steadfast love endures for ever. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago God's people had to leave Egypt in a great hurry, in the middle of the night. They were scared. But God stayed awake all night, looking after them! Many other people joined them too, because they saw that God was good. Years later, Jesus was kind in a special way. The prophet said that Jesus would never break a bent reed, or put out a little flame. Imagine a candle nearly out: Jesus shields it with his hand and it shines again. When a friend is sad or a bit broken, you can be like Jesus. Be gentle, say something kind, and help the little flame to shine.

homily: Dear friends, picture the scene. Israel has just left Egypt. They are camped by the sea, and then the dust cloud appears behind them: Pharaoh's six hundred chariots. In front of them the water, behind them the army. They cry out to the Lord, and then they turn on Moses: was it because there were no graves in Egypt? How quickly fear makes us forget that slavery was slavery. Have we not also spoken that way when things get difficult, wishing that we were back in the old life, even the old sin?

Moses says three things: do not be afraid, stand firm, and see the deliverance that the Lord will accomplish for you today (Exodus 14:13). The Lord will fight for you, and you have only to keep still. But look what the Lord says next: why do you cry out to me? Tell the Israelites to go forward. There is a time for stillness, a time for prayer, and then a time to walk into the water. God does not do for us what we can do with his help. He made a way through the sea, but the people had to put their feet on it.

In the Gospel some people ask Jesus for a sign: show us something so that we can believe. Jesus has healed and taught, and still they ask for more. He answers that only one sign will be given, the sign of Jonah: as Jonah spent three days in the belly of the sea monster, so the Son of Man will spend three days in the heart of the earth. Jesus is saying: my death and my Resurrection are the sign. Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching; the queen of the South travelled the world to hear Solomon. And something greater than Jonah, something greater than Solomon, is here.

Let us not keep asking for more proof while the Lord himself stands among us. At every Mass he gives himself to us, risen and alive. Today let us name our sea, whatever frightens us, and say with Moses: the Lord will fight for me. And then let us take one step forward. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago God's people were running away from a cruel king. They came to a big sea, and the king's soldiers were behind them! The people were very scared. But Moses said: do not be afraid! God will help us. And God opened the sea, and the people walked right through on dry ground! When you are scared, remember: God can make a path where there is no path. Say a little prayer, and then do the brave thing.

homily: Dear friends, today's first reading is the night of the sea. The Lord drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night, and the waters were divided (Exodus 14:21). Look at what happens. The Israelites go into the sea on dry ground. The Egyptians follow and are thrown into panic: let us flee, for the Lord is fighting for them! At dawn the sea returns. It is a night of terror and a night of rescue.

And what is the result? Israel saw the great work that the Lord did. So the people feared the Lord and believed in the Lord and in his servant Moses (Exodus 14:31). Faith begins with a rescue. And then they sing. That is why the Church reads this story every year at the Easter Vigil: because in baptism each of us has been through that sea. We were brought out of slavery to sin, through the water, into the family of God.

In the Gospel Jesus says something that surprises us. His mother and his brothers are standing outside, and he says: who is my mother, and who are my brothers? Does he not love his family? Of course he does. But he opens the door wider: whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother. And who did the Father's will more perfectly than Mary? Let it be with me according to your word (Luke 1:38). Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it. Mary is not left outside; she is first among those inside.

So today let us ask: do I belong to this family? The test is not that I am baptised, nor that I come to church, but that I do the Father's will. Today the Church remembers St Apollinaris, an early bishop of Ravenna, a shepherd who gave his life for his flock. Let us ask him to pray for all our shepherds, and for each of us to be a brother and sister to someone who needs a family. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know what happened on the night of the sea? God sent a strong wind, and the water of the sea moved back, and God's people walked through on dry ground! Then the water came back and the king's army could not follow. God's people sang and danced for joy. In the Gospel Jesus says that everyone who does what God wants is in his family. Mary always did what God wanted, so she is the first in that family. And you can be in it too! Do one thing today that you know God wants: share, help, or say sorry.

homily: Dear friends, the people of Israel are hungry. They are in the wilderness, far from home, and they say: if only we had died in Egypt, when we sat by the fleshpots and had our fill of bread! Hunger makes us forget that we were slaves. Hunger makes the old chains look like comfort. Do we not do the same when life is hard? How quickly we begin to say: the old days were better.

And what does God do? He does not scold them. He says: I am going to rain bread from heaven for you, and each day the people shall go out and gather enough for that day (Exodus 16:4). In the morning there is something on the ground, fine as frost. They ask: what is it? Moses says: it is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat. They did not earn it. They did not even understand it. They received it. That is how God feeds us. And it is only for one day at a time. Give us this day our daily bread, Jesus teaches us to pray.

In the Gospel Jesus sits in a boat and tells of a sower who went out to sow. The seed falls on the path and the birds eat it. On rock, and it withers. Among thorns, and they choke it. And on good soil, and it bears a hundredfold. Jesus is telling us that the word of God is seed, and our hearts are the soil. The Sower is generous. He scatters the seed everywhere, even on the path where we are in a hurry, even on the rock where we are shallow, even among the thorns of our worries. What kind of soil am I today?

Today we remember St Lawrence of Brindisi, a Capuchin friar who gave his life to sowing the word. He learned many languages in order to preach to many people, he preached to soldiers and to kings, and he loved the Bible so much that he is called a Doctor of the Church. The Lord gives us bread from heaven in the word and in the Eucharist. Let us receive both with thanks and make them bear fruit in our lives. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago God's people were hungry in the desert. And every morning God sent a special bread called manna, enough for everybody for that day! In the Gospel Jesus tells about a farmer who planted seeds. Some seed fell on the path and birds ate it. Some fell on rocks. Some fell among thorns. But some fell on good soil and grew into lots of grain. The seed is God's word. Let us listen and be good soil. And do not forget to say thank you to God before you eat.

homily: Dear friends, today the Church keeps the feast of a woman who stood at the cross and went to the tomb: Mary of Magdala. We know a few things about her from the Gospels. Jesus drove seven demons out of her. She followed him with other women and helped to support him. She stood near the cross. And on Sunday morning, while it was still dark, she went to the tomb. We have to be careful not to add what the Gospels do not say. The Gospels do not name her as the sinful woman of Luke's seventh chapter, and the Church keeps them apart. What we know is already enough: a healed woman, a faithful disciple, and the first witness of the Resurrection.

John tells the story slowly. Mary sees the stone rolled away and runs to Peter and the other disciple. They run to the tomb, see the cloths and go home. But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb (John 20:11). Everyone else had gone home; she stays. Two angels ask: woman, why are you weeping? She says: they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him. Notice: my Lord. Then she turns and sees a man standing there; she thinks he is the gardener. Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away. She is ready to carry a dead body on her own shoulders. That is love.

And then one word changes everything: Mary! (John 20:16). He calls her by name. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name. And she turns, and says: Rabbouni! My Teacher! It was not a stranger's voice. It is the voice that called her out of darkness, and now it calls her out of grief. Do you hear your name when the Lord calls you? In prayer, in the Scriptures, in the Eucharist, in the cry of a poor person: he calls you by name.

Then Jesus says: do not hold on to me. She wants to keep him as before, and he says: that way is over, now I am going to the Father. But go to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. And Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples: I have seen the Lord (John 20:18). This is why the Church calls her the apostle of the apostles. The first to see the Lord alive was the first to tell. Peter and the Twelve would announce it to the world, but a woman announced it to them.

Brothers and sisters, how do we honour this feast? First, by staying: with those who weep, with those everybody has given up on. Second, by letting the Lord call us by name. Third, by not clinging to the past, and by going. Fourth, by saying out loud what Mary said: I have seen the Lord. In this rainy season, when the sky itself seems to weep, let us remember that no tear is unseen, because the Lord was already there, behind Mary, calling her by name. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know who was the very first person to see Jesus alive on Easter morning? A friend of Jesus named Mary Magdalene! She went to the tomb very early and cried because Jesus was not there. Then a man said: Mary! She knew his voice at once. It was Jesus, alive! He said: go and tell my friends. And she ran and said: I have seen the Lord!
Jesus knows your name too, and he loves you. Today, tell somebody the happiest news in the world: Jesus is alive! And you can say, like Mary: I have seen the Lord!

homily: Dear friends, the first reading gives us the Ten Commandments. We know them, but listen to how they begin: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery (Exodus 20:2). Before any command, God says what he has done. The law is not the chain of a master; it is the road for people who have just been set at liberty. God says: I have brought you out; now live as a people at liberty. No other gods; do not misuse my name; keep the sabbath; honor your father and mother; do not kill; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not lie; do not covet.

The psalm sings of these laws as something sweet: more to be desired than gold, sweeter than honey. Do we think of God's commandments in this way? Sometimes we treat them as a list of things we may not do. But a father who tells his child, do not touch the fire, does so out of love. The commandments are the Father's love in words. And Jesus told us that all of them hang on two: love of God with all your heart and love of your neighbour as yourself. If we love, we keep them.

In the Gospel Jesus explains the parable of the sower. The word of God is the seed, and our hearts are the soil. There is the soil of the path: the word is heard but not understood, and the evil one snatches it away. There is the rocky soil: we receive it with joy, but there are no roots, and when trouble comes we fall away. There is the soil full of thorns: the cares of the world and the lure of wealth choke it. And there is the good soil: the one who hears the word and understands it, and bears fruit. It is not enough to hear the commandments; they must be received into the heart, as the prophet says: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).

Today we remember St Bridget of Sweden. She was a wife and a mother of eight, she lived in a royal court, and she was not spared sorrow. And yet the word of God took root in her heart, and it bore fruit in prayer, in service of the poor, in a new religious order, and in a long pilgrimage to Rome and the Holy Land. She shows us that the good soil does not belong only to monks and nuns. Let us ask her to help us, in these rainy days when the land is soft, to make our hearts soft too, and let us give the word of God a fixed hour every day. Amen.
kids: Children, God gave his people ten rules, the Ten Commandments, because he loves us and wants us to be happy and unafraid. They tell us to love God, to respect our parents, not to lie, not to steal, and to be kind. Jesus told a story about a farmer and seeds. Some seeds fell on the road, some on rocks, some among thorns, and some on good soil. The seeds are God's words and the soil is our heart. Let us listen carefully, so that our hearts are good soil, and let us ask St Bridget to pray for us.

homily: Dear friends, the first reading is the sealing of the covenant at Sinai. Moses tells the people all the words of the Lord, and they answer with one voice: all the words that the Lord has spoken we will do (Exodus 24:3). Moses writes everything down. In the morning he builds an altar, with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes, and the sacrifice is offered. Then Moses reads the book of the covenant, and the people say again: we will do, and we will be obedient. How many times have we said at Mass, yes, Lord, we will do it? And how many times have we done it?

Then Moses does something dramatic. He takes the blood of the sacrifice, half on the altar, and half he sprinkles on the people: see the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you (Exodus 24:8). Blood is life. The same life touches the altar, which is God's, and the people. This is what Jesus does at the Last Supper: this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many (Mark 14:24). At every Mass, the same blood is given to us, not sprinkled on our skin but taken into our lives. The Eucharist makes the covenant new every day, and it asks us to do what we promise.

In the Gospel Jesus tells of an enemy who sowed weeds among the wheat. The workers want to pull them out at once. But the owner says: no, you will uproot the wheat with them. Let both of them grow together until the harvest. This is God's patience. In our families, our parishes and even in our own hearts, the wheat and the weeds grow together. We want to uproot the people who annoy us. God waits, because he wants everyone to be saved. And he gives us time too. Whom do I judge too quickly? And who has been patient with me?

Today we remember St Sharbel Makhluf, a monk of Lebanon, a hermit who lived in silence for twenty-three years in a little cell on a mountain. He did not judge the world; he prayed for it, hidden with his Father who is in secret. When he died, God showed that this quiet prayer was not lost: many people were healed at his tomb, Christians and non-Christians alike. Let us pray with Sharbel for Lebanon and for peace, and let us ask for the grace to be doers of the word, patient with each other and faithful in secret prayer. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus told a story about a farmer who planted good wheat. At night an enemy planted weeds. The workers wanted to pull them out right away, but the farmer said: wait, or you will pull up the wheat too! God is like that farmer. He is patient with us and gives us time to grow. Today we also remember St Sharbel, a monk who loved to pray alone in a little room on a mountain. He prayed for everybody, and God heard his prayer. Let us also set aside a few quiet minutes today to talk to God.

homily: Dear friends, the people of Israel have made a golden calf, and Moses has to come down the mountain with the tablets in his hands. He sees the dancing and breaks the tablets. And Aaron, the priest, says: I threw the gold in the fire, and out came this calf! (Exodus 32:24). How like us. We make a mess and then say it just happened.

But look at what Moses does next. He does not wash his hands of them. He goes back up the mountain and prays: forgive them, but if not, blot me out of the book that you have written (Exodus 32:32). That is a leader who stands in the breach. The Psalm says it: had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath (Psalm 106:23). Every one of us has someone who stood in the breach for us: a mother who prayed, a grandfather who fasted, a grandmother who held the rosary.

In the Gospel Jesus says that the kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, the smallest of all seeds, and like yeast hidden in flour. God works small and hidden. And today the Church remembers two hidden people. We do not find Joachim and Anne in the Gospels. Their names come from an old book. But we know something certain: Mary had parents, and they taught her to pray and to trust the promises of God. How else could a girl in Nazareth say: Here am I, the servant of the Lord? (Luke 1:38). Faith is always handed on, as St Paul tells Timothy: a faith that lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, lives in you (2 Timothy 1:5).

Yesterday we kept the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly, and today we honour the grandparents of Jesus. So let us ask: who planted the seed of faith in me? And whose seed am I planting? Let us thank God for them, pray for them, and, like Moses, stand in the breach for those who have strayed. Amen.
kids: Children, a mustard seed is tiny, but when it is planted it grows into a big tree where birds can make their nests. Jesus says God's kingdom is like that. Today we remember Mary's mother and father, Joachim and Anne. They loved little Mary and taught her to pray, and she grew up to be the Mother of Jesus. So Joachim and Anne were Jesus' grandparents! Thank God for your own grandparents today, and ask them to tell you a story about when they were small.

homily: Dear friends, after the sin of the golden calf, Moses does a beautiful thing. He pitches a tent outside the camp, far from the noise, and calls it the tent of meeting. And anyone who wants to seek the Lord can go there. When Moses goes in, the cloud comes down, and the people stand at the doors of their tents and bow. And the Bible says: the Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend (Exodus 33:11).

Do we speak to God like that? We say many prayers, but do we ever just talk? Moses returns to the camp, but Joshua, the young man, would not leave the tent. Some people cannot leave the place where God speaks. Do we have a quiet place, a corner of the house, a church, a chapel, where we can sit with the Lord, who now waits for us in the tabernacle?

And what does God say about himself when he passes before Moses? The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exodus 34:6). Notice: slow to anger. Moses bows to the ground, and he prays: although this is a stiff-necked people, pardon our iniquity and our sin. He knows he is asking for a lot, but he knows to whom he is asking.

The Gospel shows the same patience. The farmer sowed good seed, and an enemy sowed weeds. The servants want to tear them out at once. But the master says: no, you would uproot the wheat along with them. Let both grow until the harvest. Brothers and sisters, God is waiting for the weeds in us to turn. We are not the judges. We are the ones who have been given time. Let us use it: weed our own hearts, confess our sins, forgive those who wrong us, and be patient with others. And at the harvest, the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Amen.
kids: Children, Moses had a special tent where he went to talk to God. God spoke to him like a friend. We can talk to God like a friend too, at home, in church and on the way to school. And Jesus told a story about a farmer who found weeds growing among the wheat. He did not pull them up at once, because he might hurt the good plants. God is patient with us too. Let us thank him today, and let us be patient with our brothers and sisters!

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, there is something very beautiful about a face that has been in the presence of God. Moses comes down the mountain, and his face is shining. And the Bible says: Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God (Exodus 34:29). The people could see it, but he could not. Holiness is like that. It does not know itself.

Today the Church in India remembers a woman whose face shone like that. Annakutty was born in 1910 in a village near Kottayam. Her mother died when she was small. She grew up wanting to belong to Jesus, and in 1927 she entered the convent of the Clarist sisters at Bharananganam. She took the name Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception. She was never strong. She was often ill, and she could do little of what the world calls important. She died at thirty-five. And the people of Kerala came to her tomb, and the Church has called her a saint.

What was her secret? The Gospel today gives us the answer: the treasure and the pearl. A man finds a treasure in a field, and in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field (Matthew 13:44). In his joy: that is the key. Alphonsa did not give up everything out of sadness. She had found Jesus, and he was worth more than anything else. St Paul says the same: I regard everything as loss because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Philippians 3:8).

And she gave her suffering a meaning. She offered her pain, in union with the Cross of Christ, for others. The Lord himself says: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). Alphonsa's life was like a grain in the earth, hidden, small, and falling. And look at the harvest: pilgrims at her tomb, sick people finding peace, young women hearing the call, a whole Church in India rejoicing, and the Pope in Rome calling her a saint in 2008.

What about us? Perhaps we feel that our lives are small and hidden, with nothing great to show. But this is exactly where holiness grows. Let us offer our small pains and ordinary duties with love. Let us look for the pearl. And let us be gentle, because, like Moses, we may be carrying a light we do not see. St Alphonsa, pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, today we remember St Alphonsa, who lived in Kerala. Her name when she was little was Annakutty. She loved Jesus very much, and she became a sister. She was often ill, but she was never cross; she offered her pain to Jesus for other people. When she died, people started praying at her grave, and the Pope said she is a saint. She is the first woman from India to be made a saint! Jesus said that heaven is like a treasure in a field. Alphonsa found the treasure. Who is the treasure? Jesus! Let us try to be kind today, even if we are tired, and offer it to him.

homily: Dear friends, the first reading ends with a great scene: the tent is finished, and the glory of the Lord fills it, so that even Moses cannot go in. God has come to live among his people. And the Psalm sings what every heart wants: How lovely is your dwelling place, O Lord of hosts (Psalm 84:1). Where is God's dwelling place today? In church, yes. But also in a home like the one in Bethany, where Jesus was welcomed.

Today the Church remembers three friends of Jesus: Martha, Mary and Lazarus. We know them as a household. In Luke, Martha welcomed him into her home, and was busy with serving, while Mary sat at his feet to listen. Jesus said: Martha, Martha, you are worried and distracted by many things; there is need of only one thing. Mary has chosen the better part (Luke 10:41–42). He was not scolding the service; he was warning against the worry. We can serve him in a hundred ways, but he also wants us to sit.

In John's Gospel Martha is the one who goes out to meet Jesus when Lazarus has died. She says what we all say: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died (John 11:21). It is an honest prayer, with a little reproach in it. And Jesus does not rebuke her. He lifts her faith: I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live. Do you believe this? And she answers with one of the greatest confessions in the Gospels: Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world (John 11:27).

What a woman! She serves, she argues, she believes. And her brother Lazarus, who never speaks a word in the Gospels, is called out of the tomb. Dear friends, in our homes there are Marthas, Marys and Lazaruses: those who serve, those who pray, and those who say little but are living signs of what Jesus can do. Let us welcome Jesus in. Let us serve with love, listen with attention, and believe in the one who is the resurrection and the life. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus had friends in a village called Bethany: Martha, Mary and their brother Lazarus. When Jesus visited, Martha cooked and cleaned. Mary sat down next to Jesus and listened to him. Jesus said that listening is very special. And when Lazarus died, Jesus cried, because he loved him. Then he called: Lazarus, come out! And Lazarus came alive again! Jesus is stronger than death. Today let us help at home, and let us also sit quietly and listen to Jesus.

homily: Dear friends, Leviticus gives Israel a calendar of meetings with God: the Passover, the first fruits, the fifty days, the Day of Atonement, the Feast of Booths. These are the appointed festivals of the Lord (Leviticus 23:4). Time itself becomes holy. The Church too has a calendar: Sunday, Easter, Pentecost, the feasts of the saints. Why? Because we forget. We need fixed hours and seasons to remind us that God is near.

And God is faithful to those hours. At Passover the Lord rescued his people. The sheaf of first fruits is raised before him on the day after the sabbath, and we know what rose on that day: Christ, the first fruits of those who have died (1 Corinthians 15:20). Fifty days later came Pentecost. The festivals of Israel are God's gifts to the Jewish people, who keep them to this day, and in them we Christians see a pattern fulfilled in Christ. The Psalm says: Sing aloud to God our strength. Joy is the proper response.

But now look at the Gospel. Jesus goes to his hometown, and in the synagogue he teaches. People are astonished. Where did this man get this wisdom? Then comes the great but: is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? They took offense at him (Matthew 13:57). They knew all about him, and they did not know him. And Matthew says: he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.

How easily this happens to us. We have heard the Gospel a hundred times. We know the Mass by heart. We have seen the crucifix on the wall since we were children. And so we can sit in church and see nothing. Prophets are not without honor except in their own country and in their own house. Let us pray today for fresh eyes. St Peter Chrysologus, the golden-worded bishop, used to preach short sermons about the oldest passages of the Gospel and people would listen as if they had never heard them before. May the Lord give us that same freshness at the next Mass, when he will be in front of us again, on the altar, risen, the first fruits of our harvest. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago God told the people of Israel to have special feast days, when they would stop work and sing and thank him. We have feast days too, like Sundays and Christmas and Easter. In the Gospel Jesus went back to the village where he grew up, and the people said: he is only the carpenter's son! They did not see how special he was, so Jesus did not do many miracles there. Do not forget how special your family and friends are. And remember how special Jesus is every Sunday at Mass!

homily: Dear friends, God gives Israel a wonderful law in the book of Leviticus: the Jubilee. Every fiftieth year the trumpet is sounded across the land, and everyone is to return to their property and to their family (Leviticus 25:10). Debts are cancelled, slaves are released, the land rests. It is a year of liberty. Jesus would read from Isaiah in Nazareth about this very year: to proclaim release to the captives, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor (Luke 4:18–19). And the Church keeps Jubilee Holy Years to remind us that God's mercy is always opening doors.

The Gospel shows the opposite. Herod is a king, and he has no liberty. He is afraid of the crowd. He is afraid of his guests. He is afraid of his oath, and so he orders the death of a righteous man. And in prison there is John, who has nothing but the truth, and he is the one at liberty. It is not lawful for you to have her (Matthew 14:4). John did not fear to say what was right, and he paid for it with his life. This is the freedom of the Jubilee: not to be spared the consequences, but to be released from fear.

At the end of the passage there is a small detail: his disciples took the body and buried it; then they went and told Jesus (Matthew 14:12). They bring their grief to Jesus. That is where every sorrow should go.

Today we remember a man who found this freedom: St Ignatius of Loyola. A proud soldier, he was wounded at Pamplona. In bed, with nothing to read but the lives of Christ and the saints, he found that thoughts of serving God left him with a deep peace. His whole life was changed. He wrote the Spiritual Exercises, and gathered friends like Francis Xavier, who came to India, to Goa, to the fishermen of our coasts. His motto was for the greater glory of God. St Paul says it: whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). Dear friends, let us ask for the Jubilee freedom of Ignatius and John: released from fear, ready to give ourselves wholly, for the greater glory of God. Amen.
kids: Children, Ignatius was a soldier who wanted to be famous. But a cannonball hurt his leg and he had to stay in bed for a long time. He read books about Jesus and the saints, and he decided to give his life to God instead. He started a group of friends who wanted to do everything for God's glory. They were called Jesuits, and one of them, Francis Xavier, travelled all the way to India. Ignatius used to say: for the greater glory of God. Today let us do something very small, like tidying our room, and say: for the glory of God!

intro: Theme: “My Lord and my God!”
The apostle who asked honest questions, the wounds of the risen Lord, and the faith that came to India.

sub: A family, a city, a house.
q: The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone.

So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.
points.apply: Learn the names of the twelve apostles and pray for the bishops, their successors, in your own diocese.

sub: I am the way, and the truth, and the life.
q: Praise the Lord, all you nations! Extol him, all you peoples!
Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”
points.apply: Where Christ asks something of you that frightens you, say this week, “Let us go,” and go.

sub: The wounds of the risen Lord.
q: so that, when they look on the one whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child,
Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.”
points.apply: Bring one honest question about faith to a priest or a catechist this week.

sub: Blessed are those who have not seen.
q: I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
points.apply: At the elevation at Mass, say the words of Thomas, and pray for a vocation to the priesthood or religious life from your parish.

concl: The Church is built on the apostles with Christ as the cornerstone; Thomas, loyal friend and honest questioner, is one of her foundation stones.
The risen Lord answers Thomas's doubt with his wounds and receives the confession, My Lord and my God, and blesses all who believe without seeing.
2027-07-03.resolve: Say Thomas's prayer, My Lord and my God, every day this week, and give thanks for the faith of India.

intro: Theme: “My grace is sufficient for you.”
A prophet sent to people who may not listen, an apostle whose thorn is not removed, and the carpenter's son whom his own town could not recognise.

sub: The son of man on his feet by the Spirit.
Faithful, whether they hear or not.
q: Whether they hear or refuse to hear (for they are a rebellious house), they shall know that there has been a prophet among them.
And he said, “Truly I tell you, no prophet is accepted in the prophet’s hometown.
points.apply: Say one true and kind word this week about your faith to someone at home or at work, and leave the result to God.

sub: When I am weak, then I am strong.
q: so our eyes look to the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us.
but he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.”
points.apply: Offer your own thorn to God every morning this week in one sentence: My grace is sufficient for me.

q: For he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, nothing in his appearance that we should desire him.
Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon, and are not his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him.
points.apply: Offer your ordinary work to the carpenter of Nazareth, and do it as well as you can.

sub: He could do no deed of power.
He goes on to other villages.
q: Have mercy upon us, O Lord, have mercy upon us, for we have had more than enough of contempt.
And he could do no deed of power there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and cured them. And he was amazed at their unbelief.
points.apply: At Communion this week, say: Lord, I believe; help my unbelief, and open my heart.

concl: God sends Ezekiel to a rebellious people and calls him to be faithful, not successful; he answers Paul's thorn with grace, because power is made perfect in weakness.
Jesus is rejected by his own town because he is too familiar, and yet he goes on teaching; faith opens the door to his power.
2027-07-04.resolve: Thank one person at home whom you take for granted, and offer your thorn to God each day.

intro: Theme: “Go, prophesy to my people.”
A shepherd is taken from his flock, all of us are chosen before the foundation of the world, and the Twelve are sent two by two with a staff and sandals.

points.h: The Lord took me from following the flock
sub: The king's sanctuary and the word of God.
A call that does not wait for credentials.
q: and the Lord took me from following the flock, and the Lord said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’
While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”
points.apply: Ask the Lord this week what he is calling you to do, and take one concrete step.

sub: Before the foundation of the world.
A plan to gather up all things.
q: Let me hear what God the Lord will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, to his faithful, to those who turn to him in their hearts.

just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love. He destined us for adoption as his children through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will,
points.apply: Write down ten blessings you have received in Christ, and read them at supper with your family.

sub: The Gospel is a shared life.
q: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up the other;
He called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits.
points.apply: Ask someone to join you in one act of service this week: a visit, a prayer, a gift.

q: This is how you shall eat it: your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it hurriedly. It is the passover of the Lord.
So they went out and proclaimed that all should repent. They cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them.
points.apply: Set aside one thing that weighs you down this week, and use the time for God or for a neighbour.

concl: God calls whom he wishes, a shepherd, a fisherman, a tax collector, and chose each of us in Christ before the foundation of the world.
The Twelve are sent two by two with almost nothing, to proclaim repentance and heal; the Church continues that mission.
2027-07-11.resolve: Do one thing this week that the Lord is asking of you, and do it with someone else.

intro: Theme: “Come to me … and I will give you rest.”
The God who says “I am,” the God who has seen, and the gentle and humble Lord whose yoke is easy.

sub: A name that opens a relationship.
The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
The Name that is not pronounced.
q: God said to Moses, “I am who I am.” He said further, “Thus you shall say to the Israelites, ‘I am has sent me to you.’”
Jesus said to them, “Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.”
points.apply: Make the Sign of the Cross slowly and reverently three times today, as a prayer to the God who is.

points.h: I have seen, and I will stretch out my hand
sub: A truthful road: a mighty hand.
q: I have given heed to you and to what has been done to you in Egypt.
And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”
points.apply: Whenever you feel unseen this week, say: Lord, you have seen; and ask him for one step.

q: Put your neck under her yoke, and let your souls receive instruction; it is to be found close by.

“Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
points.apply: Tonight, tell Jesus the one burden that is heaviest, and ask him to carry it with you.

sub: The mind enlightened, the heart on fire.
q: O taste and see that the Lord is good; happy are those who take refuge in him.
and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
points.apply: Read a few verses of the Gospel slowly each day this week, and end each reading with a prayer of love.

concl: God gives Moses his Name and joins it to the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; he has seen the suffering and will stretch out his hand.
Jesus invites all who are weary to come to him and take his easy yoke; St Bonaventure shows how study can end in love.
2027-07-15.resolve: Each night this week, give Jesus one burden to carry, and make the Sign of the Cross with reverence each morning.

intro: Theme: “He had compassion for them.”

The Lord who gathers the scattered flock, the Shepherd who walks with us in the dark valley, the peace that breaks down walls, and the compassion of Jesus who rests his tired friends and then teaches the crowd.

q: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says the Lord.
to tend the flock of God that is in your charge, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion but willingly, as God would have you do it.
points.apply: Pray by name each day this week for your parish priest and bishop, and ask yourself whom you have been entrusted with at home or at work.

sub: The darkest valley, and you are with me.
A table prepared; my cup overflows.
q: The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures; he leads me beside still waters; he restores my soul.
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
points.apply: Pray Psalm 23 slowly each evening this week, and add to it one name of a person for whom you want the Shepherd's care.

q: Peace, peace, to the far and the near, says the Lord; and I will heal them.
For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
points.apply: Do one thing this week to cross a wall: greet someone from another community, call a relative with whom you are on bad terms, or share a meal.

points.h: Come away and rest a while
sub: The Lord who cares for our bodies.
q: It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives sleep to his beloved.
He said to them, “Come away to a deserted place all by yourselves and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat.
points.apply: Choose one hour this week for real rest with the Lord, with no phone, and receive it as a gift.

sub: First he teaches, then he feeds.
q: I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will make them lie down, says the Lord God. I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed, and I will bind up the injured, and I will strengthen the weak.
As he went ashore, he saw a great crowd; and he had compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.
points.apply: Notice one person this week who seems lost or tired, and give them time, attention and a kind word.

concl: God promises to gather his scattered flock and raise up good shepherds; in Jesus he comes as the Good Shepherd and is our peace.
Jesus rests his tired friends and then, moved with compassion, teaches the crowd: the heart of the Shepherd is the model of ours.
2027-07-18.resolve: Pray daily for your shepherds, take one hour of rest with the Lord, and cross one wall this week.

intro: Theme: “Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.”
Elisha's loaves, a boy's lunch and the Bread of Life: God takes our little, gives thanks, and makes us one.

points.h: They shall eat and have some left
sub: A famine, and first fruits brought to the prophet.
How can I set this before a hundred people?
The word of the Lord is enough.
q: He set it before them, they ate, and had some left, according to the word of the Lord.
When they were satisfied, he told his disciples, “Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.”
points.apply: Bring one worry about money, food or the future to the Mass today, and place it with the gifts on the altar.

points.h: What are they among so many?
sub: Five barley loaves and two fish.
q: Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and you that have no money, come, buy and eat!
There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are they among so many people?
points.apply: Choose one small act of service you can offer every day this week, and do not wait until it feels big enough.

q: he rained down on them manna to eat, and gave them the grain of heaven. Mortals ate of the bread of angels; he sent them food in abundance.
There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to the one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in all.
points.apply: Before Communion today, make peace in your heart with anyone you are at odds with, and offer them a word of kindness this week.

concl: The Lord feeds his people from our small offerings: twenty loaves for a hundred, five loaves for five thousand.
Every Mass repeats his actions of taking, giving thanks and giving, and makes us one body in the bond of peace.
2027-07-25.resolve: This week give one gift to someone in need, and visit one grandparent or elderly person.

intro: Theme: “God himself will provide the lamb.”
The test on Moriah, the Lamb whom God gives, and the friends whose faith carries the paralysed man to the One who forgives.

sub: Your son, your only son, whom you love.
Three days of walking in faith.
God is able to raise the dead.
q: Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on his son Isaac, and he himself carried the fire and the knife. So the two of them walked on together.
By faith Abraham, when put to the test, offered up Isaac.
points.apply: Name one thing God asks of you that you do not understand, and say to him this week, “Here I am.”

q: Abraham said, “God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” So the two of them walked on together.
The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him and declared, “Here is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!
